Dad, can you tell me more about this book? I noticed you've been reading a lot of books about the English language lately. What’s particularly interesting about it, though? Ah, this one right here? It's a book about how the English language has evolved. It’s quite fascinating how words and spellings change over time. Did you know, for example, that some words, like 'colonel', are pronounced differently from how they're spelt? It's because of their etymology—originally from French and Italian. Oh, that’s really interesting! I never even thought about that. And what about words like 'centre' and 'theatre'? Why do Americans spell them differently? Yeah, that's another interesting bit about the English language. It's called the Great Vowel Shift, which occurred between the 15th and 17th centuries. It changed how we pronounce certain vowels, but our spellings didn't always change along with them. And fun fact: sometimes, the variations in spellings can be due to politics and the influence of certain groups within England during the time those spellings became standard. Fascinating! So, there’s always a story behind a word in English, isn’t there? Exactly! That's what I love about learning about language. Just like how English has borrowed words from so many different languages over the years— French, Latin, Greek, even some from other British languages, like Celtic or Norse words in the north. That must be why, sometimes, the same word can have different meanings in different parts of the country. Like, 'gutted', which can mean disappointed in London but means something totally different in the North. Right. Like 'chuffed' or 'mardy'. The influence of local dialects is huge. Funny how a country as small as England can have so much regional variation in language. Did you know that some counties in England have different spellings just for fun or tradition? I remember learning about those when we passed by Manchester and seeing signs with certain local spellings for names of places. Right. Some regions prefer certain spellings that reflect historical ties or local pride. It's all a part of the rich tapestry that is the English language. So, Dad, if I wanted to study English at university, what kind of courses would I look into? I know it’s mostly about syntax and literature, but are there other areas like linguistics and all these changes over time?

Right, so I'm going to make homemade Yorkshire puddings. Dad uses to make them when I was a kid and they're always a hit. I've got all the ingredients; chicken, gravy, roast vegetables. Want to help with anything? Yeah, sure, I can help with the vegetables. What kind of vegetables are you planning on using? I've got a bunch of fresh carrots, broccoli, and some potatoes from Aldi, right here. Oh, Sam, that sounds great! I always love how homemade Yorkshire puddings make everything else better. Ellie, I think it's a good idea to use a rich chicken gravy with those. My mum used to make it with a mixture of beef and chicken stock. That's what I was thinking too, actually. And for roast potatoes, shall we peel and chop them now or leave them until later? I think we should prep them now, so they can get a good roast in the oven. But let me just check the oven first, it's been acting weird lately. Sure, everything seems fine here. Now, back to the veg. Where is the peeler and knife, while I'm at it? Knife and peeler are on the counter, next to the sink. Speaker_2 : Can you get the carrots ready too? Slice them into sticks and we'll toss them with a bit of oil and herbs. On it. Actually, Ellie, did you know your dad used to make these during football match days? He'd always say, "A proper Sunday roast just won't feel right without a decent Yorkshire pudding." Yeah, I think that's why they're always in demand whenever I make them! But I actually grew up in Doncaster, so our Yorkshire puddings were a staple on Sunday dinner day too – more so than some other places. That's cool. I always take advantage of Sunday roasts at my mum's if I can get them! It's nice when the whole family comes together. It really is. There's something special about everyone sitting down to the same meal and sharing stories, you know? Even if now it's just us friends making dinner. For sure. I miss that now that I moved for uni and live here in Cambridge. Sundays were always that time... Speaking of moving out, Ellie, how are things at home? I know you’ve mentioned sometimes that it can be tough balancing work and uni from Doncaster, right?

Yo, mate, been a while. How's life been treating ya? Still teaching those languages abroad? Hey! Yeah, it's good to catch up. Still doing the teaching abroad. Mostly in France now, actually. The lifestyle isn't bad but sometimes I miss the UK. How about you? Still bar tending? Yeah, still doing my thing down here at the leisure centre. You know, it's not the most glamorous of jobs, but it pays the bills and there's always someone new to meet. But even so, it's been a bit stale since most people around here are just here to relax, you know? True, it can be a bit repetitive but I guess that's just the case with any job that involves serving people. Agree on that. Though I've started to get into making cocktails. It's a bit of a challenge and actually quite rewarding when a drink I make gets appreciated. That's nice. I used to work freelance as a bartender while studying. It was a good side hustle, but I didn't stick with it. What was your favorite course during uni? Literature. I loved delving into the different texts and the analysis. There's something about figuring out what the author means beyond the surface. Literature is so interesting. I took a couple of elective modules in English lit during my MA. It's amazing how varied studies can be even within one field. Definitely. And in your case, teaching - each student is a new puzzle. Exactly! Plus, I get to learn a bit myself each time. Speaking of puzzles, how's your French coming along? I've been meaning to pick it up but can't seem to find the time or the drive. Oh, I've always been fascinated by languages. French is quite a challenge, but it's rewarding. The grammar can be a bit overwhelming but once you grasp it, it's systematic. Have you tried language learning apps? Yeah, I've thought about it. But sometimes I find them a bit dry. Maybe you could give me some advice? What works best for you when learning a new language? For me, it's immersion. Spend time with native speakers, watch foreign films without subtitles. And consistency is key. Even just 15 minutes a day can make a difference. That makes sense. Film without subtitles is a good idea.

Alright mates, don't you think's it's a bit late to be chit-chatting? We've got a break time to catch up on. You're quite right, isn't it? But, the morning’s been awfully quiet, what questions have we got left to answer? Well, I did want to catch up on where we've got with the Gambia trip plan. How's that coming along? Ah, keeps coming backwards and forwards, doesn't it? We were discussing it before we had that long ramble about Driving in the rain. I know, right? Seems like we've got a million and one things to consider. But as much as we're all retirement age, I feel like we could do with a nice, relaxing holiday somewhere warm and sunny. Gambia seemed like the ideal place, but with your worries about the money... Money's a little concern, innit? But we're not rolling in it. Though between us, we might just scrape enough or even reach out to some local charity who might chip in a bit. That’s true! We could even try to make a donation box and see if the community pitches in. You know, good old English community spirit can be quite powerful. That's a bloody good idea! But while we're on the subject of money, did one of you still want to set up a small business or something? You know, something quiet, not too taxing. That's been a thought, doesn’t it? But after years of not working and the lads, we're not sure we’re up to it. Plus, what if it’s a drag? More like worry about being decently settled in, isn't it? Suppose we'd rather just keep our routine as it is. I know what you mean but we shouldnt dismiss the idea completely. It's not about getting rich, it’s about having a purpose, something to do, somewhere worthwhile to be. True, but truly so much to consider. What about zero hours contracts or small gigs? Ah, I’d almost rather collect folklore or plant in the garden. We could set up a small greenhouse. I heard Munchausen came from a wealthy family who owned lots of property. If we ain't thinking about business, perhaps we just focus on that? Love the idea of you clipping plants and me making the don’t work at all bit.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that mobile app I discovered today? Its like an all-in-one for all my favorite food spots around Peterborough. I can order meals, book tables, even find new places to try out. Really, which one is it? I've been on the hunt for something similar for ages. Let’s get into the specifics, shall we? What features has this app got? Erm, well, it’s really intuitive. You can filter by food type, by how much time you have, even by your closest friends' recommendations. It even creates a map of the best spots near you. That sounds amazing! I had no idea such an app existed. Yeah, and the best part is, it links directly to the restaurant’s orders so you can usually skip the cues and have deliveries made directly to your door. That’s a game-changer during the lockdowns when we were all stuck at home. You couldn’t even get a table, or sometimes the delivery queues were too long. For sure! We could have used that last year when everything was closed but still wanted to support local businesses. Exactly! And while we're on the subject of food, let’s order something for our dinner tonight. I saw there’s this new Japanese place that just opened up and they’re offering a discount for first-time customers. Hey, why don’t you in charge of ordering? Oh, I see how it is. You just want someone else to do the work…Fine, fine! I’ll see what the menu has. There’s a whole section for sushi and ramen. Can we also get some suggestions for ramen? I tried this one place recently and it was so hit or miss. Yeah, ramen can be really hit-or-miss if you haven’t tried it in the right place. Right, so I think we should try this spot, and maybe order a few different options to see what we like. Let’s say, two types of ramen, some sushi, and maybe some edamame to share? Sounds like a plan. And I’ll throw in a few appetizers too. As long as we don’t end up with a ramen war. Oh, funny thinking back, remember that one time we went to that new Thai place and the food was so spicy, we were all nearly...

Ah, mates, thanks for dropping by. It's been ages. You know how it is, getting old and less mobile. I've been finding it tough even getting the tea trolley down from the loft. That old tea trolley! You've always been stubborn about keeping it just so. You do know it's easier to just order a new one, don't you? Now, don't start, Eliza. That old thing has history. It was passed down from my grandad, and it still works. Well, most of the time, anyway. I’m glad you're getting your strength back, just like the car. How's the old motor been treating you? Was it the big trip to York or York making the car suffer? Ah, you remember that? It was a doozy of a journey. The Ronny, she's an old girl, but she's reliable. We've been good friends over the years. Still gets me where I need to go, even though the rarer tires squeak a bit now. The Ronny? That’s her name? I never knew! The paint job still looks great, though. You've taken good care of her. She's a Triumph Herald, 1965 model. Can't just call her 'the car', no, no. There's character in a name, you see. That's the spirit. Me and my dad used to have a Morris Minor. Same kind of character. But I do miss the freedom of the open road. Nowadays, I'm stuck with these buses and the occasional taxi. I know what you mean, really. I used to drive whenever I liked, wherever I liked. Nowadays, I'm just happy to get out and about and see you all. You both are right. It's not just about the car, is it? It’s about the freedom to go where you want, when you want. Us old folk, we miss that. Speaking of which, I had to get the bus today. And they almost didn’t stop for me at the corner of High Street and Church Lane! Said I didn’t signal early enough. Those drivers! I’ve told you, just wave like mad and they’ll see you. You're right, though, sometimes it feels like... We're not as spry as we used to be. Me, at least, if I raise my arm from the crook of my elbow, it's mostly to gesture, not hail a bus.

Ah, I hear you’re planning on moving to Manchester soon, isn’t that right? Yeah, that’s right. We've been talking about this for a while, and we've finally decided. It's been quite a process to decide on the location, the house, and everything else – but we’re really excited. Manchester’s a lovely city, I’ve visited quite a few times. It has a brilliant cultural scene and there’s always something to do, don’t you think? But moving can be a bit of a hassle, can’t it? How’s it all going? Oh, yes. It is. It’s a bit chaotic deciding where to move, finding the right area that fits our lifestyle. Yes, and then there's the matter of sorting out the logistics of relocation. I can imagine. When my husband and I moved to Ireland from England, it was a whole different story, but I recall being worried about finding the right school for the kids and how it would affect our daily routine. That’s true. It’s never easy, is it? And you know, I’ve been thinking recently... maybe we should look into this new tech for our cars. I've been reading up on electric vehicles. Thinking of making the change. How do you all feel about them? I’m a bit hesitant to jump into the electric car bandwagon yet. I mean, the technology is certainly improving, but battery life and charging points... I always worry about being stuck without a charge for a while in rural areas. Oh, absolutely. I couldn’t agree more. But it’s progress, isn’t it? Though, personally, I'm more concerned about the health impacts the move might have. The stress of it all can be quite taxing, and if one’s planning to make the trip by car... Yeah, that’s a good point. I recently read an article on how stressful moving can be on one’s health. But on the other hand, if you’re moving to a more healthy environment, it could work wonders. Perhaps changing the car to something more eco-friendly is a step in that direction too. True. I hadn’t looked at it like that before. Either way, it’s all part of the process of bettering one’s life, right? And maybe, as you said, leading a healthier and more sustainable life.

Mum, I can't believe you were able to recover my bike's passport. I thought it was gone forever! Oh, it was quite the mission, but well worth it, wasn't it? I really understood how much you loved that bike. Yeah, it was so handy for getting to and from school and around town. That's right, it was. I've also made sure it's got a brand new lock now, and we can get it registered with the police too, keeps it safer. You know, this whole thing reminded me of my social media. I posted about my bike being stolen and some of my friends from school actually saw it and they helped me track it down. That's amazing, isn’t it? Social media can be quite powerful. Though be careful what you post online, you never want to share too much information. I didn't share any personal details, just my school and the bike details. Did people from college reply as well? One or two did reach out, but it was more the general public and this group I'm part of that helps people find their stolen items that got involved. What group is that? It's a Facebook group here in Hastings, people list stolen items and others help look for them. It's been really helpful to the community, especially for bikes as they seem to get stolen quite often. That's really cool, actually. It’s a good lesson in social media responsibility and community spirit! Definitely. But it proves that social media can be used positively as well. I guess so. I just hate that things like this happen. Seems like the world's getting a bit more rough these days, isn't it? Listen, it's definitely not perfect, but it's also not all bad. We have great police and communities that really care. While you were dealing with the bike, did you manage to sit for your mid-years or was it too stressful? I did manage to focus for the exams, and I just got my results, actually. I'm pretty happy with how I did. It'll give me a good foundation for college. That's fantastic! You worked really hard and it shows. So, college plans... are they getting firmer? I've been looking at a few different options. There's a fine art course I really like, but I'm also considering something in environmental science.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was on a train from Cardiff to London and I overheard this conversation between two young boys about the dynamics of chicken and gravy? They were quite serious about it. It was just hilarious! Oh, isn’t that one for the books! I suppose they were probably part of a family headed to the big city, maybe to visit some attraction or the other. Speaking of keepsakes, I still have a photo of my daughter at 5 years old, looking like she’s about to conquer the world with a tractor she got from the farmyard we used to visit. She's 15 now, and it's bittersweet. That’s lovely! I have a picture of my little niece going on a tour of a chocolate factory when she was about the same age. It was a mess, but hilarious. She was covered in chocolate! I recall this one time when I was volunteering in a train station café. We had a gang of primary school kids on this train, on their way to a field trip. They were all different levels of "enthusiastic" about the day ahead, while the teachers were trying to keep order in a way only a teacher can. Teachers have an incredible patience, don’t they? But back to trains – I once had to explain the concept of a "peak hour" to a small class of kids. They were quite puzzled why we’re "peak" all at the same time and "off-peak" when we’re not. Exactly! The concept of peak hours to a child is quite amusing. I had to draw the London Underground map and explain the whole logistics of it. It was like explaining the meaning of life to them. Right! Speaking of train dynamics, have you ever considered what would happen if you took a very old train and changing the tracks to something more modern? You'd have to modify everything, wouldn’t you? Funny you bring that up. I once read a paper about such an endeavor in one of the historically rich train networks in Britain. It's fascinating how they integrate older infrastructure with new technology. It’s like almost re-inventing the wheel, but worth it I suppose. That’s really interesting! They essentially have to balance preservation with efficiency. It’s a challenge, but I imagine it keeps engineers very busy and content.

I've decided I need a routine or I'll continue to spend my days lounging around and watching too much Netflix. Have you ever had days like that? Oh, all the time! But I love it now and then. It's a kind of weekend ritual, isn't it? Going over the whole day and then just chilling. But I suppose a "normal" routine is healthy. What kind of routine are you thinking of? I was considering starting a bit of a morning routine, keeps me grounded. Maybe a bit of yoga, some reading, and before we know, it's lunchtime. That sounds great! I used to have a pretty strict early morning routine when we were students, even then. I had to get up early for lectures but now I feel like I've lost a bit of that morning discipline. Hence the Netflix binges! I know right? It's a bit concerning. But, you know, it's also good to have balance. I think this board game is actually part of my new routine, at least for evenings. A bit of low-key competition and friendship bonding. Absolutely. We should play more often. The last time we played Scrabble, you almost beat me. Stings a bit but I'm ready to try again. What game are we playing tonight? Tonight we're playing 'Settlers of Catan'. There's strategy, luck, and a bit of social chaos which is perfect for stimulating conversation, don't you think? I like it. But it's not just about the game, is it? The after-game chatter, the wine, all that combined makes it a great evening. Definitely a ritual we've built over the years. I noticed we've talked a lot about gaming and drinks in various cultures. Do you think we are typical of British gaming and drinking culture, or we're quite unique? That's interesting. I think we’re a bit of a blend, really. British culture famously embraces pub culture, for sure. But gaming, especially board games, has become more mainstream thanks to events like the UK Games Expo and social media. Exactly! Plus, the COVID lockdowns boosted almost all of that, right? Games like Catan or even Among Us became really popular. But I think what makes us unique is that we're not just playing for the game itself. It’s the company, the competition, the talking... it’s a whole experience.

I've decided I need to redecorate my whole house after today's insulation work. Deciding on paint colours and furniture feels so overwhelming! Are you still deciding on the ideal colour for your walls? I thought the old, beige was kind of bland. Oh don’t worry, it’s easier once you start. I’ve moved into three houses and it’s always the best part – you can actually start seeing the house come together! Right? And it’s weird how changing the colour on a whole room can suddenly make it feel like a completely different space, isn’t it? Totally, I’ve been meaning to move some furniture in our flat. Might just cosy up the lounge. You might want to get some professional help - oh we could do with that organization. Hence why I'm planning a whole day dedicated just to the project. That sounds like a plan. And you’re going to tackle this on your own, or would you like us to help? Now that’s so kind of you both. It would certainly make it more fun, but also less bewildering with multiple opinions. Where should I even start? Usually, the best place is with the colors and then let that guide your choices on furniture and such. Have you got any preferred colors or themes in mind? A neutral base with pops of color here and there. I love blue, but I’m worried it could feel too cold. You could balance it with warm terracotta shades and textures in the furniture and rugs. Makes the room cozy yet vibrant. And you could use the design wheel or apps/sites online for help choosing. They can suggest color schemes based on your preferences. Plus, remember, always check swatches. Paint can look way different on your walls than on a couple of small swatches! That’s a great idea! I should’ve thought of that. You know, it's funny how we never think of the actual process of choosing a color until we’re faced with it. Yep, when you’re renting, it’s different. I mean, we’ve lived in the same place 5 years and have just kind of grown with the spaces. But choosing everything almost from scratch is quite the challenge. Clearly, I should’ve passed on my decorating skills earlier. It’s not your fault! I’ve been so focused on the logistics of the move itself I haven’t given enough time to this... decorative side of things until the last minute.

Mum, I can't believe how much of a difference it's made having that new GPS. It's like we've never even seen this side of the city before! Everything is so different compared to when I was growing up here. Yes, it's amazing how much technology has changed things, isn't it? I kind of feel like we're losing some of the charm and character, but convenient it certainly is! True. Although I do miss the maps and getting lost occasionally. It was always so fun even if it wasn't exactly convenient! Oh, sweetheart, you always had such a sense of adventure! But I remember the times we got lost, we made some great memories. Though, let’s admit it, even then digital was not as advanced. True. And think how many wrong turns we've avoided thanks to this little gizmo. Absolutely. But looking at how London has changed... how do you think the digital vs. print debate applies to literary work? Mm, yeah, that's really interesting. So many people talk about how the digital era is this revolution, but I feel like we've lost a tactile experience that print gives. I agree, while the digital world offers accessibility and immediacy, there’s something substantial about holding a book in your hand, feeling the weight of it. But as a literary editor, I also see the need for digital as it reaches more readers. Definitely. I study book publishing and literary studies at university, we’re always talking about this. What do you think about that? Well, I think it's a balance. There's the risk that too much focus on digital could end up diminishing the quality and the existence of print. But at the same time, less people would have access to literature if it weren’t for digital, right? Right! I mean, ease of access is key, but we can't forget about the sensory experience of print. There’s a generation gap too, I notice my younger peers rarely read print unless it's specifically for class. True. I do think some are missing out. But for me, I still find digital works when it comes to initial research, but for deep reading or for pleasure, nothing beats print. Yeah, definitely. Plus, the production of print books has almost gone artisanal in some ways. I've seen some amazing designed covers and typesetting recently.

Oh, mates, remember that first trip we took to Spain? On the cheap, of course, didn’t have a lot of money after our student years. You mean the one where we almost missed the last bus home? Oh, hell yes! It was a close call. Like, we were at the hostel packing our bags and then realized the bus was actually leaving in 5 minutes. And we sprinted out with nothing else but our packs and a silly bloke wearing sandals. Aaah, that’s a good ‘un then! Did you get the whole 'I can't believe we made it in the nick of time' story? On the bus? It was more of a 'we decided to splurge on breakfast sandwiches in the terminal' story. But the real highlight was when we all got lost in the streets or Valencia, trying to find that cute little tapas bar. I mean, I thought I knew Spanish geography pretty well, but the 'streets of Valencia' are like a maze. We ended up carrying a street map, asking strangers, and nearly getting into a fight with a couple over directions, all in broken Spanish. And then when we finally found it, they didn’t even sell 'bocas'. Well, that's the real gem. We settled for 'patatas bravas' because it sounded exotic. Oh, weren’t we, lads! The 'bocas'-less tapas. It's a good thing we had those sandwiches to fall back on, or we’d’ve been starving. Aye, that were some proper 'laddurful' experience. I mean, we were all so exhausted from our so-called 'exotic' wanderings we ended up back here in Warrington for a proper Sunday roast and a good night's sleep. I still can’t believe how those trips shaped our little group. They were some of the best times we've had. Definitely. Though now we seem to complain about the rain here, like it’s a given that Warrington’s always gloomy. Well, yeah, but we managed a bit of sunshine in Spain, too, didn’t we? Speaking of sunshine, I've got another 'great' holiday story for you all. Oh, please, try me. So, remember that beach trip to Cornwall? Oh, that one where it nearly rained all the time! Exactly! But then one day, we decided to brave it and had picnic on the beach anyway. That's the one where the kids next to us were playing football...

I've decided I'm going to try winter camping. I've always been fascinated by the outdoors and found myself drawn to the idea of camping during winter, despite the less than ideal conditions. Aye now, that's a bit extreme, innit? Especially if ye haven't done it before. The conditions can be quite treacherous. I've actually done quite a bit of winter camping, though never in Britain. The challenges are real, keeps yer wits sharp, but it's also deeply rewarding. I know it sounds crazy, but I read a lot about it and even watched a few documentaries. It just seems like a proper adventure. Well, from a psychological perspective, it's a bold move, that's for sure. It pushes your boundaries and can be quite a form of personal therapy. Exactly. But it's also about safety, you need to be well-prepared. The right gear, the right knowledge, and a good plan. I've been gathering information, certainly. But I value all your input. I've been diligently reading up on it all, but I know it's one thing to read and another entirely to experience it firsthand. Aye, ye can spend years preparing for something like this, but the actual experience... Aye, that's a different kettle of fish. One thing to consider is the benefits of the cold, and the stillness that comes with it. It's a unique environment that forces you to slow down and appreciate the smallest details. That part interests me, actually. People often talk about the silence of nature. Seems like the lack of distractions would help a person recharge, spiritually and mentally. It does, but it's also about being aware of your limits and respecting the wilderness. While you're dealing with the natural environment, it's important to be mindful of your own needs, physical and psychological. I often recommend outdoor activities like this for patients dealing with stress or anxiety. It provides a healthy outlet and a real world to handle challenges outside the confines of daily life. That makes sense. There's something deeply rejuvenating about being challenged in such a natural way. Do you think it could also help with decision-making or personal growth, or is it more focused on the immediate well-being? It could definitely help with finding clarity or gaining a new perspective. Nature has a way of making the practical and abstract conflate in your mind, which can be really useful for decision-making or even tackling specific problems.

Yo, mate, did you finish reading that novel you've been banging on about? Yeah, I did. I actually finished it up last night. Had the whole book down in one go. It was brilliant! Oh, brilliant, eh? That's impressive. I'm always kind of ginger over the whole process, I find books a bit daunting. Mind sharing what it's about? It's called "The Weight of Water". It's very psychological. It's about this woman keeps coming backwards and forwards in time, not in a time-travely way, but she's struggling with her mental health and it's all quite nostalgic. She's a researcher and she goes back to her family's village and digs up stories from her family’s past. But in the process of researching, she starts to lose her grip on reality. Ah, sounds interesting! I did love "The Kite Runner" for similar reasons - the history and family secrets. But mental health? That's a pretty tough topic. Does it end well? Well, I won’t spoil it, but it's a really thought-provoking read. It's not a cheery beach read by any stretch. I can imagine. What about films? Have you seen any good ones lately? Yeah, I watched "The Lost Daughter" on Netflix. Oh, I heard that's good. I've not had the chance to catch it yet. What was it like? It’s fantastic. It’s about a woman who’s struggling with her past and her daughters, but it's not just about the relationship between mothers and daughters, it’s about her own identity and sanity, too. I was surprised at how the film keeps you off balance the whole time - it’s really a masterpiece, if you ask me. I'd highly recommend it. Yeah, I’ve had Olivia Wilde on my to-watch list for ages. She’s such a talented actress. Definitely. It’s a must-see, though a bit on the heavy side for popcorn cinema. I can't imagine it’s so heavy it’s spoiling for zero popcorn though! True that. Alright, what about you? What’s new in your world? Oh, we’re getting into the holiday season, so work has been a bit crazy. But I’ve been trying to prep some recipes from that new cookbook I got. I see! Are you talking that new...Bolton’s any good?

Right, and remember, once the Grinch stole all the Christmas presents and decorations from Who-ville, his heart started to feel so bad because he realized he was making everyone else miserable. He decided to change and return everything he had taken. But miss, why did he want to steal all the presents and decorations? Oh, he thought Christmas was about the material things, the gifts, the big feast, the decorations. And he didn't get any joy from them because he had a small heart, so he thought if he stole all these things, people would be as sad and grumpy as he was. But little did he know, Christmas is about being together and loving each other, isn't it? Yeah! And don't forget, he’s at the end so happy he gives the biggest roast beast and all the gifts back! Ah, right! The Grinch's heart grows three sizes, and he realizes the true spirit of Christmas. It’s really all about sharing and being around the people you love. Like when we went to the Brownie Promise evening last week! Everyone worked together and we had such fun, even though some of us didn't win any prizes, didn’t it? Exactly! It’s the spirit of the community and the joy in team effort and kindness to each other. Just like when we all played that Lego game yesterday, didn’t we all have to work together to build the whole city? Oh, that was fun! I really liked building the castle tower for our city. That’s so great to hear. Working together and sharing ideas is so much more enjoyable than doing things alone. Miss, do you like playing PlayStation as much as I do? I've just been thinking, you know, about how these scruffy clothes are all the rage now. I mean, I've seen people paying top dollar for the intentional-faded look. Stuck riding our bikes through bramble patches just to get our jeans just the right amount of torn. But back to breakfast - you planning on visiting the Derbyshire fruit farms this year? Ah, yes. We recently went on a trip to this abandonded medieval village between York and Scarborough. It was surreal, like stepping back in time. What a strange kind of melancholy they evoke. Reminds me of the studies on rural decline and industrial change. Exactly. Oh, I adore it! It's so comforting to put on a warm scone in the morning. Did the shop owner make it himself? Yes, apparently. Small batch production and all. He was quite passionate about his craft. Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to explain to a patient that they were actually allergic to the medication they'd been taking for years? No, that sounds quite odd. Was it because it was a medication they were supposed to be taking for something else? Or could it be a misdiagnosis? Actually, no, it was a bit different. They were presenting with secondary symptoms that didn't even seem to match the original diagnosis, and it was only when we went through their history and everything, that we realized they had started showing symptoms after they started the medication. That's quite a story. Medical mistakes can happen, but it's good you noticed the red flag. As a Head of Department, I can tell you we've had our share of tricky cases too. Sure, I recall one case where a patient was having digestive issues, and we kept switching medicines, but it was only when we actually ran a full allergy test did we find out it was the medication itself causing the problem. Exactly, so often this is about gathering and connecting all the dots. These types of situations often highlight how important it is to maintain open lines of communication with patients. If they're not telling everything, or even if things slip through the gaps, it can lead to these kinds of issues. Definitely. Like, my grandmother always said that, no matter how small you think something is, doctors need to know. One time when I was little, I had some kind of skin irritation that wouldn't go away. Mum thought it might be something simple, but the GP said "tell me everything!" and only after finding out that I'd been playing with a stray cat did it become clear the problem was less serious than we thought. Oh, I love that! The stray cat angle. Speaking of which, do you remember when Facebook started getting popular and suddenly everyone was sharing photos of animal encounters? There was one time I posted a pic of my son feeding ducks at the local park, and one of my friends commented, "Those are illegal to feed!" I didn't realize feeding bread to ducks was bad for them. Oh, social media! Can definitely spread all sorts of misinformation, and health-related misconceptions. I've almost gone into panic mode seeing some of the health advice being shared.

Oh, so many topics we've got to cover. I don't know where to start. How's your dissertation going, then? You're deep into this postgraduate life, and I've no idea. Is it all overwhelming? It's good for the eyes and the mind... and it's just plain nice to read without having to cull references or complete an essay. Exactly. Totally makes sense. I've been eyeing this new novel that won the Booker Prize. Want to pick it up together this summer while we're... should we say... relaxing? That sounds perfect. I'll definitely bring it along.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my online workout class? I signed up for this virtual yoga session last week and it was actually quite insightful. I think I'm going to be more regular with it now, you know? Really? That's great! I've been meaning to start exercising more regularly too. But I find it hard to stick to a routine, especially with the demands of work. And have you noticed house prices are just skyrocketing in this area? Oh, absolutely. It's just maddening, isn't it? Even with our current house, we're considering looking elsewhere, but I just can't believe what's being asked for some properties! It's like they're thinking we have bags of money in the bank. So, have you given any thought to selling our old house, then maybe moving to somewhere more affordable but still within commuting distance to the city? The prices aren't as bad as right here, but still... it's a trade-off regarding commute time. I'm all for compromise. I found a place in Surrey that could be a nice balance between affordability and proximity to London. It's still a big change though; finding schools, transport options, and all that. That's true. Schooling is a big deal and it really depends on each of our preferences for the kids. Speaking of kids , I heard from yours that they're doing well in their new school. Yes, they're soaking it up. The public school we chose is excellent, and they seem to enjoy the new routine. It took them some time to adjust, but they're doing great. That's music to my ears. Speaking of routines, thinking about schools reminds me I have to get back to writing this article on British cooking traditions.

Yo, mate, how's the job going? As a civil engineer, have you started working on any cool new projects since you got back from university? Ah, yeah, it’s been quite busy but fun. Alright mates, thanks for stopping by. I have to say though, you picking up some second-hand paint brushes from the yard sale last weekend was a great idea. Got some real bargains, right? Aye, yeah! What about acting?

Oh, did you see that?? That's the most fascinating thing today so far, aside from us actually deciding to take this journey. Alright, the Hay festival sounds like an amazing experience. You both have really great recommendations. I've just read this novel, though, called "North and South". Oh, it's so lovely to surprise you all like this! I hope you're not too busy. I've flown in from Kendal to see you all. Had the flight and the various transport connections. For instance, people grow older, cities change over time, but the fact that things keep changing, that remains forever . A wise observation, darling. Evolution is a constant in all things, really. You'd enjoy them! Yes, everything from old Chuckle Brothers records to funny books like The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. You could even get involved with the school's book club. Would you...? Oh, that would be great!

Yo, mate, check this out. I just got this new laptop online. Lookin' solid; quad-core, 8GB ram and a sweet Nvidia GeForce 1650. Nice! Is it better than your old one now? Yeah, way better. Oh, I'm so glad we decided to have a catch-up over coffee here. This place is lovely, and the atmosphere is so cozy. It's been quite a while since we last met and talked without distractions. Knowing that there are others going through the same thing

Oh, have you two seen this? The Dorset Steam Fair's coming to town next weekend and I thought it'd be a fun day out for all of us. Oh, it's lovely to be back in Thirsk. The weather's as unpredictable as ever, isn't it? This rain we've been having is quite something! Indeed it is. Still, though, the show must go on, as they say. Oh, did I ever tell you about's Dad's story when he took ANON to the dentist? It was hilarious! He was so nervous, insisting that his teeth were all fine. You two remember ANON's visit right? Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we had our mammoth dinner party at our place? It was a disaster! I don't know what possessed us to think that five of us could cook for twenty people. That sounds like a great idea. Our local community centre does a lot of those types of activities. Yes, it's fantastic. I've been wanting to try a bit more healthy eating, too.

Ah, I was just remembering one of my experiences as an EFL teacher. I had a student who came from South Korea. It was fascinating watching her pick up the language so quickly, and by the end of the year, she was reading English books just like the rest of the class.
