You have to be a bit of a psychologist too, I think. Exactly! Speaking of absorbing knowledge, I recall the time I lectured at sea. It was actually quite popular with the dental students to have lectures while on a voyage. The sea was calm, of course, but the whole "lecture on the ocean" gave a unique perspective. And the most interesting part? Some of my colleagues would use their free time for sailing, while I... well, I used the time to catch up on notes or simply enjoying the sea. It was a very different era, though. I remember this! I actually spent quite some time sailing when I was younger. Nowadays, the NHS doesn’t provide those kind of perks anymore. You’d think about it, in the past, as a dentist, we were entitled to really nice travel benefits. I used to take advantage of them to travel to places like Prague. The food, the culture... it was amazing. Ah, Prague! We really need to plan a trip there soon. It’s a beautiful city and prices are pretty reasonable these days. I went there a few years ago and marveled at the architecture and the history. And do you know how we could get into those fully booked performances? We managed to get into an opera at the last minute by just arriving early and asking politely. True. I used that trick whenever I could. And speaking of unique experiences, last time we were in Prague, we managed to get into a gallery by showing a previous boarding pass. You’d be amazed how often that works. Fascinating. I’ve had similar experiences in theaters here. Just showing up a bit early can work, but truly, the best experiences have always been the spontaneous ones—like the time I got into a show at the last minute because the previous person didn’t turn up.

So, I've been thinking over the past week while we've been here in Australia. We're in a really unique situation. We've got a sweet setup here with this beautiful house and all the time in the world to brainstorm. You know, we talked about this before but now I think we have a better chance to do something about it. What do you think about starting a business in the education sector? Like, focused on developing materials and case studies that use moving images and visual storytelling right? Absolutely, that sounds like a fantastic idea! We've both had loads of experience with teaching and education. You in training entrepreneurs, and me, well, you know, in the classroom. Plus, with the advancements in technology, we could do something really innovative. Exactly, the potential to combine our skills in a way that could actually make a difference. I've seen how impactful moving images and visual storytelling can be when trying to convey complex ideas. And with all this technology available now, it's not just about film, there's animation, graphics, even VR and AR applications. That's right, and speaking of visual learning, it's really underestimated how much of this is missing from our current curriculum. I use a lot of visual aids in my classroom, and the difference it makes is huge. I think this idea could really bridge the gap between traditional teaching and the way kids learn things now, you know, through screens and whatever. Ah, and to make it even more interesting, we could tailor it to different age groups or subjects in school. For example, history lessons could become immersive experiences, and math or science could be explained through interactive visuals. I've been looking at some of the tools and software that are used for this kind of thing. The potential for interactive, digital learning materials is huge. Right, and we could create something that's flexible, accessible online, and, if we're really ambitious, it could be made available to schools for free or at a very low cost. Just think of the impact that could have, especially in schools that might not have the resources for fancy software or equipment. Absolutely, and because of our background, we can also teach teachers how to use these tools and materials in their curriculum. A service side of the business could be offering workshops for educators on how to integrate these resources effectively.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen Grace and James lately? It's been ages. Yeah, talked to Grace last week. They've just landed a new job at the university in Brighton. Apparently the weather and the sea air have been treating them well. Oh, that's wonderful! I'm surprised though, I thought they preferred staying in London. I'm right there with you, but I guess Brighton's got its own set of charms. Speaking of keepsakes, I still have the photo frame you gave me. Oh, the seashell moment from our trip to Cornwall? I'm glad you like it. It's always there on the mantle when I need a reminder of our cherished summer spent by the sea. Speaking of which, I've been thinking of a fun retreat. Ron and Sarah are planning a little getaway to the coast and they've invited us along. Would you like to join? That sounds lovely! So, where were they thinking of? We might end up at a small B&B near Whitby or maybe Bournemouth. The sea views would be wonderful. Bournemouth’s a lovely idea, we could enjoy the long beach walk and maybe do some surfing or paddleboarding. I'd love that! We haven’t had time for an activity like that in ages. I'm sure they’ll organise it all. Plus, it's always fun to see them and catch up on the latest from their travels. Absolutely. Ron has been to so many places since his sabbatical. More reason for us to join them! I noticed Emily and Phil were also getting into water sports now. Did you know? From playing frisbee on the beach to paddleboarding in the sea? You'd think after all the mishaps Emily's had on the water, but I guess she finds it therapeutic. It's always good to see people trying new things, especially if it means being active and enjoying nature. Agreed. And they almost lost their camera in the sea once. Oh no, did it survive? Oh, funny story. They were doing a bit of underwater photography and it got a bit too involved. I suppose it makes a good anecdote now. That's a great tale for our beach stories collection. Yeah, and they now make sure to keep their phone secure in a waterproof case. Well, we've got all these plans for getting out to the sea, don't we?

Oh, did you see that?? Did Kim Kardashian just wear the same dress twice to two different events within a week? I don't know, I think it's so unrealistic. You can't just keep reusing one outfit for almost the same occasion, can you? Oh, Kim Kardashian and her team make those choices for a reason. It's all about brand synergy and maximizing their public appearances, right? Exactly! It's about creating a conversation starter, keeps her in the news, people talking about her. You'll probably see it on every magazine cover. I get that, but personally, I think it’s just a bit too much to expect us to be as fashion-forward as that. I mean, I feel like I can't even make an invitation to a party without hours of deliberation over outfits. Well, speaking of which... how’s that dress you bought last week? Did it come in alright? Yeah, it's lovely. I really loved it when I tried it on in the shop. We’re going to Emily and Matt’s dinner party next week, so that’ll be my go-to. Great! You should show us. If it’s really nice, we can even help you think of some accessories to match. I used to have quite the knack for that when I was in college. I could use the help. You know how it is, we always have these great plans but never know what to wear until the last minute. Just like the day we were supposed to go to the end of term party in uni, and you changed your outfit three times before going out. Ah, that was a long time ago. Speaking of which, have either of you booked tickets for London Fashion Week? It's next month, I’ve heard it’s supposed to be quite a spectacle. Yes! You know how much I love fashion. I've already got my tickets. The schedule says they're showcasing some of the new trends for spring. I thought about it, but I’m not sure if I’ll be able to make it. The timing with work is a bit tight this month. Though if I could just get the day off, I’d love to go. I heard they’re showing some really avant-garde designs this year. That would be amazing. I've never been to a proper fashion show.

Mum, I've been meaning to show you this photo I took. I have been trying out this new photography technique I read about online. Ah, that's great, sweetie! You love your technology, don't you? Show me the picture now, let's see how you're doing. Oh, that's really good! I can see why you'd be interested in photography, there's so much detail and depth. But even better is how it makes you look at ordinary things in a new way. Thanks. I've been trying to capture moments like this all the time, but I'm really worried that I'm not good enough to do this as a job. You're good enough, of course. It's just about making yourself better, isn't it? And even if it doesn't turn out to be a job, photography is a wonderful hobby. But speaking of creative work, have you got any ideas about college yet? Uhm, yes. I'm between choosing film or journalism next year. So many jobs seem to require that, so...I don't know, it feels like a safe bet, but I worry I won't be good enough. A safe bet isn't always the best choice, but it's not a terrible thing if it is aligned with your interests. I used to have similar fears about my own work, whether I'd make it as a receptionist or not, especially after grad school. Really? You were scared about your job? Oh, absolutely. I felt like I could've been doing something more… interesting, you know? But over time, I found my own ways of making it interesting, like connecting with people, and using my education in unexpected ways. That’s really comforting to hear, I guess. I feel like I keep looking for the ‘perfect’ path, but maybe there isn’t one. There really isn't. What’s important is you keep trying new things and embracing learning. We all have fears, sweetie, but it's how we face them that matters. I'm sure you'll do great in whatever you choose. Thanks so much, Mum. I guess what really scares me though is not being able to show my work, and what if no one likes it? There's always the risk of rejection, but that doesn't mean you aren't good enough.

Ah, marvellous to see you both! Just got back from the garden. On the road, I found those young birds in the nest. Thought it was just the little ones, but there was a proper cockerel in there too! Oh, that’s quite a surprise – a cockerel in the nest? I didn’t expect that. But then again, nature can surprise us at times! Yeah, very much so. I read somewhere that it's not uncommon for a rooster to get cooped up with the hens. Crazy how societal norms can apply even in the animal kingdom, isn't it? Speaking of animals, have you seen the latest 3D printing designs online? Some of those digital patterns for cats and dogs look almost life-like. I’d love to get one for my niece’s birthday. Ah, yeah! I did see those designs. But with our generation, sometimes it feels like we’re racing with the tech, don’t you think? Can’t quite keep up with the pace. Absolutely! But that’s the charm of it, isn't it? It keeps us young, even if we're running the wrong way most of the time! Like trying to fill out that council application form for the new library space. They made it so complicated. I must’ve read it five times and still didn’t understand half of it. Oh, for goodness’ sake! Young people probably whip through it in no time. I despise these forms nowadays. Everything is online and… and… well it’s just awful. Online, but then you get the design flaws and shabby workmanship. Seems like the young ones may do it faster, but the quality isn’t matched with the speed. Exactly! Just had my phone screen replaced last week and it’s already sticking! I swear, changing the world and losing quality at the same time. Well, I suppose we can’t have it all. But it’s funny when you think about it. I mean, we didn’t have phones or 3D printers when we were young and we still found ways to be happy. Maybe it's just about perspective. I teach and I see it all the time. Our youth these days are so used to instant gratification, they sometimes miss out on the joy of process or slowing down to appreciate things. That’s a good point. Maybe we do focus too much on the ends rather than the journey.

Ah, I've been meaning to talk to you about it, Susan. I've finally made the decision to bring my daughter back to live with me here in Brighton. Oh, really? That's great news! You must be really excited to have your daughter closer, after all this time abroad. I am. It's been a while since she and I have been under one roof. And to think that now I'll get to share those quiet, cozy mornings with her, just like old times. Are you still a bit worried about the transition, though? I know she's been living on her own for quite a while now. Yes, I do get a little anxious. It’s like I have to re-learn how to be a part of each other’s daily routines again. Also, making sure the house feels like a welcoming home for her is important to me. Absolutely. Trust me, it’s also a bit of an adjustment for the kid when they decide to move back in. You're not alone there. I suppose what worries me most is adjusting to her new schedule and this new life she has built for herself. I want her to feel comfortable here, but I also don’t want to overstep or interfere. That’s a delicate balance. But remember, your home is also hers, and she’s coming back because she trusts you’ll keep her safe and happy, right? Exactly, and that's why I’m a bit apprehensive about making changes to her space or routines without talking to her about it first. I'd say that’s wise. It's a two-way street. Perhaps you could have an open conversation about finding the right balance? Let her tell you what she’s comfortable with and what she might need from you in terms of support or space. Yes, I will. She's a confident and independent person, so I’m expecting her to assert her preferences. That’s exactly what should happen. She’s also probably got a lot to share about her experiences abroad, so be open to hearing that too. Yes, I’m sure she’s got a world of stories and perspectives to share. I just hope she’s willing to tell me about her struggles and triumphs. She could have had some amazing experiences and ups and downs, just like all of us when we venture out into the world.

Ah, I hear you've seen some of the latest news regarding the Scottish referendum. Quite a surprise; I mean, people didn't think it was going to go that deep, did they? Oh absolutely, you've no idea. I was up late last night waiting for the results, and I must say, it was quite stirring. You've given it much thought, have you? Absolutely. As a lecturer, I've been following it closely as it ties into some of the topics we cover in political science. But even beyond that, it's a fascinating representation of how societal and demographic changes can truly shake up the status quo. Right, and with the way things are, it's been a real eye-opener for many, including my pupils here. They're asking all sorts of questions about it, and it's quite the opportunity for a valuable discussion. It most certainly is! It also raised its head during a recent job interview. One of the candidates asked about my thoughts on the matter, and I had to improvise quite a bit. It wasn't on my radar as something I expected to discuss. For me, it's been a mixed bag with students. Some are fully engaged and see it as an opportunity to express independence. Others are quite nervous, while the rest seem oblivious. It's good that it at least sparks interest in politics, right? Certainly. Well, politics aside for a moment, how have you been otherwise? A bit chaotic around here, still teaching from home isn't it? Indeed, it is still quite restrictive and a bit chaotic. But it's been manageable. I've been holding regular classes online, adapting where I can. How about you? How’s the new role treating you? It's been... interesting. A few more responsibilities than I anticipated, but I'm enjoying the challenge. Plus, the crowd of students is really enthusiastic so far. However, it's been a learning curve, getting used to the new teaching environment and making sure I'm still meeting all the curriculum requirements. Accustoming to new environments can be a challenge, especially in our advanced years of teaching. I recall my early days in this profession. Funny how things just keep evolving. Anyway, I've heard your daughter is applying for jobs now that she has finished her degree? Yes, she is. She’s been going through this whole process just over the past month or so.

Alright, I remember when we used to play Mousetrap. It was always quite chaotic, but so much fun. Indeed! Made for some great memories, Alison! Though I must say, it was quite the challenge, wasn't it? Always something breaking or not working just right. I've heard about Mousetrap! It's one of those classics right? Yeah, but have you guys ever seen how complicated it keeps getting? It's almost like a puzzle in itself, right? Absolutely! Even today, it’s a fun challenge for the family. Though I must admit, it’s getting harder with all the new and modern games out there. Well, from what I've observed, children today are exposed to so many complex games and tech. Mousetrap seems relatively simple in comparison. That's true, but sometimes we need those simple, classic games. They help build teamwork and problem-solving skills in a more tactile way, don’t they? Yeah, it's true. I actually met this American exchange student last year who was completely fascinated by it. He tried setting it up with his friends but funnily assumed we only used 'trap' and 'mice,' he had no idea it was a game! That's so cute! Ah, speaking of Americans, I had a pretty interesting story, actually. Last year I worked at a bistro in New York for a few months. The kids, and even some adults, were always curious about our dishes. I mean, doesn’t everyone in the States know about Fish and Chips? Well, you’d be surprised! I was in Atlanta visiting the Johnson family. Their children were absolutely intrigued by the concept of just chips, meaning fries to them. They kept asking if we also had burgers or hot dogs with them all the time. While you were dealing with the cultural food gap, I struggled with the American sense of distance and space. I mean, I spent weeks trying to convince my colleagues that not every public transport here uses miles, but metric, and they just couldn’t wrap their heads around it! Haha! That reminds me of when I was in California. The way Americans quantify almost everything in feet or inches was quite the adjustment for me. Clearly, I underestimated how deeply embedded it is in their daily life. That’s a great point. I heard from Mark that in general, Americans seem to be quite often puzzled by this ‘metric system’...

Oh, did I find bargains or what? I was just today shopping for a few things and found this stunning outfit. . You love shopping. What did you get this time? Just this dress and a few accessories. I found this beautiful silk dress at this new shop near the market. It's got this amazing pattern, fits like a glove, and the best part – it was actually very affordable. Which pattern is it? I'd love to get a look. You know how much I admire good textile designs. It's this intricate floral pattern, quite nostalgic, reminds me of something traditional Chinese but in a very modern twist. Ah, that’s really nice. I feel like that could be a theme for many things here. So modern and traditional at the same time. Exactly! And the fabric is so fine, yet very appropriate for the local climate. And these earrings, I found these matching ones. They match so well with the dress. For me, it's always about finding that perfect balance between local culture and modern aesthetics. How did you notice the store? You’re becoming quite the local while I’ve been here teaching and so in my own world at the university. It’s just part of exploring, right? But seriously, a colleague from work told me about it. She’s always on the lookout for unique, culturally nuanced pieces. And I love how the store also supports local designers. That’s fantastic. Supporting local artisans is something that speaks volumes about cultural sensitivity and progress. I might need to check it out myself sometime. Please do! She’d be thrilled if you dropped by. And, speaking of matched sets, I also found a nice blouse to go with my other dress. It's classic but with this one unique detail... You mean like how I find matching ties for my suits? Exactly! But these little touches make all the difference in my world. Anyway, I was thinking, maybe we could look for a nice restaurant for dinner tonight and debut this dress. That sounds like a plan. There's this new place I've been wanting to try. It's supposed to have excellent traditional Chinese dishes but with a modern twist. Could work really well with your dress and the current mood. I’d love that. And maybe this dressing up might just... be a nice change?

Ah, lads and lass, did any of ye catch the Six Nations match last night? It was a cracker, if I do say so myself. Wasn't it? Yeah! I watched it with my mates at school, and England won! Go England! Oh, now don’t be cross, but I'd have to argue that. Ireland took them out to the cleaners. Indeed. The Irish boys played out of their skins that day. Ah, it was a fantastic match. Full of suspense until the very end. What did you like best about it, Owen? Oisin, I mean.. sorry, dad. No need to apologize, lad. Just call me by name. So, what caught your eye? Well, it was when the Irish team started scoring tries! It was like they turned the game on its head. Aye, but he was firmly For England before that point, it seems! I prefer the Irish spectacle. Their style of play is always so entertaining. Indeed. Especially the way they work the ball out wide. It’s a joy to watch. I agree. Aye, Ireland has a flair about their rugby that England could sometimes learn from. But you never know, we might have a good shout if we keep working harder. That doesn’t come from nowhere, mind you! Helen, didn’t you hear? Scotland’s performances are getting better too. Aye, I’m very proud of the Scottish Rugby team. They’re getting confident again. So, Mr. . . er, Chief! Can I ask something? Don’t be formal, Oisin. What's on your mind? Are we going to send a card to the players? Like, if one of them is having a birthday or something? That’s a grand idea. Even just to say well done. We could all sign it. That would be lovely. We could include a message of support. I like that. We’ll do that. You can all sign it this evening while we’re... Yay! Can I design the card? If you want to, why not? Just keep it simple and appropriate, please. So, Oisin, are we still planning to go stargazing tonight, given it should be clear? I’d absolutely love that! It’s going to be a beautiful night. You’re not too tired for it, are you? Don’t need to go to bed too late. No, not at all. I've had some practice already. And if we do go, can I bring my new telescope?

So, I hear you're expecting. Congratulations! How's everything going? Yeah, super excited! The pregnancy is going well, thank you for asking. We're due in a few months but I still can't quite believe it’s happening. That's completely normal! Both exciting and overwhelming at the same time, right? I remember when my sister had her first baby, she was in a similar boat. Exactly! I keep trying to process everything and it’s just so much to take in. Are you still with Simon in Aylesbury? Yeah, actually. We've been there for about a year now, just before we got the opportunity to move back from London. The village is just lovely. You know, quiet, peaceful... That sounds wonderful! I'm making the transition from living with my parents in Lincoln to a new flat with my boyfriend in Norwich. It's all a bit of an adjustment, but I'm trying to set up the new place. That must be quite stressful. You'll love it, though. I know I love the new place we've got. So different from this bustling city and it's provided some much-needed tranquility. I’ve been decorating most of my free time though, while the research job still gives me so much joy. I hear you, the last few years have been a whirlwind. I'm also really looking forward to having more space for crafting and, you know, baby preparations. Crafting? What are you making? I'm all about handmade and unique items these days! I've started making a couple of things for the baby - baby blankets and a knitted hat or two. I’ve also started collecting second-hand maternity clothes since they’re less wasteful and usually in better condition. Have you done anything similar for your future family? Oh, absolutely! Clothes sharing and reusing is such a sensible idea for the environment and our bank balance! Especially now with a new changing body. Definitely. I also borrowed a bunch from family and friends. Plus I’ve been reading up on local baby groups and playgroups, getting excited for all the social stuff. That’s great! You’ll love meeting other new moms and dads. We’ve got a fantastic group in Aylesbury just for local families. We could set up something in Lincoln and I’ll hook you up if you’d like?

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new board game from's been on everyone's radar. Its' quite possibly gonna be the next big thing. Thoughts? Yeah, I've heard about it. It's got quite a mixed bag of reviews but I'm intrigued, though I kind of do love questions on linguistics. It's got this mechanic that tests your knowledge and understanding of different words and idioms across different languages and dialects. I'm actually considering using it in one of my language classes, to get my students more engaged with dialects and even how language is perceived socially. That's a good idea actually. Like how we're sitting here, all from different parts of England but having entirely different accents. I'm thinking of that game just like how my job shows me, as a gardener, the nuances of regional plant species and techniques - though maybe not the best analogy. Exactly, dialects and accents are really interesting because they tell you so much about where a person comes from, traditionally. But it's fascinating that even within these relatively small regions in Britain, there are so many variations. So true. My accent is a bit different compared to some of the boys from up North, or even from London. I’m from the south, Bedfordshire specifically, and sometimes I get comments about it. But it's cool, really. It’s part of who I am, right? Absolutely, and it's similar to how dialects in Greek, which is my second language, show regional differences. There's this beautiful variation in Cyprus, where I have roots, that differs from the mainland Greek. Shows language is never static and always evolving through geographical and social influences. But it's not just about the how we say things; it's also about the kind of words and expressions we use. I've noticed things like different words for basic things in different parts of England. Like a bread roll, for instance, is called a bap in some places, a cob in others, but here we just call it a bread roll. That’s so true! I remember changing the word for something simple like 'zip' to 'zipper' when I moved out of Bedfordshire. People had no idea what I meant. Funny how those little things can throw you. It’s indeed interesting. It also reminds me of how students struggle with understanding colloquialisms and slang.

I've decided I need a new car. The commute to work is becoming too stressful. Well, that sounds familiar. I was thinking of getting a new one too. Want to discuss the ideal type for our needs? That'd be great! So, you've been driving for a while now and I'm just starting out. I have some ideas, but I'm not sure they're practical. Like what? I'd be happy to share my thoughts. Well, I've been thinking of getting an electric car. They seem to be getting more popular and I've heard they're cheaper to maintain. But, I heard charging can be a hassle sometimes. That's a good point, but the infrastructure is getting better all the time. What about hybrid cars? They seem like a good balance between electric and conventional. Hybrids are definitely a good option too, especially if you need to travel longer distances that electric cars can't cover on a single charge. Yeah, I hadn't thought of that. For me, a lot of it is about the daily commute. I understand. I use a hybrid myself and it works well for the shorter trips. For longer journeys, I use a commuter train to save on the costs and the hassle of finding parking. That's a clever idea! I hadn’t considered public transport for longer trips. But isn't the train network expensive? For the most part, yes. But if you buy a season ticket, it can work out quite efficiently in terms of cost and time. Plus, the train is stress-free because you can work or read while you travel. That sounds really appealing. But I just got my first job as an administrator and I was thinking of having a car for independence. Independence is valuable, but it's worth considering whether the cost of a car really justifies it, especially if public transport is convenient for the bulk of your travels. Hmm, fair point. What about the cost of buying a car in general? I know I have a bit of debt from uni, and so I'm trying to save money for a deposit. We can definitely talk about finance and budgeting. Before you buy, check if you're eligible for any government incentives or employee benefits. Yeah, I've looked into that but still, everything seems pricey. Especially with trade-ins and new registrations.

Ah, barge on in then. It's always lovely to have you here. How was the journey from York, lad? Right good, aunty. It wasn't too bad this time. I got to read some questions for my Maths GCSE while I was on the bus, and I think I've got a real good grip on percentages now. Thou should be proud of yerself, lad. That's hard work for an 11-year-old, innit? Even when I were at school, we didn't need to learn all them fancy maths. Aye, times have changed, eh? But good on him for keeping at it. I'm proud too. But before we get on to any maths talk, have you both had a good visit? And have you had a chance to see grandad's old pictures in the study? He was meaning to show you his Hull City collection before. Yeah, grandad showed me all his old Hull City memorabilia. I saw the old shirts and pictures. He told me about the St. Andrew's ground and how it used to be. It was really interesting, aunty! Ah, the good old days at Boothferry Park. Speaking of which, lad, do thou know thou should be really good at that? They say the fans are as passionate there as they used to be over at Boothferry. True enough. I used to go to every match, and the noise, the crowd, it was electric. I remember the time they won the old League. The floodlights were lit up all over Hull city. It was a sight to see. Win what, aunty? You mean like a football prize? Aye, lad, that's what I mean. A big tournament. Funny how those games stick in yer head, isn't it? Reminds me, we should see if there's a good match on the telly tonight. Would you be interested, you two? We could put it on in the living room if you like. The light's good in there for the afternoon. That sounds like a brilliant plan. I might sit with you too, lad. I never used to watch much but any excuse to be with you lot... No, no, now come on, let's not make it a burden. Grandad, you keep your afternoon quiet, don't you? Take your time, and if you fancy watchin' the match later, that's fine too.

Alright kids, are you enjoying this pirate story about Captain Blackheart yet? Oh yeah! He’s so fierce! He’s on a ship with a flag with a skull and crossbones! That’s right! So, who here knows what a pirate is? A pirate is someone who steals things from ships and boats! Right? Like Captain Blackheart here. Close, but not entirely accurate, sweetie. Pirates did sometimes steal from other ships, but they were also fighters and even explorers, sometimes. But they didn’t do nice things, right? They didn’t share very well, did they? No, pirates weren’t very good at sharing, that’s true. But some pirates, like Blackbeard, were known more for their bravery or their reign over certain seas than their niceness. Is this the ship that Captain Blackheart is on? Yes, it probably is. It looks like a galleon from the illustrations, which are a type of ship pirates often used. So, are we all pirates today? For today, doesn’t that sound like fun? Arrr! Arrr! But the book says that pirates used to hide treasure! We’re going to search for treasure today in this very kitchen! But won’t the treasure be hidden really well? You know, jewels and gold? No jewels for us today! But we’ll have treasure of a different kind. Treasures of imagination and fun! Now, about those adventures. We’re almost ready for Shakespeare Week at school. Did any of you learn anything about Shakespeare and his plays? We did learn. He wrote Romeo and Juliet. And it’s really sad but also really good. And we might get to go see a play in the theatre! That would be so cool, if we can! That would be a brilliant plan. How about after that, we also make it a weekend trip and head to Stratford? Stratford? Where Shakespeare lived? Yes, exactly! It's a town famous for theatre and also where you can see Shakespeare’s house. Can we also go to the circus there? There’s one we visited once and it was amazing! It might be closed for the season, but there is actually a circus workshop in a real circus we can go to. They offer training sessions like trapeze and tightrope walking. Interested? Oh, yes! Trapeze would be so fun! Me too! And speaking of new adventures, how did you like our Easter egg hunt last week?

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about the time I got arrested in Saudi Arabia trying to sail from Jeddah to Cyprus? It was a bit of a farce, really. Aye now, the old sailing days! You've always been daring, haven't you? So what happened? Well, to make a long story short, I was teaching English as a Foreign Language there, and I decided to take a break with some mates during Ramadan. We thought, “Why not sail to Cyprus for a bit?” After all your adventures, I had no idea you used to sail. And in Saudi Arabia of all places! That's quite daring. Yeah, well, I didn't realize the implications of that. As a foreigner, sailing without proper permission is quite a serious offence. And did the authorities react when they found you? Oh, absolutely. We were arrested as soon as we docked, thinking we'd pull off a quick getaway. I mean, it was a small boat but still... The border control was quite diligent. You didn’t realize that’s a no-go, did you? Well, at the time, I did, but the thought of a bit of an adventure, you know? It wasn’t all in vain, though. They gave us a bit of a talking to and a stern warning. So, what was it like teaching in Saudi Arabia? It must’ve been quite an experience. Oh, it was. The students were brilliant, very eager to learn. The culture shock was the biggest challenge for me, especially when I first arrived. I can imagine. The cultural differences would’ve been quite stark. Did you have any trouble adjusting to life there? Yes, quite a bit, particularly with the alcohol ban. I do miss a good English pub sometimes, let me tell you. I always take a case of wine with me on long trips now. Speaking of alcohol, I recall a good anecdote. When I was in Manchester, one of my students once sent me a stack of dental magazines disguised as books. They thought customs would be less suspicious of a professor with a bunch of dental magazines than a few bottles of fine wine! That’s hilarious! I hear you, that's... quite a creative solution. Customs can be picky, especially with alcohol. That’s why I’ve always liked the less rigid countries, like Cyprus. Speaking of which, I've never had a cheeky little sailing adventure like yours, but my sailing days were limited to weekends around Ramsgate.

Oh, did I ever tell you about's Dad's latest bathroom catastrophe? He's trying to install that new smart toilet he bought online, but I think he may need more than just a manual to figure it out. He sounds like he's in over his head! You know, I once went on a work trip to the Warwickshire countryside and saw some pretty quirky public loos... But I didn't think a bathroom could be THAT challenging! Are you serious? That would make for a funny video if it were recorded, right? What was he trying to fix exactly? I think he was just trying to fit in that new water-saving feature, but then he got stuck when he read that the seat needed battery power. Then he thought "oh, how many AA batteries does a toilet even use?" Ron, creative yet very literal in his approach to DIY, isn't he? I bet it's funny to watch. Do you think maybe that was before his years of youth working on cars and before he got into marketing and proofing? Exactly! He assumed if the toilet needed power, then it would be like his old cars - uses a simple battery to make things work. He's probably writing off buying a new one, or just marking it as a "teaching moment". Can you imagine? The life of a British man and all those "can-do" moments that sometimes get slightly complicated. I'll have to remember that when I grow up and end up like him. I mean, if I ever end up working on a career in DIY or commerce, maybe those skills will come in handy, right? On that note, did your mum say anything about your plans or holidays before schools end? We're planning something in Cornwall this summer but we'd love to include you. You've never really had a sit-down meal in a beachside pub, I imagine? Yeah, she mentioned something about it. It sounds wonderful! A proper beach soaking, maybe some snorkeling if the weather is good. It would be awesome to have a break and enjoy the sea. Lovely idea! We often meet up with families in Devon over the summer and if you're up for it, you could join us. It's always great having more kids around to keep the older ones company while the parents chat.

Alright Dad, I just can't believe these truffles. I've never seen such varieties before! I talked to our local chef back home and he said they're all here because the soil here in Istria is just perfect for growing them. Wow, I knew Istria was known for its truffles, but I didn't know it was this big of a deal! I've never had them before though, and it's bizarre how much they cost keeps changing based on supply and demand, isn't it? Yeah, and they're supposed to be really delicious, but I've been questioning if the price is worth it. Especially with the economic situation back home. Exactly! And the chef I spoke to gave a pretty stellar review though. He's been here a couple of times and he raves about the truffle hunting experience too. Interesting! Did he explain why the soil here is so good for them? And I heard truffle hunting is quite the adventure. Oh, he spent quite some time explaining it but it includes the different types of soil, the climate, and even the fact that the area is relatively untouched. It makes a big difference. It's a bit like wine country over there, isn't it? Like specific regions known for specific grapes, this region is known for these truffles. An area known for specific truffles and they're rare. I don't think we have anything like that back in the UK, do we? No, not that I know of. And speaking of rare things, do you remember when we were in America and Dad was explaining those stem cell research articles he was reading? Oh yes, I do. It was quite a controversial topic that one wasn't it? There was a lot of ethical debate around it. Yes, and Dad was quite opposed to the use of embryonic stem cells, right? Yes, I remember he felt it was pushing the boundaries too much. And I thought, coming from a medical background, it would interest you more. It does. The potential for medical breakthroughs is huge, but the ethics... well, it's a complex topic. And what about the football? How's Man United doing? I heard they're finally getting their act together after that rough patch. Oh, it’s been better. Just the other day I was watching the match, and they actually looked like they had a game plan.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you ever had your work featured in these books we print? I've always wondered how it must feel to hold something you've helped create in your own hands. Actually, yeah! Just this past month, our digital marketing firm designed some kind of infographic for the Cambridge Encyclopedia of Language and Linguistics. It was a fun project! I've never had anything published, but I set up a lot of the meetings and communications for projects like that. It's pretty rewarding to see everything come together, even if it's not your name in the byline. It definitely is. I've just finished a research paper on English dialects around the UK - focusing on the differences in places like your hometowns, Cambridge and Aylesbury, by the way. That's fascinating. We've actually worked on a few creative projects highlighting local dialects in English for educational materials. Ever noticed how different people from Cambridgeshire and Bucks use different words and phrases for the same thing? Absolutely! In Aylesbury, for instance, people sometimes use "nineteen's" instead of "-teen" for 19. It's one of those little regional quirks that make our research so exciting. Well, in Cambridge, we say "flat" for "apartment". I noticed that visiting friends in other parts of the country sometimes get confused by it. Oh, "flat" is quite normal for us doesn't it? It's these kinds of differences that I find so interesting. I've even looked into how some of these regional idioms get incorporated into educational content. It's great for making the learning process a bit more fun and relevant. Absolutely! We've been working on some interactive learning modules that use humor and local dialect to engage younger learners. You'd be surprised how well it works to teach a bit more complex concepts! Sounds like we're all pushing in the same direction, trying to make language accessible and enjoyable. Exactly. I think those of us who deal with language in our work just have an innate appreciation for the little variations that make communication so rich and interesting. Well, I can't speak for all of us, but I just enjoy when it helps to get a bit more attention for the products we're promoting. Don't worry, I'm sure your work is definitely noticed! You know, it's interesting that despite how different these places are, we share so much when it comes to work and interests.

We've hit traffic gods today. I hope we make it to Joe's place before the late afternoon darkness deepens. No, the road’s fine, Sue – we're not far off. I just got a bit nervous. Haven’t driven in a campervan for so long and this one of yours, as lovely as it is, can be a tad unpredictable. Are you still adjusting to being back in the UK? Yes, adjusting. I’ve been out of the loop for a while and I’ve been relying mostly on part-time TEFL work just to keep my English up. But as much as I adore the language, I feel like I've lost a bit of my edge. It's okay, Sue, I’m sure you’ll get back into it. You were always very good at TEFL, and it’s such a rewarding job. You just need to get back into it. So, where were we before the traffic caught us this morning? You and me planning our next trip? Ah yes, the travel plans! The basics are still the same – we’re driving down to Tarnow to meet at Joe’s place, then we’ll decide whether we want to do anything else. I had a thought – since we’ll be in Poland for a while, shouldn’t we really plan to visit Krakow? It’s so much closer and they said the Wawel Castle is worth a stop. Well, it is the closest major tourist site to Tarnow and it'd be a shame to skip it if we're in the area. We could grab a side of pierogies in the old town and see the castle. Exactly. And while we're in town, we should look for some of those local specialty foods. There must be some amazing bakeries or street food stalls in Tarnow itself. Absolutely, but let’s not book for anything until we’ve seen Joe’s place and had a bit of a rest. We don’t want to tire ourselves out for the trip ahead. Right. And we’ll need to see about those campervan parking spots once we get to Tarnow. Last time I checked, parking in those historic areas can be a nightmare. We’ll figure it out. Joe’s connections should be able to help us with that. But now, let’s enjoy the ride. This countryside is beautiful this time of year.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen these new Nike shirts for Tottenham? Oh, yes! They're quite something. I mean, I'm a bit concerned about the new design. Black and white is classic, but those blue stripes do something odd to the overall look. I see what you mean. But you've got to give them credit for trying something different. I'm just hoping the stripes don't clash with the darker tones of their traditional home kit. True, but sponsors can get too much influence sometimes. You know, those adidas shirts with the oversized numbers? It's all just about sticking logos on, really. Oh, those are ridiculous. I read that some teams are getting big money from sponsors though. Hence the problem. It's a game of money now, not just football. Back in my day, jerseys were simple. You couldn’t even see who was on the front of the shirt! I’m sure they were. But it's the sponsorship culture that's driven the change. Even the referees have extra logos on their shirts now. Exactly. Speaking of which, I saw a report on sports sponsorship at work. It's interesting how companies are using football leagues to brand themselves. That makes sense. Football is a global brand itself, really. But have you seen those McDonalds and Coca-Cola signs around the stadium? Of course, it's unavoidable. I was talking to my colleague the other day about that, and he mentioned that McDonald's actually sponsors more football teams around the world than any other company. Really? I didn't know that. I noticed more McDonald's ads at the World Cup this year. Absolutely. It's all about reach. While I agree with changing the football strip designs for sponsorship, football needs to keep its identity. Like, I mean – I know it’s for the money but these new designs sometimes just… look silly compared to what they were. Totally agree. It's good the adidas and Nike stuff almost always looks good, but sometimes... like the Northampton Town strip with those sleeve sponsors. I mean, it works for some but occasionally looks a bit tacky. I heard their company makes those novelty socks for babies and that was their branding idea. Oh that's terrible! But, if it brings in revenue for the club, maybe it's worth it.

Ah, you've really got to see the state of the job market, Sarah! I've been on about six interviews today and nothing so far. It's like they'd rather fill the job with a part-time student than take a risk on someone with minimal work experience like me. Oh, really? That's so disappointing to hear. You're putting in a lot of effort. Yeah, well, at least I had a bit of a laugh at the train station. This young lad just thought I was purposely making him uncomfortable when I read his eBay order from across the carriage—he thought we were on the wrong platform. Then when we chatted, he realized he'd mistaken me for someone of a completely different race. Hilarious, really... Oh, I can just imagine. It's like those old sitcoms where someone gets thrown completely off by a misconception. So, what about the eBay order? Was everything delivered okay? Yeah, all good there. It was one of those little day trips with the kids over the weekend we were discussing, right? The George Foreman grill. Worked like a charm for our impromptu barbecue at Margate. Exactly, that was really fun. I never realized we'd use it so much. What do you think about maybe trying to plan another one soon? As much as it brought us together, part of me wishes we could afford more than just day trips. You know, side of commerce, try those theme parks or just treat the kids to something a bit more... grand. Listen, it's not just money either, it's about being able to plan for the future. That and the benefits claim isn't exactly a sustainable solution. You know how it feels to sit there wondering if people are resentful of others spending their inheritance while you're struggling to pay the bills for gas and electricity. I get it, totally. It must be tough seeing others seemingly coast through life while you're still paddling hard. But, you know, this is a time for all of us to support each other. That's easy for you to say, Sarah. You're a student, you've got your whole life ahead of you. I'm stuck here, trying to figure out if I should cling to any semblance of a career or just accept the benefits and hope for a miracle.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I drove past a minor road and got completely lost? I was trying to use my sat nav, but it told me the wrong way! Made me miss my client meeting. Oh dear! That's quite something. I've had days like that too, though I usually stick to what I know. I'm right behind you there, dear. I once took the wrong road in Norwich and ended up in another city altogether! Oh no, I can imagine. It was such a hassle. Sat navs are just so convenient but I swear, they sometimes forget how London roads work. Well, we can't all be from big cities like you are. And to be fair, they’re a godsend. I’ve heard of people going so far off course that they’ve ended up on the wrong side of the country! And these modern-day maps. I'd never use those. I’d still carry a proper map or a guidebook. Now that was before the days of smartphones. I prefer the old ways too. Less reliance on technology, I think. Indeed. Speaking of which, I saw there was a plane crash the other day. Well, relatively near London, at least. Oh, really? That can’t be good news. Any details? I only heard through my neighbor. Just said there were casualties involved. That’s terrible. Terrible that it had to happen, and tragic for those involved. It’s strange, isn’t it? We rely so much on these machines for our daily lives and transport but they can still let us down so badly. Exactly. Especially with so many people changing the world of transport these days. You'd think after all these years of flying, we'd have that sorted out but clearly not. That’s so true. Reminds me of when we used to travel by ship. Gran, you’re almost upsetting me with the old times! Ah, but there’s something to be said for the sense of adventure and anticipation with sea travel. Quite true. You’d often see more of the world that way... and meet interesting people. Speaking of sea travel, I miss seafood. You know, fresh fish, from the coast, not just some imposter from the supermarkets. Oh, I agree completely! Nothing beats fresh fish from local markets. You know what, though, I was at this excellent fish and chips place recently, I’d say as good as anything from the coast, but their regulars might disagree.

Yo, so I had this absolute craic of a first year's art lesson today. We were supposed to do some designing and I was trying to come up with an idea using this old chicken coop out back. Made me think about sustainability and all that. That sounds cool! You know, I've always thought questions on sustainability are just so overused in school tests. But then again, it's quite a serious topic! True! But I guess you never know when your chicken coop might set you apart. Anyway, how was your day? Did you have a moment like that? Yeah, actually. Our science lesson was kinda about climate change today, just like we discussed last week. The teacher brought in this model of the water cycle. It was actually pretty interesting. Yeah, our teacher tried to do a model of photosynthesis too. She started acting out parts of the plant, which was a bit embarrassing, but at least she's trying. Oh, that's pretty funny. You couldn’t have painted it. Someone should make a video of that and post it online. You and me both. But come on, even if she’s a bit... silly, she’s kind of nice, you know? Totally. And our teacher for English is also really nice, but apparently the new trainee teachers are supposed to start next week. Can't wait to see what that's like. Oh really? I heard that as well. But you never know, they might actually be good. What if we get some new styles of teaching? Maybe we can finally learn something that's not the same old stuff the whole time. You're right. And what if one of them knows things about different cultures or something? It’d be pretty cool to learn a bit more about the world outside of England. If they're as open-minded as our geography teacher, that's for sure. He's always got these amazing anecdotes from when he traveled. Yeah, he does. Like that time he was in India? The story he tells about people not having public transport and using just rickshaws everywhere. It's such a different world! It's wild, isn’t it? It makes you think about what you take for granted back home. Anyway, have you heard any gossip about these new teachers? Not really. I heard one might be American or something, but that's all I’ve heard.

Yo, Dad, did you hear about that stuff with the matrix's film? I mean, like, how it's super cool and all about how the world is like, not real? Oh, that's quite a deep subject. It's just a movie, kiddo, but it does bring questions about reality and perception to the surface. Goo goo gaga! No, but seriously, it's really interesting how it's keeps coming up in school, people talking about if our reality is just a simulation or not, you know? Even our history teacher brought it up in passing. And have any of you ever thought about what's the point of life? You know, big questions like that? Well, most of us have thoughts about that, even at a young age. But you know, your mum here, she might have a different take on it, right? Mummy! Mummy? Okay, okay, but no need to jump up just yet. Your uncle here was just asking about things to do with life and religion. But for me, perhaps I'd say that, no matter how we feel or what we believe, as long as we're kind to each other and ourselves, that might be the real 'point'. At least, that's been my takeaway from all the things I've learned and the people I've met. Yeah, I guess so. That makes sense. But what about people who believe in things like scientology or, I don't know, other religions? What's their take on it? Well, for each person, and especially in religion, it's a very personal journey. Some people find meaning in diving deep into one faith or practice, while others might try on different hats before finding what fits. The important thing is, it's usually about finding what brings peace and connection, whether it's through faith, community, or understanding the world around them. That makes sense. So, it's like, whatever works for you, right? Not quite that simple, but close. It's also important to respect others’ beliefs and not force our own views on them. You know how your grandfather used to talk about that? Yeah, the old man was pretty interesting. He always told stories about when he was a young man in the army and met all sorts of people with different beliefs from around the world. He said it made him realize how much we have in common.

Yo, mate, did you finish reading that paper for Uni? Nah, nearly there though. Been caught up with a few things at work, you know? You're always working, you've really got to pace yourself. Remember, the old saying about a tree – you can't keep giving without recharging. Haha, yeah, I've heard that but my projects just keep piling up. Well I'd be there for you if you need a break. Speaking of keeps changing, I've started taking up dancing lessons. You'll not believe it, sweetheart, but I've always wanted to be more graceful. That's really cool! You're so quick to just try new things. How's it going? It's harder than I thought - oh we're on the wrong road aren’t we? Sorry, I didn’t realize. No worries, no worries. What about you, you've got your football training on Saturdays, right? How's that going? It's great! For a guy who doesn't usually stick with sports, I've surprised myself. It’s different training when you're focusing on the fun of it all, rather than pressure to perform. Absolutely, that balance is key. Have you seen those videos of people dancing on their way to work? I'm working on doing some of those moves in my free moments. I love those videos, really lifts your spirits! They’re so cool, and they have fantastic energy. Exactly, and who would’ve thought it? It’s great for exercising that creative side of the brain too. Except, I've been struggling with remembering all these different steps. More steps than in engineering? Haha, kidding. Haha! You know me too well. So, are you planning any holiday trips soon? We're thinking of going to Cornwall next summer. You know how much I love the sea, and the kids would love it. Cornwall is beautiful. You’ll love it, take me too next time. Definitely! You’ll have to show me those engineering and health things. Yeah, I'd love to. I've been getting into more medical research. I started reading about new stuff in surgery using 3D printing. It’s mind-blowing thinking about how it will affect medicine. Sure, but I suppose it makes sense given that you're a consultant engineer. Exactly, I think combining engineering and medicine is really where the future of healthcare is heading.

Okay so apparently these are some super cool places to visit in Istria. There's this little town called Motovun that's famous for its truffles and art fairs. It says they have the most beautiful old town squares and a fantastic view of the Mirna River Valley. Ah, yes! I've actually been there before with my husband. It's truly idyllic. And the truffles are fantastic. You must try a truffle dish while you're there if you can, they're a must-try. Truffles? Like, like the ones in Sons of Anarchy? No, sorry, Mom—no guns required! What's that like? Do you get to dig them out of the ground? No, not exactly like Sons of Anarchy, but you can actually take tours where they'll show you how truffles are hunted. It's quite interesting. For me, the view is the real highlight. Have you two seen how these little towns blend seamlessly into the countryside? It’s breathtaking, the way nature and architecture mix. Speaking of which, we should really stop by Groznjan sometime. It's another arty little town but it's more laid back. We could take a stroll through one of their small art galleries, really get a feel for local life. That sounds dreamy. Have you taken part in any art tourism there? Or is it mostly for the locals and the backpackers? It's open to everyone. During peak season, they have festivals and the entire town transforms into one big outdoor gallery. It’s really a must see, if we can time it right. Art festival? Like, with music too? Can we combine that with a music festival then? We could crash a few of those, right? Well, if we can align these plans. But I have a better idea. Why don’t we suggest we stop by at the end of the trip? Maybe we can catch an evening event if it doesn’t conflict with other plans. That’s a great idea. I've heard about the Pula Arena. If we head towards Pula later, the festival grounds are across from it. We could catch both the history and the modern art atmosphere. But now, let’s enjoy where we are. I see we're approaching Rovinj... should we stop and explore the old town or drive through? I say we definitely stop. There’s the St. Euphemia’s Basilica to see and the old town architecture across the narrow streets is quite picturesque.

Yo, lads! How've you all been? We're all good thanks, just been super busy with uni and stuff. Yeah, Uni is a lot to take in. Still trying to get used to this whole adulting thing, isn't it? Yeah, totally. It's like a whole new world. Speaking of which, I've been meaning to show you guys this game I've been playing. Oh, which one? It's called Squirrel’s Escape. Hilarious fun, really makes you think on your feet. That sounds good, share it with us next time we all meet up, yeah? Sure, sounds like a plan. Also, have any of you watched that new episode of 90s football analysis? They talk about Leeds United there, you might be interested. Leeds United? That’d be brilliant! Yeah! But I was actually looking this up, on that new episode they've got a whole analysis section on Sheffield United's comeback. I didn’t see that. That's interesting, I'll make sure to check that out. Speaking of Sheffield... have you guys heard about the new recording studio they opened in Doncaster? A friend of mine has been using it and says it's amazing. I'm dubious. I'd be curious, though. Doncaster does need some cultural upgrades, lads. Totally agree. It’s time for Doncaster to step up in the arts and culture sector, you reckon? Definitely. The town’s got a lot of potential. Yeah, but who’s going to invest in something like that? Good question. Maybe we can start by talking more about it? Like, who's interested, what would we do, etc. I like where this is going. We could take advantage of local initiatives or crowdfunding if needed. We could show our friends, family. You could even talk about it at uni, raise awareness. We could also do more regional stuff. I mean, there are local events but sometimes they feel... not very Doncastrian or whatever. I know what you mean. Sometimes I feel that there's too much focus on the bigger cities... True that. We could also look at DIY events, low-cost, locally sourced stuff. See if it takes off. And it’s a great platform for us to gain some experience too. Brilliant! Let's pool our minds together and see what we can come up with. We’ve got some brainpower here!

Right, so I'm going to treat myself to a Greggs's pasty today. Nothing beats their Northern Spice and Cheese, and Manchester has some of the best Greggs around! I love a good pasty, isn't it the perfect lunch option? But I swear, they do vary depending on which branch you go to. That's true, I remember when I worked in Manchester, right near the Trafford Centre, I'd grab a pasty before or after my classes. There was one store that really nailed the consistency of the hot water crust pastry, but another one on the other side of town – well, let's just say they were fan's of very loose pasties. Sounds like you're a connoisseur of Northern pasties then. I never thought about making pasties at home. Anyone ventured into that territory? Actually, I tried during the lockdown, following a recipe from a food blog. It wasn't terrible, but it was definitely no Greggs. There's something about the way they cook them in that commercial kitchen that gives them a certain something. I'm with you, homemade pasties are never quite the same. It's like anything coming out of a motorway service station – it's about the whole experience, not just the food itself. Yeah, it's about the ritual – grabbing a pasty on the go, maybe sitting outside in the sun if it's one of those rare warm days, really enjoying the food without much fuss. That said, I did discover through my efforts at pasty-making that getting the pastry right is the hardest part. The secret, as I found out, is keeping it very cold before you roll it out and handling it as little as possible. That's useful to know! I've tried making the pastry for other things – like pies – and yes, cold is key. But with pasties, you want it to be pliable but not too soft. Speaking of good food making, did either of you hear about that new bakery on the university’s second floor? They're offering workshops on how to make traditional British treats. Might be worth a look, given our line of work. Ah, that's the Bridgewater Bake. I've seen the leaflet they put out. They’re offering a pastry class soon. I might consider signing up. I've always been curious about how certain types of pastries are made.

I've been meaning to ask you lot about this. I've been meaning to set up a group chat for all of us at work to discuss work-related matters and perhaps even share some of our personal life. Social networking platforms have really evolved haven't they? That’s a great idea, questions are easily asked and answered over there. Plus it keeps everyone updated and connected. But do you think setting up a work-related group chat might also give you more work to manage, you know, answering all the messages and stuff? As librarians, we're actually really supportive of information exchange. It could indeed be an interesting solution to improve our internal communication – and keep everyone in loop with the day-to-day running of the library. Right, but what about ensuring our work life balance, we can't be staring at the phones even outside work, can we? Hence the importance of setting boundaries. I totally agree. We need to be careful not to blur those lines. But, there are ways around it, like setting specific office hours for the group chat. That's what I was thinking too. Perhaps we could schedule a few times a day and only discuss work-related matters during those hours. That might help maintain some balance. Good thinking, guys. Also, in terms of the medium itself, I was thinking we could use something like Slack or whatever platform the university already uses. Should we propose this to IT? Possibly, but it's always good to discuss in advance any changes like this with IT to make sure we're in line with company policies and security. I'd say doesn't hurt to reach out to them. On the topic of work life boundaries, does anyone else ever use social media for work, beyond just keeping up with news in the library or LIS field? Ah, of course, we are librarians after all. I've even attended some professional development webinars via Facebook Live or LinkedIn. And recently, I joined a group on LinkedIn dedicated to library services where we share best practices and occasionally discuss job openings. Interesting, that’s something I hadn't thought of for professional development. I tend to keep my personal Facebook separate from work, but I do follow a few library memes for some comic relief. Oh, I know which ones you mean.

Ah, I see you've seen the latest proposal for the business case. I'm still getting to grips with some of the figures, but from what I've gathered, the key rationale for the new location of the hospice seems to be the growing population in this part of Kent and the strain this puts on the existing facilities. Exactly. You've hit the nail on the head. As the population expands, so does the demand for elderly and palliative care services, right? We need to plan ahead, really. The local health services are already feeling stretched even with the current capacity. This new location would not only alleviate some of that pressure but also allow us to provide a more comprehensive service – offering not just end-of-life care, but also day services and respite care. That's a great point, but ensuring our planning reflects the needs of the local community is also crucial. Have you had any feedback from the local authorities or other stakeholders? We've had some positive feedback from Tunbridge Wells council, actually. Their response highlighted the need for a forward-thinking approach to end-of-life care. But we've also received some feedback suggesting that their priority at the moment is on recycling facilities and new housing projects. So, they've got their hands full with different projects. Makes sense. I suppose this kind of planning would also require working closely with the existing local hospices? Absolutely. We can't just parachute in without making sure there's effective cooperation and coordination with local healthcare providers, including hospices. We're looking to forge strong relationships with existing hospices, as well as with charities and community groups. It’s all about ensuring a seamless and continuous care experience for the patients. Which brings up the question of how the new hospice might look. Any particular design or operational model in mind? We're thinking of creating a more community-based, garden-style setting that incorporates a focus on both comfort and function. Ideally, it should be warm and inviting, while also allowing for various treatment modalities and communal spaces. That sounds like a great approach. I’ve seen similar models elsewhere working really well. It might also be good to include some advanced facilities – I know there’s been a lot of interest in innovative ways of providing care at home. Exactly, indeed.

Ah, I've been meaning to catch up on some non-fiction. I have "The Power of Now" by Eckhart Tolle on my wish list. Ever read it, Dougie? I finished that one quite a while back. That's a great point, Dougie. And I think that concept applies even more broadly. Now that I think of it, it explains a lot about our preconceptions and judgments based on past experiences rather than the current situation. The guy has a great way of bringing it home. Absolutely. Do you also follow any travel or hiking blogs? I've become quite interested in them lately, especially the ones focusing on less touristy areas. Oh absolutely! I follow several, but really enjoy  Affording Travel  by Ankur and Vasudevan. They're always writing about these hidden gems around the world and tips on budget travel. It was breathtaking and we were one of the only people there. I can imagine! The Highlands are full of secrets just waiting to be discovered. We should plan a hiking trip up there for the summer. That sounds great! It was lovely the other day. We ended up having this wonderful conversation with a local farmer about the history of the land.

Instead of just listing your qualifications, tell them why you're passionate about this particular area of architecture. Show them what drives you, and what you can bring to the company. Okay, so instead of saying "I designed a green roof," I should be saying something like "As someone invested in sustainable architecture, the green roof project I co-designed at university was a complete game-changer for me.

60-69, M, British, dialect: UK, England, South, Eastern_engl, born in Norwich, civil engineer , graduate, long-term unemployed. - 70-79, M, British, same dialect, born in Costessey, retired without work, keeps to himself mostly. - 60-69, F, British, similar dialect, born in Harrow, childminder , with Sixthform education, also long-term unemployed.   Conversation:        Ah, well, you know the way things are going these days, makes one wonder how we managed before all these new-fangled changes.      Quite right, old chap. For me, it's the youth. They don't seem to appreciate the foundations their parents and grandparents laid for them. I remember the '60s and '70s, everything was simpler, perhaps more to the point, more predictable.      Possibly, John, but isn't that a bit of a romantic view? Life was never easy, even back then. We might not have had the "problems" we have today, but they were different problems.      Indeed, dear, you're right of course. But it's the pace of change and the seemingly lack of control over our lives that irks me.      Exactly! Things move so fast now; we can hardly keep up. I still find myself turning to the physical newspaper for my news. Can't seem to wrap my head around everything these digital platforms do.      I know what you mean, but it's also about adaptability, isn't it? I've taught children who knew more about technology than their parents did. It's a double-edged sword; you can't stop progress, yet sometimes it feels like the world's spinning too fast.      That's a good point, Sarah. But thinking back, when I was working as a civil engineer, there was change, alright—but often it was incremental. We could see it coming and prepare. These days... I feel like we're all just along for the ride.      I remember when Norwich was still a center for manufacturing. People had work, youth had apprenticeships. Now it's all about service jobs and retail. Don't get me wrong, I’m not one to turn away from progress, but it seems uneven, doesn't it?      Uneven indeed. And it affects housing too, doesn't it? Rents are through the roof, especially for younger people. I've seen it with some of the families I worked with as a childminder. Those big cities—London, but also even places like Norwich—are becoming less and less attainable for most young people.

Right, so I've been thinking. I believe we've got a great opportunity here to really upscale The Brix and make it a go-to community space in Brixton. What if we converted that unrealised studios space into a community centre where local artists could run workshops or classes and people could rent it out for events? We could even have some kind of store selling local art and crafts. But first, we need to make sure it fits the fire escape standards and arrange maintenance and storage... right? Absolutely, and it’s a fantastic idea! We'd want to get a reputable contractor to check out the fire escapes before we start, and storage would be a good plan – we seem to always be running out of space here, despite our efforts. Perfect, speaking of which, have you noticed the carpets in the meeting rooms? They need to be replaced. And the seating, perhaps some new sofas and chairs could add a homelier feel? Definitely. Ron, our volunteer, seems to have a knack for these things. He refurbished the office furniture last year. Maybe he could help with that? Plus, he or even a local college could help us generate income this way. A side project for them, and good exposure for The Brix. Brilliant idea! And while on the subject of generating income, what if we began a subscription fee model for regular users, or even started a crowdfunding campaign for the space conversion? We already have a nice following on social media, especially since our bird-watching group is growing so popular in the area. Crowdfunding, I like that. And with the bird-watching group, I wonder if we could create a window into the garden from the new space? There’s always birds flitting about behind that wall. Plus, with the right marketing, it could become the next big thing in Londontown. Oh, the birds. Our local feathered friends do bring in a lot of visitors. Just this morning, there was a group of school kids here, really interested and respectful. They asked so many great questions. You know, it's things like this that remind me why we do what we do – it’s not just for us, but for the community. Couldn’t agree more. And speaking of the community, how are we with our relations with the other tenants? We have those B and B’s upstairs, and the yoga studio...

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to explain what a "bubble and squeak" was to some of my non-British students? They were all confused about why we're still making something out of scraps. It’s just tradition, right, but also kind of heartwarming. I remember once, I had to do a "Pembrokeshire Puff" workshop and I'm like why, why do we still make these? It’s so time-consuming, but it’s still a part of our culture. You know, it's fascinating, isn't it? Even with all the modern world, we still cling to these recipes. Absolutely! I mean, even here in England, the food we cook in the southwest is so specific to the region. And each region, everywhere has its own traditional dishes. It’s incredible, really, how the food can tell you where a person is from, or where they grew up. Exactly! I travel a lot for work, and every time I go to a new place, or even just a different part of the country, I try to stick to eating local dishes. It's amazing how much different regions have in common, but how specifically they've developed their own unique recipes. I grew up eating Welsh Rarebit all the time. It’s a bit different from the traditional cheese on toast, isn’t it? Like, my grandmother always said that, you know, the leek and the cheese, it really is a recipe from another time. Speaking of comforting food, have you guys tried the salt beef done right from Morecambe in Lancashire? I just tried it for the first time last year and was amazed at how tender it was. Oh, that's interesting! I’ve heard it’s supposed to be quite a famous dish. You know, working with our charity, we often get food donations and it's interesting to see the different regional specialties. Our people used to make salt beef a lot, but it's not as common as it used to be. It's like that with so many recipes and dishes right? Some of them are dying out, others just adapt to new times and ingredients.

Yo, mate, did you seen any of that new advert from Weetabix? On the telly? Yeah, it's been talked about a lot. Ah, thanks so much for inviting me over to your place, Susan. It's been ages since we last caught up and I must say, your flat looks lovely. Thanks, I've been working on it bit by bit. Remember that time we went to Japan and almost got hit by those school kids on bicycles? Oh, yes! We were so close! They were all shouting 'Gomenasai' as they cycled by us! You can't really go kayaking or rowing without proper rain gear. I always recommend going to the outdoor gear shops here in Cambridge, they have the best selection of water sports clothing.
