I've been trying to keep up with my own fitness from home now that I'm working from the London office. It's tough because sometimes it feels like the day just lapses away into nothing when you aren't looking. But, it's good you're staying motivated! Exactly! That's why I thought about it. Someone should be organised enough to handle a massive event, right? Definitely. It's all about setting goals and holding yourself to them. Speaking of which, how's your relationship with Alex still going? You mentioned last time we spoke that there were some troubles. Ah, Alex... It's complicated. He's nice and all, but I sometimes feel like we're not on the same wavelength. Like, sometimes he really understands where I'm coming from and supports me and all that, but other times, it feels like we're from different planets. Yeah, relationships can be tough. It's like we're on the same page one day and then things just shift and you're left wondering what's happening. Have you talked to him about how you're feeling? Yeah, we've had some conversations but it doesn't seem to change anything. Maybe I just need to accept some things as they are or decide if it's something that really works for me in the long run. Definitely talk it out but also listen to what your gut’s telling you. It’s important to feel seen and understood in a relationship. You're right, of course. It's just hard. I've always invested so much in this relationship and the thought of potentially having to re-evaluate it is scary, you know?

Alright, James, you've got your pizza. Look after today's delivery driver like you do with every Domino drive. Well done! Auntie, you've really understood our ritual by now! Did the pizza arrive on time? Of course it did! That’s the Domino’s guarantee, isn’t it? I wish they could make life guarantees like that, as easy and reliable. Aye, that’s a thought. Back when I was hauling livestock, we had our orders to deliver, but not quite as quick as your pizza! Oh yes, Uncle, just like you have your trucks, Domino’s have their vans. But faster and cleaner! True enough, lad! Though I prefer my work with the animals. Still, it's fun to see you liking these... Pizza drives. It's his only Friday night excitement, between homework and sports. Sometimes I think you're more excited than he is! Uncle, it’s just different! We don’t often get to try new pizzas while the rest of the family is busy. It’s our bonding time. Aye, bonding time. Well, I'm happy to support you both as long as you show the same commitment to your studies and activities in return. Of course, all work and no play and all that! But seriously, James is holding up his end well. Very true! And I like the new toppings they have here. Maybe next time we could try something different? That’s a great idea. I noticed a new vegetarian option. You could try that or even the new Hawaiian. While you’re at it, a pepperoni for me. You sure know how to pick toppings! Uncle’s classic! But Auntie, I have a question. Do you think my haircut looks alright? I didn’t want to bother you last week when you were busy. Your haircut looks fine, dear. It’s the same style I’ve had for years, and I think it suits you well. But if you want a change, we could look at some pictures and get something new for you during the Easter holidays. Hmm, maybe that could be a good idea. Just to... be part of the Easter celebrations, I suppose. Absolutely! And speaking of Easter, how’s your school project going? Going great! We're working on a history project about what Easter might have meant for our ancestors. It's fascinating! There’s so much to learn.

I've decided I need to try and visit as many regional pubs as I can before I turn 30. It sounds bizarre maybe, but they're just so quintessentially British. You know? I completely get it. There's something special about sitting in a traditional pub with a pint of real ale and a plate of pub grub. Absolutely. I'm actually planning to start with those in and around Sunderland, where I'm from. Which pubs do you think I should definitely visit? Well, I don’t know those pubs particularly well, but have you considered the Black Bull in Birchwood? It's supposedly been around since 1870 and has a bit of history. Brilliant! Yeah, I've heard of that one. What's it like? From what I’ve read, its food and ales are very well-regarded, and they often have live music. But, it depends on your type of pub experience. Some are more beer-focused, others more food. Beer-focused sounds good to me! I love a good ale, especially if it's locally brewed. You’re definitely going to want to try 'The Shipper' if you're in the area. It's a craft brewery right in the heart of the city. Ah, excellent. I’d been wanting to try some of those craft beers. Craft beers have really become popular over here, and they have fantastic local flavors and unique notes. I'm also curious to try some regional pub dishes. There’s always this rumor about the ‘maggie pie’ in the Northeast. Oh, I’ve heard of the ‘maggie pie.’ It’s just a meat pie, right? Yes, but apparently, they put this special layer of potato on top before baking. It's said to be really good. Sounds interesting. I was reading about British food traditions and I found out that the concept of a 'pie' is actually quite popular. Funny how different regions have their own versions. Exactly! And if anyone does British comfort food right, it's the North-east. The 'pie and peas' is another favorite... but this 'maggie pie' sounds worth a try. As for greens, are you still doing your five-a-day? . You know me too well. I did try making a bit of a resolution to eat more veg but any suggestions on how to make them interesting? I heard of a vegan guest recently at a local restaurant who raved about their 'vegetable baskets.'

Alright, I don't think I've ever seen Grace so determined to win a game of Articulate! No kidding! She's not just playing, she's really diving in. It's like she's been practicing all week! I guess that's what happens when you have a bit too much time on your hands! Now, don't start, Glyn! We know she's been up early every day to watch episodes of “Pointless.” Oh, don't mind him! He's just jealous because he got tripped up by that 'accessibility disabled' word just like the rest of us. Well, it's a tricky one - "accessibility-disabled" is definitely a modern phrase. It's a very good word, actually. It's nice to see the game reflecting current social issues. But, I must admit, this game does make me wish I had watched those educational shows more. For once, we're glad it wasn't about history or geography! Those were always Glyn's strengths. Glyn, you don't even count St. David's Day as a historical event, right? Oh, shut up. I'm just as good at religious festivals, especially if they involve leeks and daffodils! That's right, "Daffodil Day" is likely to be his next winning term! Perhaps we could use that one for our next round if it comes up. But the point is, this game is definitely more fun together as a family! I agree. We don't get to do this much as we live far apart usually. It's great to have this time and it really makes me realize how much I value the little things like these game nights. Absolutely, family time is precious. I'm sure we can all agree on that. And it truly brings back memories of those childhood game nights we had with our parents when we were growing up. You could even say it's like... a bit of a 'throwback', maybe? Yes, and who knew we'd learn so much about “Influencer” terms too? Sure, but I suppose it makes sense given that nearly every social platform uses that word nowadays. It just goes to show how far we've come in terms of what terms we consider common now. Yes, youth culture is so quick to adopt new words. I've been trying to keep up by having fun with what we call successful challenges – what we've decided to call “Lexi-quests!”

Alright mates, let's get this game started. Who else is still up for a game of cards after all this delicious dinner we've had? You know I'm always up for a game, especially after that lovely roast! But shall we go for something simple, or do we want to mix things up and try something new? I'm all for a simpler game right now, perhaps something with no strategy required. Sounds good to me. We've had enough complexity discussing school stuff all day, right? Definitely. I wasn't sure if we'd manage to avoid talking shop among family members. How about a round of UNO then? It's fun and easy to pick up again after a while. Sounds fine by me. Though I hope no one holds it against me if I cheat occasionally for the fun of it! Cheating is practically encouraged on family game nights. Now that we have our game, who has the cards? I brought the cards. Do we also need papers for scorekeeping? Oh, nice! I'd take scorecards as an extra challenge. Keeps it competitive and in good spirits, really. That's a great idea, thank you! So, we're going for UNO, scorecards, and "minimal cheating" as the rules. That's settled. Now who's got the most beginner’s luck tonight? You're asking the wrong person. I’ve won all family game nights since I was a teenager. This is where we really test our family dynamics then. Let's shuffle and deal! Ah, 29! That's definitely lucky. Did anyone else get a lucky UNO? Wait, hold on! I got a wild card! That must count as cheating since we're adults. I thought we agreed to minimal cheating? Oh, you've got to share that one, then. That's what family is for, right? Though we must keep score, I'd say it's cheeky but clever. Groaning! But that still puts me ahead, right? Well, only if you keep it up. Speaking of families, have you all heard about that new community centre opening up in Cardiff next year? Yeah, heard about that. They even mentioned something about some of the leadership positions? Yeah, I saw that too. Maybe we could even try out some new roles or volunteer there? It could be nice to give back to the community. That would be a great idea.

Oh, did you guys see last night's episode of "The Crown"? I just can't believe how far they've taken the story from the real history. Yeah! I was like, "Is that even true?", but it's drama, so I guess questions are kind of irrelevant now. Honestly, that's why I'm glad I took a break from TV and focused on my accounting coursework. It's so much more... factual. Hahaha, I can imagine you immersing yourself in balance sheets and accounts, very realistic. But seriously, I think "The Crown" does a great job of blending history and fiction. It gets people interested in the real history, right? Definitely! It's a great conversation starter with family too. My grandma was talking about how the actual royal family would react to it last Christmas. She couldn't believe the Queen would ever swear like that. I know! But it's funny, it's almost like a whole separate world. I mean, I'm studying for my graduate entry exams right now. It feels so different from what the show portrays. Yeah, it must be so intense. But hey, have you thought about what you'd like to do after university? Like, do you plan on starting as a trainee accountant or something? Well, that’s definitely a thought. I've been looking at apprenticeships in accounting, it seems like a great way to get experience straight away. Plus, it'd be a bit less daunting if I'm planning to enter the job market. That's smart, I did an apprenticeship for a local firm. It was a tough but rewarding experience. You learn so much more practically and personally meet people in the industry. Also, it helps you decide if it's really what you want to do in the long run. Definitely. I've had friends who went straight for jobs after graduation and some who decided to take a gap year. Personally, I’m lucky my job is quite stable, but I can see the benefits of both paths. What about you, you being in the military job, would you say your work and university studies were closely related or totally different? Hah, you could say that. I focused more on engineering at university for my engineering degree, but my work is more about systems and... well, naval combat systems to be precise. But sure, there's a connection with troubleshooting and problem-solving that helped.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I drove from Essex to Glasgow? Not that I remember, Sylvia. What happened? Well, I was just starting to drive, and I thought I’d be daring and go on this cross-country trip. It was in the 70s, of course, so the roads weren’t as good then and there wasn’t as much signage. I had a map, but still managed to get lost several times! I can't imagine! Oh, it was a nightmare! I must have been driving for 10 hours just trying to find the right road. And did you finally get there? Yeah, eventually. But I was so exhausted when I did. You should have taken the train, Gran. I was young and curious. I wanted to see the country for myself, on my own. I love driving when I’m not in a rush. It’s pretty relaxing. Where did you go after Glasgow? Ah, the Highlands, the Lake District. It was beautiful, but I must admit, I did love to stop at all those classic English pubs along the way. Did you ever think about cycling instead? I always hear that’s quite the popular thing now, especially in the countryside. No, sweetheart, that wasn’t really on the agenda back then. Cycling wasn’t the same then. Nowadays, people are more health conscious and cycling is lovely, isn’t it? It is. I’ve had my fair share of cycling trips, especially in and around Cuckfield. But I’ve always found driving to be more practical for grocery shopping and such. Grocery shopping. Yeah, for sure. Oh, don’t be so glum, Raymond. It’s just a small part of life. Gran, you’re right. There’s more to life than just grocery shopping! That’s right. Like these lovely family dinners. You know, I’ve been thinking... Maybe next week we could plan a family drive or bike trip somewhere close? Me? On a bike? Oh come on, Raymond. It might be a bit of a challenge, but it’ll do you good, and we can all go together. Groovy! I thought we could do a day trip to Cambridge. There’s some lovely cycle paths and we can take a picnic. Sure, why not. If you can handle me on a bike... It’s a vote then. A family outing! So, I’m thinking this area from Grantchester to Cambridge.

I've just been to Wales last year. It was fascinating to see the number of languages they have. You know about the Welsh language being resurrected, right? Oh yeah, but I've never actually visited Wales. I've only read about it. The idea of a country with multiple languages is quite intriguing, isn't it? It's not just about Wales, though. I've had the opportunity to study how languages have evolved in diverse cultural contexts. For instance, the Basque Country in Spain. You'll find it fascinating how Basque, along with Spanish and French, have coexisted for centuries. Basque! Absolutely, it's such an interesting case study. I read that Basque has a lot in common with Celtic languages. And the preservation of it has been quite remarkable, despite all the history of migration and influences from other language groups. That’s true. I wonder how it continues to thrive today in the digital age. Spain has done a good job in supporting linguistic diversity, I think. For sure. We've seen it happening across the world - from Wales to the Basques, from China's myriad languages to the languages of indigenous peoples in the Americas. It's about sustaining the language and cultural identity at the community level, which is also why we can't underestimate the role of local government initiatives and language policy. Speaking of China, it's one of the most fascinating cases, really. With dialects that can differ so much, and all those minority languages. I always find it surprising how different the Mandarin doesn't sound in different regions. Exactly! Just last month, I listened to some recordings of rural dialects in China and it was like a completely different language. The diversity is just staggering. I just wish more people were aware of it. The thing with languages is that they are so much more than just communication tools. They carry culture, heritage, and identity. It's heartening to see how passionate people are about preserving these. I hadn't looked at it that way before. It makes sense though, isn't it? And it's not just about the official languages; the dialects and local nuances are such a rich part of the culture. Yeah, and it's not just about preservation. There's also innovation and evolution. In London, for instance, you'd hear so many different languages and dialects, it's like a city that acts as a melting pot.

Oh, mates, it's been ages. I have to say though, the last few years have been quite eventful. Remember that viral Facebook ice bucket challenge? Had the whole family down on my mum's garden, getting soaked. Oh, that was hilarious! Especially when dad nearly froze his foot off because he didn't let us warm the water up properly. "Practical jokes" they call it, right uncle? Yeah, and it for a good cause too! keeps coming back to how it actually raised awareness and funds for ALS research. Exactly! Speaking of causes, have you guys seen any of the recent charity campaigns that've been making waves? Might have to give to a new one. As an admin for a dental practice, I'm always getting leaflets and such. Hence, I'm kind of aware of some local initiatives, but nothing that really caught my attention as much as the creative ones online. Right! And you won’t believe it but the recruitment company I work for organised something similar, a dress down-to-work day to raise money for a local homeless charity. One of my candidates even promised to donate all their income for a day for it. Wow, that’s amazing. You know in my job as a language instructor, we sometimes organise sponsored language courses for charities too. That's thoughtful, perhaps I could participate in one of those next time. For sure! But you should also consider the diet, I mean, you're always popping into that café round the corner for a Diet Coke… I know, I know. It's just hard to resist all those tempting pastries in town. More like hard NOT to resist. Listen, we all need to think about our health. Exercise is key. I joined a local triathlon and it really changed my life. That's impressive! I might aim for a charity fun run next year – I heard there’s one for the local hospital. Either way, it's good to hear we're all finally putting health first. It does get harder to summon that energy when the little ones are around. Totally. Even as an instructor, I meet many parents who struggle with advising and guiding little ones towards healthy habits. Oh, definitely! My niece and nephew are always asking me why I don’t play tag with them as much anymore. I suppose I’m getting old...I mean, senescent.

Ah, I can't believe how much of a hassle it's been getting these removals sorted. The removal company is charging us an absolute fortune! I don't know how people even afford moving these days. I know what you mean. Especially now, the cost of storage is outrageous too. I'm working on transcribing conversations for this company that specializes in property and moving companies. It's amazing how much profit they make out of our relocation pains! I had to deal with moving very large equipment for work when I was in the oil industry. Think about it - whole cargo containers full of stuff to move, and it always was such a hassle. But at least then it was part of the job. Now, moving in your personal life, just trying to fit your whole life into a couple of trucks, it can be horrendous. [chuckles] Well, your job sounds fascinating though - you must have learned so much about logistics and organizing big operations. Oh, you have no idea. But even that experience doesn't help much now. It's just another reason for resignation - how businesses and companies exploit or prey on people's necessity. [nodding] Yeah, it really gets under my skin the way certain companies just see moving as an opportunity to charge excessive prices. They don't even provide reliable service at that rate. [looking around the kitchen] Speaking of hassles, hasn't our coffee machine been acting up again? I swear, no matter how carefully we use it, it still clogs up. Oh, the coffee machine! Yes, it's like some kind of temperamental old creature. Always problematic when you really need it. Last week I had to use my son's ancient coffee maker from college to make some coffee for visitors. That reminds me. Did one of you see any ads for decent coffee machines in the area? I keep looking for a more reliable one but everything seems overpriced or poor quality. Not that I've seen. But you might want to check online. Sometimes online reviews can save you from buying a dud. True. I might just do that. Online reviews can be really helpful. But it just adds to the whole process - so much research for something so simple as a coffee machine. [chuckles] This is what modern life is. Even choosing household appliances feels like a major project.

Oh, Mum, I haven't seen you in ages! It's so good to catch up and actually talk without rushing. Nor me, darling. There's just so much to talk about now that we have the time. How's life in your new job as a TEFL teacher? It's been a roller coaster, but I love it! I’ve learned so much and met some lovely people. I had a class with a very lively group last week — even managed to get through a whole lesson about Christmas traditions without too much chaos! Oh, Christmas is always such a busy time for TEFL teachers, isn't it? Everyone wants to talk about it, even if they're not exactly Christian. Exactly! But it's also so nice, hearing all the different perspectives and how Christmas is celebrated worldwide. Yes, it's wonderful for cultural exchange. What about you? How's the rest of your life? Is your partner still nursing and his job at the uni still hectic? So, yes he's still a nurse and yes, his shifts are still quite demanding. But he's holding up well and I’ve adjusted to the TEFL schedule now too. And the kids? How's your week with the grandkids been? Oh, they're delightful! They were here Friday for a baking session – we made gingerbread houses. It's chaos but it's absolute joy. That sounds lovely! Alright, I'm green with envy. I always feel like I'm missing out on some of the fun stuff. Don't worry, we'll have you and the kids over for dinner on the 23rd. We can have a proper family Christmas dinner the day before festivities officially start. Plus, I've always wanted to teach you my grandkids a Welsh Christmas tradition or two. Yes, that would be great! I'd love to hear about it! We could even make it an English-Welsh Christmas festival! Well, that sounds like a plan! Let's say we do that and make it an annual thing, alright? Absolutely! And have you planned the big one? The family dinner on Christmas Day itself. Yes, of course. This year, the whole family will be here — complete with a little livestream session with the ones that couldn't make it. It's going to be a full house, but I love it when we all get together like that.

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about the time I discovered that the tin of Richmond sausages that I bought at Waterfields expired a week prior to when I actually purchased it? No, you've just reminded me! You bought those sausages at Waterfields because they're supposed to have the best and tastiest rolls and buns in the area, right? Exactly, that's why I bought them. But, turns out it was a bit of a keepsake for me alongside a whole bunch of useless information... knowledge about expiring sausages, that is! And what's with this pub, mate? This is the Poachers, in Gorse Covert. It's the best we've got around here. Though sometimes you get the locals here who talk about snoring as if its some sort of a tragic pollution. One of the old regulars, Dave, he barely speaks over his own snoring. It's like this constant battle between him and the world. I can imagine! I mean, it's funny how some people just never notice their snoring or even think anything of it. Yeah, and its even weirder when you meet people who apparently do it on purpose or don't even care! Speaking of, I still can't believe the handkerchief story... Oh, you mean the time you used a gran’s old handkerchief and didn’t wash it and then... ...you went to work the next day and everyone could tell what you'd done? Yeah... that one was just unforgettable. The smell was ridiculous. Honestly, Gary's handkerchief story could be a bestseller. While you’re on changing the topics, did you guys see that Andy’s done a new jacket? Andy, the one from Leeds? I thought his style was stuck in the 90s! He may look like he still has the Leeds nightclub scene in his bones, but this jacket... it's worth a look. Clearly, he's outgrown his previous fashion phases. Fashion or not, he still can't execute a handshake without it turning into a fist bump... that takes some getting used to. Yeah, fashion forward or not, some things are hard to change. Absolutely. Speaking of changes, have you guys noticed how much the area across the youth club is changing? It's all new apartments and fancy little cafes now. Right, it's like the entire character of the place is shifting.

So, how was your weekend? Did you manage to get some rest or was it just as hectic as usual? It was actually quite good, thanks for asking! I got some well-deserved relaxation. We spent some time at the farm. It’s just so peaceful out there. Oh, that’s wonderful! I sometimes wish I could spend a day out at the countryside, but my schedule just won't let me. Well, if you ever need a break from the hustle and bustle, you know where to find me. There’s nothing like a bit of countryside air to clear your head. That’s very kind of you, but I don’t know if I could handle farm work, to be honest. No, no, but just being there does wonders for the soul. What did you do this weekend then? Ah, I spent most of it working, as usual. But I managed to squeeze in a film night with friends and we saw that new mystery film everyone's been raving about. That sounds like a good one! For me, a more relaxing weekend would be hard to find, but I still managed to sneak in some reading. I love the way you can still find time to read. I often wish I could do more reading, but papers and reports keep me busy. Ah, the world of management is always full of paperwork. Speaking of which, how is your new project going? It’s been challenging but rewarding. We’re nearing the end of the initial analysis phase and everything seems to be falling into place. It’s great to see that my team is holding up well under the pressure. That’s great to hear! Managing teams can be tough, but it’s also a real privilege, isn’t it? To be able to watch your team grow and prosper. Yes, definitely. It’s really fulfilling and it makes all the stress worthwhile. I couldn’t agree more. I remember when I was first out of college, I was managing a small team at a local business. It was just as tough but in a different way. And later, running my own farm was a real challenge too. It sounds like you have a lot of experience managing people and projects. Well, you learn as you go, don’t you? Although, I still wish I’d have had someone to guide me sometimes back then.

So, how have you been enjoying your new job? Oh, it's been a whirlwind. I've moved from teaching primary to secondary, which has been a bit of an adjustment. The children are older, so the dynamics are very different. But they're all so keen to learn, it's been very rewarding! That's wonderful to hear. I've had the same kind of change myself, moving from teaching adults to tutoring language right here in Birmingham. I love meeting all the local people who want to learn English or another language. It’s amazing to see them grow in their abilities. That does sound like a fantastic change for you. I've had a bit of a language project going on in my spare time too - trying to learn Spanish. Really? That’s great! I've always wanted to try another European language, perhaps Italian. Hence, I hope to start soon. Have you found the learning process challenging at all? Yes and no. It's been tough, of course, but rewarding in its own right. I was never very good at languages in school, so I never thought I’d ever be comfortable speaking a new one this side of 30! But it's made me realize that different learning techniques work with different people. And it's made me appreciate the kids' struggles in my classroom in a new light. That's exactly the kind of thing I've seen too. Everyone's learning style is so different. I even had a course participant recently, who pointed out that she needs to see visuals as well as hear things to learn, which I’d never considered before. And that changed how I taught her! I wish more teachers weren’t afraid to try new methods. I've been looking at finding local language groups too, hoping to practice speaking more. Maybe we could meet up or join together? Oh, that would be great! I'm sure we could meet at a local café. Speaking of skills, did you hear that Sarah is getting married soon? Really? That's great! I knew she was seeing someone but didn't think it'd move so quickly. Yeah, they were both so surprised. And speaking of surprises, I have a baby on the way, which is so surreal. I thought I was going to have a midlife crisis, but it's been more of a midlife embrace.

Ah, did you see that robin's nest we spotted yesterday? It's practically an architectural masterpiece! Oh, yes! I did see that. It's fascinating how they work isn't it? All those grass and twigs, beautifully woven together. Exactly! And have you noticed the one in the apple tree over there? Yes, right there, under the branch. I hope they'll be coming back for it this year. You know, it's like they have knowledge handed down to them, isn't it? Even the young ones know exactly where to build. Absolutely. Though, have you noticed how different birds make their nests? Some are quite precise, while others seem a bit more... "relaxed" about it. Exactly! It's like some birds are the Kirsty Allsopp of the bird world! Quite right! Now, onto something entirely different - have you heard any news or seen much recently on bird feed? I’m thinking of perhaps putting out some more next spring. Not much from me, but I did hear that this year the peanuts seem to be particularly in demand. That's right, the last time I fed them, it was peanuts that went fastest. But remember, we need to be careful about how we set it up so the squirrels don't nab it all. Of course, all about timing and placement. And maybe we should consider a squirrel-proof feeder next time. Squirrels! They’re a right nuisance. But, if it’s any consolation, they’re great fun to watch, aren’t they? Very true. Speaking of fun, did you see those puppets I made for the grandchildren last week? Yes, I did! You’ve always had a knack for that sort of thing. I remember when... Yes, and I just decided to dust them off and put them to use finally. Speaking of which, have you given any thought about perhaps showing them off at the community center or something? It’s such a lovely activity and the kids these days don’t get enough of that stuff. Oh, that’s a wonderful idea! I might just do that. Maybe there could even be a workshop or something. Brilliant idea, I can see that going well. It certainly would bring some pleasure to the community and keep you engaged. Maybe even help us make some new friendships. Yeah, I've been feeling a bit lonely since retiring from childminding.

Oh, did I order anything else besides the grilled halloumi? I hope I didn't confuse the waiter with all the noise around. Don't worry about it, dear! The waiter isn't going to let you starve, even with all the chaos around. You've asked for so many things already and yet, nothing has been brought out. I guess we've been chattering too much, discussing everything except the meal itself! Indeed, we have. You know me too well. By the way, did you hear about John and Sian's recent misfortune? No, what happened? They're both so lovely. Sian's mom passed away last week. It was sudden, she never mentioned any ill health. Such a shock to all of us. Oh no, that's so terribly sad. Sian didn't seem very forthcoming about it when I last spoke to her. But these things are usually so private. Yes, quite true. And on top of that, John just started this new job on the mainland and they've both been adjusting to that. These busy lives with unexpected setbacks... I can imagine. They've always been good about telling us when they're stressed or worried, but we can't always know what people are going through. Exactly. Speaking of health, how is your brother in law doing? I heard he had some trouble with his hearing, couldn't hear you anymore. Yes, he did. He's actually considering getting a hearing aid now. It's been quite an adjustment for him and our family, but he's all for it. Late in life hearing issues really bring home how fragile the body can be. I understand. My dad went through the same thing and he swore he would never use one but then... he's never looked back. It's really changed his quality of life. It's interesting how these health issues can change our view of life's priorities, isn't it? No wonder some people seek out spiritual or holistic paths to handle such changes. Reminds me of shamanism teachings I've read about. Embracing the unknown and the interconnectedness of life. How about you? Ever gone on one of those new age retreats or anything? I did once try dowsing. It was a fun weekend course. I liked the connections it made to earth and the idea of destiny or at least guidance.

Oh, Dad, Mum, it's so great to see you both again. It's been ages. How are you both doing? We're doing well, thanks for asking, dear. It's lovely to see you. How's life in London treating you? She's settling in quite well, isn't she, dear? Though I'm sure you've had your fair share of chaos, what with the big city life and all. But that's how it goes, right? Oh, you have no idea! London's been a whirlwind, but I'm adapting. I've been really enjoying my project coordinating job. It's been challenging but rewarding. That's good to hear. And how's your project going? Is it related to education or something else entirely? It's a bit of a mix, actually. It's creative and very hands-on, which I love. We're working on refurbishing a local community space and it's coming along well. So, business as usual then. I'm sure this is a perfect fit for you. Now, tell me, any interesting stories from the job? Well, one of the most awkward moments was when our team accidentally painted half the wall the wrong color. We ended up having to redo the whole thing over a weekend. But you'd be surprised how much bonding we had during that time! Oh, bless. That sounds like quite the adventure, dear. But you survived, and that's what matters! Well, it's the little things that make the job interesting, I suppose. And you, Mum? How's teaching going? The students must be keeping you on your toes. They do! You wouldn't believe the skills some of them have. But personally, teaching's one of the most rewarding jobs. I love seeing the kids grow and learn. It really is a great career. Although I'm sure you're busy with your own work, but it's nice when you can manage to catch up with friends or go watch a game of football or such. Exactly! Did you know the Six Nations are almost upon us? I just read the fixture list. I’m excited to see how England performs this year. Ah, yes! Rugby. Always a highlight of the year. I went to a couple of matches last year. It was great fun. I know! And don’t forget the Six Nations also signals the start of a few nice family gatherings.

Yo, lads, have you heard of this latest Catfish's episode? I was nearly in tears watching it. Yeah, Catfish is so sad but addictive at the same time, right? Aye, I agree! It's a kind of sickly fascination we've got with these sorts of shows. Absolutely! But honestly, some of the stories they share are just... ruinous, you know? I mean, to think someone could set up a whole fake online persona and lead people on like that. Crazy stuff. Definitely, and it's equally fascinating and sad to see the reactions of the people being catfished, like they just can't believe what's happened to them. I read that in the latest episode, the girl was catfished by her best friend. Unbelievable. That's exactly what I thought! How someone could do such a thing to someone they supposedly care about, it's just mind-blowing. Yeah, and that's what makes these shows so compelling. They really strip away the facade this online world we live in creates. Exactly, it's a weird paradox, isn’t it? The internet bringing us together and driving us apart all at once. Absolutely. And do you remember the episode with the couple who thought they were in a relationship for years but it turned out to be all fake? It was a real tear-jerker. For sure. It’s all about empathy and realizing these "profiles" could literally be anyone doesn’t help much with that feeling of betrayal and the real human connection they thought they had. I don't understand how people can do things like that. Deceit just for the sake of it? I just don't. Neither do I, but it's clear they think they will never get caught, but nowadays, they usually do. True, but changing the topics slightly, have you all watched the newest episode of Jeremy Kyle? Not yet, but I’ve seen previews. Sounds like another explosive episode. Yeah, I heard it’s about family members who’ve sent thousands to a fake charity, and it’s about those internal conflicts and stuff. I might need to catch up on that soon. I heard it's quite intense. Definitely is! Those shows really get under your skin, don’t they? You feel for everyone involved and sometimes can't believe what people are capable of. Definitely true! But at the end of the day, whether it's Catfish or Jeremy Kyle, these shows bring real life issues to light and make us question how we interact with others and the internet.

I've decided I'm definitely going to study French during my next spare term. It sounds like it's going to be such a challenging language to learn, but I'm really looking forward to it. Ah, French isn't so bad now, is it, dear? But I do remember when you were learning German and you were always making fun of the grammar and the pronunciation. Oh, the German language... I had to laugh at myself when I found out that "der, die, das" still changes depending on its gender. You'll tell me to relax, but it's a brain wreck! Well, you have to remember that in your youth, the complexities like that don't seem as daunting as they do now in retirement! Yeah, maybe, but I still think German and French grammar is a bit of a puzzle sometimes. But you also love puzzles, don't you? And you're quite good at them. You'll do well, I'm sure. Thanks! We should go to Paris sometime, see if my newfound French skills can get me anything but a silly look. Where did you go in France the last time you traveled? We went to Paris several times, but also to the south. The Côte d'Azur was beautiful. The sun, the food... and of course, the people. You'd love it. And you'd talk in French, as good as your Italian is getting, by the way! I don't think anyone would ever mistake me for a native! Do you have any good stories from your times in Italy? We've talked about your artistic career, but less about your travels. Oh, there was one funny incident... we were on a train in Italy, and we were speaking in English. Suddenly, a passenger next to us starts speaking in perfect English. She was from Trieste! We ended up having the best conversation about art and culture, and after a while, I asked her if she could talk in some Italian so we could practice for our upcoming art workshop. She obliged. We laughed about it so much, mixing Italian and English for hours! That sounds like something right out of a movie. Speaking of art and cultural exchange, have you kept up with any language learning or are we just reminiscing about languages now? Language learning? Well, I've always tried to keep up with languages in general.

Oh, don't you just hate it when the traffic is like this? These idiots driving! I really wish people would learn to indicate properly. What did you just say now? Irritable, as ever, I see! I'm just saying, it's not rocket science! You know, when you're on a two-lane road and you need to pull out, sticking your indicator on at the last possible minute isn't just rude, it’s dangerous. People should be more considerate. Considerate? You’re a student and you’re telling me this? Alright, alright... Well, I’m more concerned about the side view mirrors. Some people seem to think they’re just decorative or something. Oh, don't even get me started on that. I once had to parallel park and the guy next to me... He nearly drove into me because he didn’t see me, all because his mirror wasn’t adjusted properly. Look, it’s not just mirrors or signaling! These modern cars with all their tech… sometimes it's safer not to have too much of that stuff. I went to pay for an appointment and I ended up typing everything in because the system wouldn't work. I reckon Windows 8 just added more stress. Don’t even say that now, young thing… You and your generation always complaining about the tech. Yeah, but seriously, it's a bit more than that. I’ve been in these new cars and I have no idea what half the buttons do. "Nav! Nav 2? 5? Again and again." Five hundred and ninety-nine! You just have to press it 599 times! Ah, but seriously now… You know I’ve realized though, that old Sat Navs never had... ...Navigation? Exactly! They just had maps and your sense of direction. But youth of today… You’d get lost without a Sat Nav saying “Turn at the next blue door.” Well, it’s true. We found ourselves on a wrong road last week trying to find the house, because the Sat Nav mispronounced the street name. But what can you do? But we still managed! We just used the phone, like my mum taught me. Your mum was right, as she often is. Your mum and I would have been hopeless without phones. They’d have equipped the police with phones before driver training. But, you know, even with all these phones, sometimes it feels like less talk and more distraction.

Ah, marvellous weekend we've had haven't we? The weather was just right. Felt like we were back in the 70s again. Indeed, it has been lovely. I've spent most of it in the garden. Nothing like fresh air to clear the mind, although I do have a bit of backache today. Speaking of the garden, have you noticed how the daisies have started to bloom early this year? Yes, they have. Seems like nature's got its own rhythm now. I've been meaning to get out and do some gardening but, you know, the body just doesn't want to cooperate anymore. I’m sure you're getting your share of rest just like me. You're right, but when you've spent your whole life making sure other people's days were properly started and ended, it's a bit difficult to fully retire. Still, it's been good having you here. You’ve kept me quite company. And you’ve done it for all these years. Childminding can't have been an easy or a lucrative job. No it wasn't, certainly not financially rewarding but it was very rewarding in other ways. Watching the children grow and seeing them learn new things every day. It made the long hours feel worthwhile. Absolutely. Though now, let's face it, we’re both at a stage where the jobs we had are simply not an option anymore. How are you finding it in retirement? It's quite a transition, I'm finding. Haven't gotten used to having all this time on my hands. I keep trying to find ways to occupy myself, but nothing seems as engaging as childminding was. I know just what you mean. Before I retired, I worked at the local market, mostly doing odd jobs, nothing too strenuous. I used to keep myself busy, but without that structure, it feels quite empty sometimes. I've noticed we both speak a lot about the past. It's good to sit back and reminisce but maybe it's time we make the most of these years too. True, we should, but it's hard to find something new to get into when we've had a lifetime of routine. Perhaps we could try something new together? Like perhaps a painting class? I've always wanted to learn but never had the time. That's a good idea.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you listened to that new album from The 1975 yet? It sounds so different from their usual stuff but I think it really grew on me after a few listens. Yeah! I listened to it a couple of weeks ago. I'm not sure I agree it's that different though. I'd say it still has that characteristic The 1975 sound. Oh, it definitely does. But like, it feels... darker and less upbeat than their other work. Right, I think the subject matter's a lot heavier this time round. They're tackling some pretty serious themes. Exactly! And while it's intense, I think they do it so well. They're really good at conveying those emotions. I'd say they're one of the few bands out there who can pull off a concept album and make it feel cohesive and engaging. You couldn't say that for everyone, for sure. No, definitely not. Now that you mention albums... have you seen the new Foo Fighters album come out? It was different as well but I thought it was fun. Yeah, I did. I loved the Stampede of the Disco Elephants track, really catchy. Though I have to admit, their older stuff is still my favorite. Aye, same here. There's just something about The Colour and the Shape era for me. It's timeless. So, is the garden still blooming? I heard it's been a great year for all the plants here. Oh, absolutely! The weather's been perfect. Our roses are looking particularly lovely. The variety we planted last year is now fully mature and it's just stunning. That's great! Gardening must be therapeutic after all the studying I've been doing. It's good to sit back and watch something grow without pressure of deadlines. It definitely is. Though sometimes it can be just as stressful as any other project. I've had my fair share of figuring out what's wrong with the hydrangeas and why the begonias won't flower this year. I can imagine. I've heard gardening can be quite frustrating when things don't go as planned. Exactly! But when it does go right, it's incredibly rewarding. I must admit though, this year has been pretty much perfect... except for the rabbits that keep trying to eat everything.

Oh, so I was reading an article about this fascinating study they did in the UK about unemployment and how education affects it. Have you ever heard about this? Ah, yes! I had a look at that, too. It's quite compelling – suggesting that even postgraduate degrees don't always guarantee job security or better pay, right? Exactly! I couldn't believe it, right? I mean, with all those extra years of studying and debt for my postgrad... I keeps coming across loads of stories about graduates not finding jobs in their field or being underemployed. It really makes me question the value of all that time and money, you know? 100%. I mean, even here in Cambridge, the job market can be really competitive. I've lost count of the number of job applications I've sent out since finishing my master's. It's scary sometimes, wondering if it's going to pay off. And that's not even considering the potential rise in university fees. Someone should be screaming about those, really. So, you were saying how the article suggested that this trend isn't just specific to us, it's across the board? Correct. The researchers found patterns across different regions. They pointed to the employment uncertainty as a substantial factor even within high socio-economic groups, like us. It's not just about the job market being tough, it's also about jobs matching what people study. Like when I study human resources and end up in research management, which is cool and all, but not exactly 'what I studied' if you know what I mean… Exactly! I mean, I'd like to think my PhD will make me more desirable in the future career market, but the truth is, it’s all a bit uncertain, isn’t it? It does make me feel a bit...disillusioned. You and I, we've both done a lot of 'useful' work on our own projects, but do you ever worry that it's more about personal fulfillment for us than actual job prospects? I think that’s part of it for sure. It does give us a sense of purpose, which is great, and it’s certainly a joy. But if I’m being honest, the financial struggle and job uncertainty can put a bit of a damper on that sometimes. Oh, absolutely. I remember when I was just about to start my postgrad, I had a big long list of 'career goals'... and honestly, any of the practical career paths that felt most 'guaranteed' just seemed so... dry.

I love this picture! Look at this one, mum! The kid is practising his magic spells, but he's not very good! Yes, that’s quite funny isn’t it? It reminds me of when your Uncle Alex and his friends used to get into all sorts of mischief when they were your age, right? Ah, yes, let me see... They were full of energy, always seemed to need a bit of supervision. You didn’t tell us about that. What kind of mischief? Oh dear, they were lovable naughty children. Once they thought it would be a hilarious prank to fill the neighbor’s garden hose with jam! That’s really funny! So, mum, was that the kind of stuff this book reminds you of? Well, yes and no. It’s silly fun but also kind of neat, the way this book talks about family. It’s not just about mum and dad, it’s also about step-parents and different kinds of family structures. Speaking of which, it got me thinking about our own family tree. Your grandfather never spoke much about his family but I wish you boys could have known them better. What do you mean? Yes, your grandfather’s family was quite big and spread out, unlike our current structure. I just thought, maybe we could do a family tree project with you kids. That sounds cool! We could write and draw everything down. Indeed. It might be a good way to learn about your family’s history and also understand different kinds of families. Some have just mum and dad, others have step-parents, single parents, or even three parents if you count grandparents! Gran, what about... what if we included things like we’re not together with dad? Does that make our family different too? Yes, it does. And that’s okay too. This book shows that there are many kinds of families and they all have their unique stories and love. That’s what I meant. Each family has its own special way. And it’s important to make sure we share those stories, both the good and the not-so-good because that’s part of our history. Maybe we could write that into a story. About different kinds of families and how they’re all special. That’s a wonderful idea! Why don’t we start with some notes? Even if it’s just for fun, collecting stories and ideas.

Yo, how's studying going over at your end? Oh, you know; it's been alright. Just trying to get through this final period before summer. Exactly. It's all quite stressful isn't it? Especially now, the days are getting longer and we're supposed to be studying. Totally. But have you tried any new tips or strategies to manage your time better? Yeah actually, I've started using this app to keep track of how much time I spend on each subject and it's been a game changer. Oh, that's really good! I might have to check that out. Yeah, totally worth it. Okay, so I wanted to talk to you about something else. Sure, what's on your mind? About body hair and shaving. I've been thinking I might start shaving more often. Ooh, really? Like, all over or just certain areas? Well, I've been feeling really self-conscious about my armpits and legs, so I thought maybe it would be less stress to just shave it. I completely get that. The last thing we need right now is one more thing to worry about. Exactly! But I've also been thinking... have you noticed how everyone's doing it differently? Aye, right, it feels like there's a new movement suggesting that women really don't have to shave if they don't want to. And that it's all just a societal expectation. Yeah, it's actually quite liberating isn't it? The freedom to make our own choices without having to conform to what's expected. Absolutely, but at the same time, I also feel... I don't know, it can be quite alienating if you do or don't fit within certain beauty standards. That's true. While I agree with changing the expectations and letting women make our own choices, there can be a pressure to conform to the new norm too. Like, if you don't shave, it's seen as being part of this new movement, but if you do, you're being too traditionally feminine or whatever. Exactly. It's like you're damned if you do and damned if you don't. Yeah. I guess my point is, it should just be about personal preference and comfort. If I feel more comfortable shaving, then I should be able to do it without fear of judgment either way.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you ever had your beer spill all over your notebook while working in the lab? Oh, well, that's just classic, isn't it? Yes, I have and more than once, I might add. There's something about the mix of science and ale that leads to unlikely incidents, and I suppose this is one of them! I can imagine! Speaking of science, did you hear about how they're trying to use alcohol to solve certain medical issues? Oh, like ethanol, you mean? Yes, exactly! They're testing it for its potential to dissolve certain types of plastics. Could be a breakthrough! That’s really fascinating. And in a way, it’s quite fitting. As much as I enjoy a pint or two, it's funny to think that one of the things causing such accidents could potentially help address a global issue. Absolutely, it's all about balance and context, isn’t it? You know, between the fun and the serious side of things. So true. Speaking of balance, have you been following the debates around alcohol use and young people in the UK? There's a suggestion that we might need stricter regulations. I have. I think it's interesting because we can't ignore the cultural aspect. In many places in the North like Sunderland, pubs are community hubs. But at the same time, there is a real concern about the level of binge drinking among certain groups. That's a fair point. I come from Birmingham originally, doesn’t have the same pub culture as the North but the issues are similar. The influence of environment and social groups can't be ignored. We also need to consider the issues of underage drinking and the availability of alcohol in certain areas. Absolutely. I've seen studies that show it's less about stricter regulations and more about education and making healthier alternatives available. Also, and this is where we should talk a bit about the football scene in Birmingham, there was this really passionate debate about racism in football. Did you catch that? Yes, I did. It’s something we need to tackle head-on. I’ve always found it disheartening when football players of different ethnicities face abuse from their own fans. It's just so appalling. I mean, I remember when I was younger and we would watch football matches, it was always a community event

Ah, marvellous weekend. I hope you've had a chance to relax after that exhausting exhibition at the Old Jefferies Estate. I must say, I talked to quite a number of potential clients who were interested in your extensive work with heritage sites. Oh, thank you for the kind words. It was quite a success, wasn’t it? But even with the increased interest, securing funds can be a challenge, can't it? There are just so many competing projects and I often find myself explaining why older buildings need particular care and maintenance to keeps its history and character intact. That's very true, but I've found that there's always a way if one is well-prepared. I have been working on a project of my own, trying to renovate an old listed building in our hometown of Stratford-upon-Avon. Stratford-upon-Avon? That's a treasure trove of history! What do you plan to do with the building? Will you be opening it up to the public? Yes, actually. I'm contemplating turning it into a small museum or perhaps a business space that preserves its original structure and aesthetics. I'm curious, what’s been your experience with heritage buildings? I understand you have quite a bit of experience with this, coming from a job as a heritage building consultant. Well, it's interesting you mention that. I do come across a lot of older buildings in my line of work. The most important thing I always stress to clients is to balance the old with the new. You see, if you keep everything exactly as it is, the building might not be functional and may fall into disuse. On the other hand, if you change it too much, you lose its historical value. The trick is finding that sweet spot. Yes, absolutely. I've been reading about the measured decay approach in conservation, weren’t you involved in a project that applied that method? Yes, we did use that method for the restoration of Denham House in Buckinghamshire. It was a beautiful project where changing the modern elements that didn't fit was more feasible than saving everything. It was all about making choices that were both historically sympathetic and functionally practical for the current era. That sounds truly fascinating. And I believe applying for funding was a large part of your project's success, wasn’t it?

I've been meaning to ask you, have you started your literature review for your thesis yet? Oh, talked about it recently. Got some of the main concepts cleared out, but I really need to dive deeply into the material next. It's a bit daunting, to be honest. It always feels daunting, but once you get started, you'll find it gets easier. That's probably true. And I got some really interesting resources from a seminar at a conference in Edinburgh last year. One paper about phonological variation in the East Midlands is particularly relevant to my research. That sounds fascinating. I did some work on regional accents and dialects during my postgrad. Really? Which regional accents were you working on? Mainly on the North East and partly on the Midlands, so the project had a lot of overlap with your interests. I studied the similarities and differences in pronunciation in various communities from Sunderland and the surrounding areas, for example. So, you were looking at the Geordie accent? Indeed, it's such a unique and delightful accent with its own colourful vocabulary and pronunciation. I remember this one speaker I interviewed, he told me he often says 'hyem' instead of 'home'. It's such a quaint local variation. Ah yes, I've heard that one before. Speaking of which, did you find any significant differences in the way folks from Sunderland and Newcastle pronounce certain words compared to those from surrounding areas like Durham or Middlesbrough? Interestingly enough, despite being geographically close, there were some notable differences. For instance, the Sunderland accent tends to retain more archaic features or pronunciations that have since died out in Newcastle or the surrounding areas. Fascinating. The local history and migration patterns probably play a huge role in those differences, right? Absolutely. Sunderland's insular position, surrounded by the sea, likely slowed the natural linguistic evolution that came with increased mobility and external influences. Definitely. It’s these kinds of intricate details that make linguistic anthropology so compelling. It can indeed get quite addictive. And speaking of influences, did you have a chance to go on the holiday you were planning to the coast this year? We did eventually make it! We went to Cornwall, which was amazing. The scenery and the accents there are so different yet still English. I've always found it fascinating how even within a small country like the UK, the dialects can vary so much depending on where you are.

"I've just got the menu for next week's school dinners and it looks like they're serving fish fingers and chicken nuggets again. You two remember what they were serving at Granny's the other day? "Oh, yeah! Granny made us lasagna and it was absolutely delicious! She said she took a new recipe from her old cookbook. "And she gave us milkshakes after. "That sounds like a very fancy picnic at Granny’s. School just can't compete with that. Speaking of which, did either of you get the money for the tennis tournament from your piggy bank yet? "I did, but it's £2.00. Do we need more than that for the registration and things? And what if we get in the top three? Do we get a prize? "Can we really get a prize? "Well, I don't know the exact details yet, but usually, the school does give out small prizes for the top finishers. But the registration is indeed £2.00. It covers the basic cost of the event. If you want to, we could set aside a bit more as an 'emergency fund' in case we need any more money for accessories or something. "Oh, can we? I'd like that! But what if we weren’t good enough and we don't get any prizes? "Yeah, and the piggy bank is empty now. "Don’t worry about it, even if we don’t win or get any prizes, it's about participating and having fun. That’s what sports are all about, right? "I know, but I do want some prize. "That's alright. But let’s focus on playing our best. It'll be fun either way. "Do you ever think clowns at the circus scare you? "No. I think they're funny. But I liked the jugglers and the tightrope walker more. "I know what you mean! And don’t you think being in the circus must be a really cool job? Not just the clowns, but all the performers. Maybe one day, watching them inspired you to learn juggling or acrobatics? "Can we learn that at school? "Possibly! We've had a guest come in before and teach some gymnastics basics. You could ask Mrs. Johnson if they plan on having more sports or arts workshops during the year. "That would be amazing! Can I even be a performer though?

I've been thinking about that film we saw last week. Did you really think it was as ridiculous as I did, or was I being too harsh? Well, dear, you've always been a bit of a history buff, haven't you? But I do think questions were raised that made us think about the way we teach history today, don't you? Absolutely. I've been thinking about it ever since. I've never been too impressed with how history is taught in schools these days. It feels so... sanitized. You know, all the interesting bits are taken out, and it becomes a list of dates and names. I couldn't agree more. When I was at school, even up to when I was in university, history was a lot more engaging. More than just memorizing dates, it was about understanding the context and the whys of events. Exactly! But now, it seems like it's all about rigid educational standards and meeting those benchmarks. It's so dry and doesn't allow for much discussion or debate, which I think is where the real learning happens. And that's what I've come across in my work as an advertising director. We're always looking at how to engage the public in meaningful ways. The current national curriculum seems to make learning history feel so... uninspiring. It's surprising, given how rich and diverse our history is. Speaking of engagement, did you hear about that debate at Cambridge? I read about it in the Guardian. An interesting piece on how they're looking at incorporating more practical, project-based learning into the curriculum. Oh, I didn't catch that. Tell us more! They're thinking of integrating more vocational aspects into the curriculum, lessening the divide between theory and practical application. I think that's a fantastic idea, really. When I was in school, getting some form of work experience was a big deal for us. It made all the difference and it really helped me decide on a career path. Makes sense. In advertising, every project is unique. You learn as you go. But for younger people, it's just as important to structure their learning so they can make those connections early on. It could also help students who want to go straight into industry, without needing to go through a university degree. That's an interesting angle.

Ah, mates, remember when we used to talk about these subjects? It feels like an eternity since we last met and just slumped about our views. You wouldn’t believe the stories I've uncovered since we last spoke, you know. Oh, I'd love to hear about them! I've been clearing out the old house, and I stumbled upon some of my grandad's war letters. It makes me think about how things have changed, doesn't it? Indeed! Speaking of keepsakes, I still have my grandfather's old armchair. It's comforting seeing that, surviving generations and witnessing history – wars, conflicts, all that. You know, I was going through some old family photos the other day, and there were images of our grandparents during the Blitz. It’s stark to see the contrast with today. Absolutely, man. It’s remarkable how we lived in a completely different world. And now, our children and grandchildren couldn’t imagine it. And it's not just the wars and this sort of stuff. We should also talk about our beginnings. The different parts of the country, the jobs we did… Yeah! For instance, I retired as a childminder, bringing up many a bright young mind. And Speaker 1, you know, never really worked as such, always struggled a bit, didn’t you? Ah, yes. Costessey was always a bit of a working-class town. I grew up surrounded by Norwich’s textile industry, but the factories closed and the jobs dwindled. Never found my footing, unfortunately. That’s a true story, ain’t it? I lived in Harrow, a very different world compared to Norfolk. Our family ended up in higher management, but even then, we were always aware of the struggles of others. That's why we all have such a strong bond, I think. We've all had our share of struggles in one way or another. But look at it this way, it’s made us stronger, better people. Speaking of strength, I recall when the police used to patrol more frequently in my area. There were more local bobbies, knowing everyone by name. Yeah, I remember those faces too. Always a friendly word, a handshake. In those days, everyone looked out for one another. That feels a far cry from today’s impersonal, tech-filled world. Sometimes I wonder if that’s improved things though… Wait, let's not get too negative, guys.

You know, Dad, even though the drive is usually quite short, I still can't quite believe this time. It feels like the end of an era, kind of. I know, mate. All these years and it's hard to believe how quickly time flies. You're really not just leaving mum's house, but a chapter of your life you've been in for as long as you've been alive. Yeah, just trying to wrap my head around it. Do you remember when we used to do these drives every week or so when I was younger? And going on camps and stuff with the family? Those were good times. Oh, those were some good times. But, let's admit it, you're growing up now. It's time for you to start your own chapter. I'm just glad we could do this drive together one more time before you leave. Yeah, I know. I just don't know if I'll ever be able to make it back here as often as I like now that I'm moving for my job. Aye, but there will always be Skype or Facetime, or as I like to call it, video calls. It’s not the same but it’s better than nothing. And don't forget, us getting older isn't a bad thing either. Means you're gaining more independence, responsibility and hopefully, you’ll make your own family one day. Yeah, I know, I'm just a bit nostalgic today I guess. It's normal, son. But you know you always have a home here no matter what. Thanks, Dad. I know. So when are you moving in at the new place? Did you get all the paperwork sorted? Ah, yeah. I should almost be there. Just got to finalize the job contract and the lease. But everything's been pretty smooth so far. Good. Always a bit of a bureaucratic nightmare when it comes to such stuff. Reminds me of when I first bought this house. How’s the mortgage anyways? Mortgages... they never change really do they? Still finding it a bit steep from what I initially thought. But the area seems great and the flat's close to the university, so I've made my peace with it. That sounds wise. I remember your mum's and mine, we were quite stretched as well when we first started out, but it does pay off in the end.

Right, so I think it's time we start making concrete plans for Mum's birthday dinner. It'd be lovely to do something special for her. Have you given any thought to where we could host it and what kind of menu we could prepare? Actually, now that you mention it, I was thinking we could have it here at ANON's place because it's spacious and close-by. As for the menu, I did some research and found some great recipes from the Great British Bake Off. I know how much Mum loves watching it. That's a great idea! She absolutely adores that show. She's always saying she wishes she could be contestants – always baking and cooking for fun. Exactly! I thought about preparing some signature dishes from different series, like the showstopper cake, some of the dishes that were part of the "Foodie" challenges. And maybe a traditional English dinner as a nod to her preferences. That's very thoughtful. Since she loves traditional English food, we could also have fish and chips or perhaps a Beef Wellington. But we should also consider her current dietary requirements due to her dementia. For sure! We should keep it simple and nothing too overwhelming for her. Perhaps just a few dishes to choose from, so she doesn't feel overwhelmed. And for sure, no complicated recipes. Also, think about the lighting and the seating arrangement to make it comfortable for her. Too bright can be quite jarring, right? Absolutely. A more subdued, cozy ambiance with maybe some scented candles, really set the mood and help her feel relaxed, and less confused. Photos of each dish, and changing the labels to something more identifiable could help reduce confusion. Plus, her favorite photographs up around – it might bring back nice memories and make her feel more at home and less anxious. Agreed. I can look for some of her favorite family photos to display.

Yo, I've gotta get my wisdom teeth out next week, I've been dreading this so much, lol. "Oh, look, I found these lovely lactose-free cookies! They're so nice isn't it? I knew one of you might have enjoyed them." "Lactose-free? You mean like no milk in them, Mum? Like in our yoghurts?" "Exactly, that's right! They're very special, just like you." "Could they still be fun for playing with? Like using them as money?" "Well, maybe not money, but we could use similar food items for another game idea. For instance, we could play a game where playing pieces are oranges, crackers, or cute little cookies like these. You have to move them across the board, and if you reach the end, you get to eat them!" "Oh! That sounds fun! But what about the ones that we use to make money with?" "Remember the chess pieces we've been using? They're quite nice as play money as well, especially if we assign silly prices to them. For example, if you land on a certain square, you get a 'chess knight', which could be worth two crackers." "Cool! So it's the same but with different pieces?" "Exactly, and if one of you can make the other pieces less important by the end, you win! But I just thought, maybe we could do something a little more fun tomorrow. Something to celebrate another culture or tradition. Since it's getting close to Chinese New Year..." "Oooh, Chinese New Year! Can we do something like that?" "Absolutely! I was thinking, for acts of kindness and because we're talking about money, maybe we could make some traditional Chinese New Year buns or dumplings and share them with the neighbours or maybe even have a mini party. It’s about giving and sharing, isn’t it? Plus, we could put little notes with good wishes inside, like we do with fortune cookies!" "That sounds awesome! But I heard Chinese New Year has dragons and stuff?" "Yes, it does! We can do a bit of a dragon dance outside, like the ones you might have seen in videos. I'll help us make some simple costumes and we'll make up a dance. We could also make a dragon puppet using old cardboard boxes and paint. You both love crafting, right?" "I love crafting! Can we paint them really bright colors, like fire and water?" "Yeah! And we can make the dragon's eyes shiny!"

Mum, I was browsing on the internet yesterday and came across an interesting online workshop about how to learn how to read books more efficiently. Do you think it's worth it? Ah, I was pondering over something yesterday when we last spoke. We have these wind turbine applications; these are truly insidious, aren't they? It frustrates me so much that the council doesn't see the full picture of how these turbines can ruin our countryside. Yes, entirely! That questions the competency of our local council really. You know, I've been following this local protest group fighting these planning applications, and it's incredible the amount of effort they're putting into it. But, dear friends, you have to ask - how far can we actually go with simply protesting? Is there not another strategy we can adopt? Oh, oh yes! What I was thinking last night was that maybe we should dive deep into understanding the various project proposals more thoroughly. Maybe looking for loopholes, or conditions that could be introduced to minimize the impact. We could compile scientific evidence on wildlife or landscape impact. Sometimes facts and data can sway decisions quite effectively. For sure! We could also perhaps reach out to local universities for support. They might be able to provide some diligent students eager for some real-world study while adding 'official' backing to our case. Stampeding over the politicians with facts is the way forward, isn't it? Absolutely, and while we're on the subject, I'd love to hear more about your engagement with the previous local group regarding the solar panel applications. What key strategies did you suggest and how did they help? First, we focused on socio-economic impact - clearly showing the potential loss of the area's tourist appeal due to 'industrialization'. But then, we dug into environmental impact, bringing in the fact that less land would be harnessed for alternative green spaces or agriculture if the panels were to be installed. Ah, I see, linking it back to tourism and the local economy. That could resonate with the council more than a purely environmental stance. It’s all about making them see the bigger picture, isn’t it? I recall in my experience of leading a company, we always had to intertwine our corporate goals with community betterment to get support. Maybe local business owners and residents could also show their concern, appealing to the council as stakeholders.

Right, so I've been reading about educating children on driving. It's fascinating how today's generation learns quite differently from how we did back in the day. Oh absolutely, and I've noticed that. Especially here in the UK, new driving laws have now required all new drivers to undergo some kind of formal questions before gaining their license. It seems like a safer way to go, don't you think? Yes, I think so too. But I remember when I learnt to drive, there was a very traditional approach with a driving instructor and an old Vauxhall alongside a lot of hands-on practice. Yes, indeed. Speaking of which, did any of you get any good deals on your car insurances? Well, my insurance is actually quite high due to the nature of being in a city, but sometimes you get creative discounts if you're a young driver, freelance language teacher type. Oh, that's true. And isn't it time we all think about our plans for the holidays? Anytime anyone plans anything interesting? Ah, definitely, Woburn Abbey and Gardens are lovely. I remember taking the children there when they were young. Such a serene place, and the walks are lovely. That does sound delightful! Perhaps we could make a family trip out of it. It might be a good change of pace from the city. Yes! Or maybe we could just have a country weekend. We always take too much stuff with us when we travel, but a weekend away would be nice. Again, agreed. Or perhaps you could go and spend some time at my brother's place in Wales.

Oh, Dad, remember when you used to take me to those horse races when I was a teenager? It was always such an adventure! Ah, yes! You were quite the keen participant. Right, I’ll look into that. Now, while we're talking about cities and planning, have you set up a Facebook page for your job search? I find that Facebook really helps these days for jobs, especially for people looking to connect with the community or groups related to their industry. No, I hadn’t thought of that! That’s a great tip, thanks. It’s good for those job searching groups and almost as good as newspapers were in my day. I’ll definitely look into that. And don’t worry, I’m also still thinking about how to turn my account into something that won’t bombard everyone I know with notifications every five minutes.

I've got an incredible story for you. I was at this Shakespearean acting workshop last week and one of the participants clearly hadn't read the script. He just turned up, and when asked to do a Hamlet monologue, he started reciting the Macbeth soliloquy! Every single word! Oh, that’s hilarious! And to think that the workshop centred around minimalist Shakespearean techniques! Exactly! The coach was so calm about it until he pointed out the mistake with the best sarcastic tone, “Ah, we’re focusing on Macbeth today. Slight difference.” Classic! I had a similar incident with a botched line delivery in my theatre class. The whole class erupted into laughter and our teacher just shook his head and said, “You’re on your own from here.” It's amazing how quickly the intentions behind your voice can be misconstrued, isn't it? Absolutely! It's funny because we're so often taught to deliver lines for the "right" emotion or tone or volume, but sometimes the best reactions come from this sort of on-the-spot improvisation. Totally agree. I reckon that kind of mistake shows the human element in all these performances. It’s awkward, but kind of charming. Exactly. It's all about making the best out of a worse situation, or in this case, turning a mistake into a moment. I've got one about cricket, actually. I couldn't hit the ball to save my life until my dad started calling me “Hitmaster” . It was the funniest kind of sarcasm and it actually kind of helped. I started hitting one or two more balls the next time. Oh, that's brilliant! The power of sarcasm and nicknames. I once had a nickname from my mates at college for missing penalty kicks in soccer. “Miss-hit Miller.” Not so flattering but it worked. It sure motivated me to improve. No way! I'm sure in another universe, I'm sitting there just hitting goal after goal as “Hitmaster”! It’s all about the meme of the moment, innit? Absolutely! Now, this leads me to wonder... Have either of you taken up any new skills recently or been trying to improve at anything? Well, I've been trying to learn to play golf. I just watched all these YouTube tutorials but I must admit, I’m more determined to “look the part” than actually hit the ball...

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about my week at work? It was a whirlwind. I've been working on this new conference and talked to at least three different caterers who each told me their chicken dish is the best in all the land and then the client changed the menu three times before settling on something completely different!
