But seriously, I think it's going to be good for all of us. That sounds great. And did you figure out the plans for the week? We were supposed to go to Aunty Carol's this Sunday, right? Oh yes, I’ve been meaning to finalize that. I assumed we’d still be going. Should we confirm the time? I think so. Just to make sure we're all on the same page. Also, how’s the weaning going? I know it’s been a challenge. Oh, you know how it is. One day things are going well and the next it's the baby's first reaction to solids or finding the right bottle again. Honestly though, seeing him try new food really warms my heart. More food for his growth, a few less tantrums at mealtime. Oh, I know that stage all too well. Last week it was like Timmy decided he was allergic to the world. But sure enough, he’s back to normal today. Exactly! It's all just part of the adventure. Speaking of adventures, have you spoken to anyone about the family trip to the Peak District? Not yet, but I've been thinking about it. I've got a few more free days next month if you're up for it. It's been too long since we all went out together. That would be lovely. Timmy loves the outdoors, and it's been... a bit of a blur the last year or so. We could use a break. Plus, it’s good for us to spend time away from this little area.

Oh, isn't this wonderful? I never thought these hills would be so beautiful. I know, right? You love walking in the countryside, don't you? It brings back so many memories, though a bit different for me, I've always been from London. Indeed, Norwich and London are quite different. I've grown up with these tall green hills, and I couldn't imagine not having them. Norwich is so much smaller and keeps its history really well, don't you think? Oh, yes. I love how each village here seems to have its own little history, and I've been really enjoying exploring them. This village near where we're walking is called Happisburgh - did you know it has a medieval village feel to it? No, I didn’t! I need to look that up. You know, when I was a child, I used to read books about English villages, and now I feel like experiencing them firsthand. It fills me with so much joy. So, do you think that growing up in a more rural setting has shaped who you are? Absolutely. I think it has influenced my love for history, the environment, and the slower pace of life. It’s a privilege to be able to enjoy the simple things like a clear night sky and the local wildlife without the noise of the city. A stark contrast to metropolitan London, but it seems to have kept you grounded, really. For me, I couldn’t have imagined anything else than living in London. The energy, the opportunity, everything was there. Well, it’s good that we bring different perspectives to our relationship. I often find myself wanting to escape the city to the countryside, and together, we get to experience both. That’s one of the things I love about us - we balance each other out well. So, what do you think of the walking paths here? They’re very well maintained. You'd think so, wouldn’t you, given that this part of Norfolk is popular with walkers. But actually, I know a few hidden gems if you’d like. There are some paths that are off the official routes which take you through tiny villages and show you the real unspoiled side of Norfolk. Oh, tell me about them! I’m always up for new discoveries. Alright, follow me! We’ll take a slight detour.

Oh, did you see that last Avengers film? I was so impressed by the way they wove that plot together. It was so different from what they've done before. What did you think? Yeah, I thought it was great! I loved the way they incorporated all the new characters and gave some of the old ones some really interesting backstory. Absolutely! It felt like they were really pushing the bar of what superhero films can be. And Thanos? He still stole the show. But even with how big those characters are, they managed to make room for some really interesting smaller players, like Thor. Totally, Thor had some amazing scenes, despite being absent from most of the third act. I think his line towards the end about the "Asgardians of the Galaxy" was hilarious - "Two words: galaxy. Asgardians." Yes, that's one for the ages. What do you think about the film's themes? I found it pretty philosophical. It's not often you get a superhero film pondering the end of the universe or the nature of time. Definitely. It's certainly provided some food for thought. The different universes and the consequences of actions across them was fascinating. It's a bit hard to wrap my head around but it definitely felt like a worthy progression to the story line. Agreed. And it's amazing how they can tackle such complex ideas while still delivering an action-packed blockbuster. Yeah, and considering we’re talking about a multibillion-dollar franchise, that's a real testament to the prowess of the crew. For sure. Speaking of jobs, how's your consulting work coming along? Late nights or things are going smoothly? It's been decent. We won a project for a local bicycle manufacturer so we're quite busy. It's exciting though - we get to do something practical that's actually making a difference in our community, rather than just serving a corporate entity. That’s great to hear! I'm all for supporting local manufacturing. Plus, I'm intrigued by cyclist culture and sustainability in general. Sunderland has some great spots for cycling by the way! It's getting quite the scene here, isn't it? With the cycling paths and such. Though, I've heard the infrastructure could still use a bit more work to keep up with the demand. Very true. I’ve heard some of the paths are a bit narrow and dangerous during peak times.

Oh, look at this pretty wildflower. I have no idea what kind it is, but it's so vibrant and full of life. Lovely, isn't it? Right out of a painting. It's probably a species of wild marigold – they love these open meadows. You'd think you'd have some knowledge about them, living up here. True, but I've always focused more on the cash crops and economics side of things when it comes to agriculture. These wildflowers are just a delightful bonus. Well, they're a subject of my research, actually. I've been studying the language of early British botanists to highlight how they described and perceived these very flowers. It's fascinating how language can influence our understanding of the natural world. That’s quite interesting. I can see how that would be a unique angle. We talk about pollution and environmental issues, but how we conceptualize the natural world in the first place is deeply rooted in our language and culture. Absolutely. I found some old texts where the word "natural" often meant something entirely different from what we think it does today. It was more about order and cultivation, rather than wilderness. Quite the paradigm shift in how we view 'nature.' Exactly! It’s a bit like how we talk about language families too. Do you know, I had a fascinating lecture about how all Indo-European languages have a common ancestor, much like how all these flowers here have a common ancestry, despite all their diversity. I'd love to hear more about that. Well, linguists have been able to map this linguistic family tree by finding similarities in grammar and root words across languages like English, French, German, and Hindi. It’s incredible to see the deep roots of communication right there. It’s funny, isn’t it? Language and plants are so intertwined in human society. From cash crops to concepts of language changing the way we view the world. It's quite poetic. We use words borrowed from agriculture for so many things: for example, "culture" from "cultivation." Absolutely, and it's also telling of how significant agriculture was to early societies. It still is. Economic development often starts with agriculture, yet it’s often overlooked. I complete agree. Just look around us – these fields are still the backbone of our economy. And yet, our thinking about them is often outdated.

Yo, mate, did you manage to sort out the tickets for the match on Saturday? Yeah, I managed to snag a couple of tickets. It's the Newcastle Match, isn't it? Aye, and I thought we'd go watch together – do something we used to do back home. You remember The Angel of the North, eh? Haha, that's the one! I'm right behind you on that. I'd love to see it again. Right, so, parking. That's always a nightmare. Wonder if we should try and park on the outskirts and walk – less hassle at least. Yeah, that sounds like a good plan. Not like down here in London where you can pay through the nose for parking but can't find a spot anyway. Exactly! Anyway, what's the exact time? I'll make sure to check the weather as well – didn't know how it would turn out for the weekend. It's 3 pm. And it should be sunny, at least according to the forecast. But yeah, check the weather closer to the day just in case. Also, I might be able to grab a few good seats, so we’re not too far from the action. Brilliant! I'm looking forward to that. I also really need to sort out the car – the break light's been faulty for ages and I need to get it fixed before I go. Oh, can I take a look? I'm sure I can help you out, and it might save you some pounds. That would be brilliant! But it's probably just a loose bulb or something. Though, last time I messed around with it, I might have made it worse. But the problem is less about the bulb than the whole sensor being wonky. Don’t worry about it – I’ve fixed a few cars over the couple of years. It’s just a bit of elbow grease and maybe some technical knowledge. But first things first, we need to sort out our football tickets. True – I’ll pay for them right now. Just give me a few minutes. Take your time. I’m on zero-obligation mode today except for sorting out the car. That's almost as bad as being a consultant. Anyway, job first, football later! That's the spirit. By the way, have you thinking about where we will be staying while we’re up there for the game?

Oh, did you hear about that celebrity's trial? I mean, what a circus it was. Whole town talking about it. Yeah, I've overheard bits here and there at work. I don't think I'll ever understand why those kind of folk get into so much trouble. Well, you've got to remember, everyone has their problems, and sometimes they just can't seem to stay out of trouble. Speaking of keeps coming to get into trouble, would you look at those geese in the park? They're always making such a commotion! Yes, they're a right nuisance, just like the celebrities. But you know, they're fascinating creatures in their own right. What's so fascinating about them? They're just birds. Oh, they are much more than just birds! Did you know they migrate thousands of miles every year? It's quite a journey. They've got instinct for timing and navigation that us humans can't even fully understand. I'm aware they migrate. But I didn't know the exact distance or the fact that most of them return to the same nests. Yes! It’s incredible. And the way they fly in formation - it’s like they’re coordinating an air show. Some species travel from as far as Canada to the Caribbean, avoiding hunters and predators, finding food and shelter along the way. An air show? That must be quite the spectacle to see. I've never been one for bird watching but that does sound interesting. It is! You should check out some documentaries or videos online. It’s really awe-inspiring the way they’ve adapted to survive. Plus, the fact that they keep coming back to the same place year after year, despite all they’ve seen or had to overcome. You know, it's things like this that remind me why nature is so amazing. It’s easy to get caught up in the everyday routine of our lives and forget just how wonderful and complex the world is. You’re right. We often take it for granted and don’t appreciate those kinds of things until...until we actually take the time to look. Just like with celebrity trials. People are always so quick to condemn. But if we took the time to understand the context, their journey, their struggles... Maybe then we'd have more empathy.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that job interview I had today? The school principal was super cool, but I was practising my lingual foibles before I got there and ended up saying "maths" instead of "mathematics". That's quite English of you! I had the same issue once when I first moved down to the Midlands, but my colleague just explained the region’s accent quirks right there and then. That would've been helpful! Anyway, keeps coming up in job interviews. You ever experience that? Yeah, actually. Like when I started teaching here, I had to get used to the local dialect. They say 'bairn' instead of 'child', for example. But it was lovely, really. Made me appreciate the regional variations more than I even did growing up. Ah, you’re so right about that. I love regional dialects, especially how they often carry history and culture in a way standard English doesn't. Exactly. And it’s funny, after you get used to the local way of saying things, you start to realize how it actually helps you see the underlying culture and identity. I completely agree. Where I'm from, the accent can change so much from town to town; it's almost like a linguistic map to the local history and customs. Absolutely. But back to job interviews – did you get the job? Oh, I don’t know yet. They said they’ll let me know in a week or so. And to be honest, I need it. Just been through a real rough patch, and the new job is the light at the end of the tunnel. I’m so sorry to hear that. But the fact you’re getting interviews is definitely a step in the right direction! And, if I'm completely honest, it sounds like you were doing your best despite the lingual hiccup. It’s just practice they want, really. That's a very comforting thought. It's easy to forget that when you’re in the moment. Plus, I think in these interviews, they often want to see how you think, adapt, and communicate, rather than if you get every single word perfect. You're right. I could have probably justified my "maths" slip as just being relaxed and real. You know how it is when you’ve been teaching for a while – certain terms just become part of your everyday vocabulary.

So, I've been thinking a lot about the future lately, coordinating things have changed so much since I started working. Yeah, it sounds overwhelming. I'm the same way. I mean, I finished my postgrad and got this admin job but now I feel like there's a kind of expectation to have it all figured out and I'm not sure I do. Exactly! It feels like everyone's prepped this perfect roadmap and somehow I'm supposed to know where I'm headed. Which is so not true! I've heard loads of stories about people not knowing until later in life too, but that doesn't make it any easier right now. Honestly, I feel the same. Everyone around me just seems to have it together. My family members keep asking me about retirement plans when I'm still trying to figure out my summer plans. And to be fair, even though I'm managing okay, it sometimes feels like being in a career that's sometimes not as creative as I'd want. And the pressure from potential careers or family doesn't help. I had a meeting with my director the other day and was firmly told that I need to develop a five-year plan by next quarter. As if! The industry I'm in is pretty cutthroat too, so while the pressure isn't about creativity so much, it’s about adapting rapidly and that feels stressful. I can relate. Well, technology-wise my work is changing all the time, but my role is more about being efficient and organized. I do enjoy the structure sometimes, but if I’m being completely honest, sometimes I wonder if there's more to me than just processing emails and organizing files. Well, there is more to you. For sure. Perhaps finding something on the side? I've started doing some freelance work in the creative field. It's just enough to keep those creative juices flowing and, surprisingly, it's given me a little perspective on my production role. It actually makes me appreciate certain things about my job that I wasn't really seeing before. That's so interesting. I've been considering taking some online courses or maybe volunteering. Anything to make me feel like I'm not just going through the motions. But it's hard when you feel like you should be focusing on 'advancing' your career right away.

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about that stupid lad called Billy? I swear he's more Jealous than a Manchester City fan after losing to Manchester United at home! Right! Jealous isn't the half of it! He’s like a one-man soap opera, isn’t he? Going on about who's dating who and who’s talking to who. It's like a full-time job! Honestly, I think he’s more troubled than a dog during fireworks night. But, on a serious note, does anyone else think it's a bit messed up to be that concerned about who’s dating who at uni? 100%. I mean, is it really that big of a deal? As if we can't mix with friends or whatever without having an affair. And to be fair, it's partly understandable, I want my space too, you know? Totally. But at the same time, it's good to spend time with friends. You can't just lock yourself away because someone's got or doesn't have a boyfriend. That would be really odd, wouldn't it? Exactly. Plus, if everyone's assumed we're up to no good just because we're hanging out, that puts a lot of pressure on the friendship group, doesn’t it? Absolutely. Honestly though, I think it’s also about growing up and learning to understand boundaries really. But it is annoying when people jump to conclusions all the time. I know what you mean… last week, I went for coffee with the lads from my course, and we were just talking about our modules, and oh my god, people assumed the worst. Oh, the blurred lines of friendship and ‘affair’. It's like everyone automatically assumes we’re couple goals or something. That’s so true! I swear, the world thinks we’re all on Love Island or something. Plus, I don't know about you two, but I find it really annoying when my friendship group gets split up because of one person's jealous boyfriend. Right! And it's like, if the person you're with can't trust you, then maybe there’s something worth asking about that relationship. 100%! It should be easier. But I guess it’s a learning process all round. I suppose it’s a part of growing up and understanding better ways of communicating, huh?

Alright, boys, who was the first one to finish their main course? Oooo, I think it was me! I love this fish. It's got the right amount of seasoning. Ah, well done, young Master! You and your appetite make us all proud. He's been right hooked on fish since... I don't know, forever! Yes, indeed. Fish it is! And, speaking of eating and appetite, have any of you been following the recent hockey match I saw on the news? The London Lions just pulled off an incredible comeback. Yes, actually! I saw a clip on my phone. It was pretty cool. Ah, was it? I didn't catch it unfortunately. What happened? They were down by three goals in the final period and managed to even it out. But the real magic happened in overtime. One of their players scored a beautiful goal from about 30 yards out with just 20 seconds left. It was nail-biting! Wow, that sounds exciting! What team scored the winning goal? It was a local lad, actually, from Birmingham. It wasn't a small feat, as I said, they were down by three goals, and all of them in the last period. Can we watch it later? Maybe we can look it up online and watch the highlights? That sounds like a great idea! How about after dessert? Sounds perfect to me. Just one more thing before we dive back into hockey highlights. How are your friends doing? Any new updates you want to share? Well, Ben is coming next Friday. I'm pretty excited for that. He's been saying he’s trying out for the school hockey team. Ah, so the hockey bug's spreading? Seems like it! And speaking of friends, how about our plans for the summer? I was thinking we might head to the coast for a bit. The weather's projected to be fine, and it'll be a nice break. That sounds lovely. I hear the coastal path along... ...along that little bit of coast is really scenic. Yeah, from what I've read; it's beautiful. We could take a tent, set up at a campsite, and just enjoy the sea for a few days. Ooh, camping! That would be a blast. Yeah, camping, seaside, fish for dinner... sounds like a family tradition is taking shape, isn’t it? Well, that's the spirit!

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we drove through this exact same area when we were at university? No, you never did! What happened? Well, it was the summer of 2010, and we decided to take a road trip from LA up to the Redwoods. We packed up the car, a very old and rickety van, and off we went! I can picture it. Sounds like it was an adventure! It was, but also quite stressful. We kept breaking down, and we had to pull over at this little village to get it fixed. The mechanic was this quirky guy who spoke in this very thick, almost like rural American English. Yeah, I can imagine the culture shock! What happened then? Well, we realized we were low on cash and had to go into town for help. The shop owner, an older lady, heard us talking and asked if we were alright. We explained our situation, and she kindly offered us a room in her guesthouse for the night. She was so sweet and this is where we spent the night before driving further into the Redwoods. That’s kind of neat, the way strangers can become such unexpected friends in a moment’s notice. Did she tell you anything interesting about the place? Well, she did tell us about a couple of secret trails nobody knew about. We explored those the next day. But the best part was that she really opened our eyes to life in the countryside, and all the stories and characters you meet along the way. I would love to hear more about those secret trails. They’re kind of hidden off the main routes, but they lead you through really dense areas of the forest, where you can see all sorts of wildlife, and the trees are so tall it feels like you're in another world. Sounds incredible! We should try to find those trails sometime. You know, it's funny how we never mentioned these trails to anyone back home because we were so caught up in our own little adventure. But now I really wish we had. I know, right? This trip is reminding me of that 2010 road trip and all the places we've been since then... Yeah, I was just reminiscing about that period. We've had so many adventures since. How is work treating you, by the way?

Alright lads, who was surprised by the Irish national rugby today? The way we ran those Wallies around was superb! Ye don't say? I was watching it with my mates at the match, and we were all stunned! We didn't see that coming. Indeed, it was quite the performance! I did enjoy watching that. Though I'm more of a fan when Ireland plays England. The matches are always so competitive. True, nothing beats an Ireland vs England game! But we've had our fair share of successes. I have to say though, your chicken kievs tonight were a bit of a surprise as well. They were actually really good, though I'm still wondering how you make them so crispy without using your usual pan-frying method? Ah, that's a well-kept secret! But, I'll let you in on it. It's all about the right amount of flour, baking them in the oven, and a good old bit of patience. You know, it's amazing how many different ways there are to make a basic dish like that. I remember my mum used to pan-fry them and they were always delicious but a massacre in the kitchen. Oh, absolutely! But this way, the kids can help prepare them as well, no flinging oil around the kitchen! Anytime you want tips on cooking, feel free! I'm always up for learning something new in the kitchen. Anyways, on to other matters. Did anyone hear about the planning for visiting the granny this weekend? She’d love to see the both of you again, and I'm sure you two would enjoy her warm hospitality. Oh, that sounds great! Last time I saw her we went out picking up hedgehogs from the garden. I was surprised they’re so cool to interact with up close. That's right, and she’s always got biscuits ready so we can snack all afternoon! Though if anyone is going to eat too much, it's me most definitely. There's always room for biscuits when it's with Granny! Just remember she might not enjoy the “backchat” as much as I do! You mean the banter? Yes, any type of banter you've got going. Though if anyone can keep up with my Dad’s jokes, it might be Granny herself! Yes, youth can't beat experience, can it?

I've decided I need more vintage stuff in my life. Got a bit carried away on eBay last weekend browsing through old cups and saucers. You wouldn't believe the tea sets I've seen! Carried away? You mean you spent hours going through questions on status updates and now you want to deck your kitchen out with antique cups? Exactly! It's not just about the monetary value... I love how they tell a story. Every set has so much history, even if it's just about a bygone era of tea-drinking traditions. That's quite romantic. But isn't collecting just stuff gathering dust? I’m more into meaningful experiences. Sent your friend to that local community market last weekend, by the way. Was good, but wish I’d known earlier - would have taken you with me. It was good, wasn’t it? I sometimes miss out on those things. But, you know, it was just a last-minute plan. Your friend texted you at the last second, right? For once I’m glad I didn’t have much planned. It was a lovely market. Lots of good food, quirky crafts… and I even scored this delicious buckwheat bread. Buckwheat bread? How was it? I keep hearing about it being healthier but never tried it. It’s good! Not too sweet, but has this really satisfying grainy texture. I actually used some of it in my salad dressing and it added this interesting layer of flavor. Oh, that sounds different. I might have to get some. Have you thought about if it’s worth bringing some to work? Everyone could benefit from healthier options at those leaving dos. Speaking of which, your leaving do is coming up soon, isn't it? Yes, in two weeks. You’re invited, of course. It’s going to be a smallish gathering because of COVID. But hopefully we can still make it fun. I’d love to come! Can we maybe arrange for some of that buckwheat bread as a surprise for the team? That sounds like a brilliant idea! We can make it a little parting gift or a treat for the team. You know I just realized something. You seem to enjoy collecting little bits of the past while I’m more about experiencing... I guess I feel our lives don’t mesh that way? On the contrary, I think these differences make our evenings like this perfect.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that money laundering business's owner who was just issued a huge fine? Yeah, it's shocking, innit? I mean, we've got a right to speak about this in Doncaster. It's just, the system, you know? Yeah, it seems like a big problem. Don't you think this is a part of a bigger issue? Exactly! It’s never just about one case; it says a lot about how even banks keeps money laundering alongside us. Crazy when you think about it. Absolutely! Even our own city’s not immune. These kinds of activities can affect everyone, even if we’re not directly involved. So, what about the kids? What’s the best way to teach ‘em about finance when they’re growing up? Good question! My mate did this cool thing with his kids, got ‘em a piggy bank early on, then when they were big enough, started giving them weekly pocket money. It teaches ‘em responsibility and saving. That's wise. I'm thinking this is a perfect moment to start giving some finance-related responsibilities to my sister’s kid. I’m sure she’d be interested in learning. That's the way forward, make ‘em understand money’s value, not just the concept. Absolutely, and while we’re on the subject, I always find it alarming how little people my age talk about their finances, really. It’s like it’s still a taboo subject or something. I know what you mean. It's like it's not just about the money itself, it's the whole environment behind it, banks, accounts, all of it. Maybe people feel the system is daunting or just lack the education in it. Totally right. I noticed a lot of my mates at Sixthform didn’t even know how to budget properly. That’s bonkers! I mean, changing the world takes individual actions. What if we did a little workshop for local kids or even adults on basic banking and money management? I’d like that, but realistically, it’s probably harder than we think. Need to find a way to make it engaging and inclusive. True. Maybe we can turn it into a workshop series or something over the summer. We could even involve local banks and services to make it more hands-on. That’s a plan! Maybe we could start a Facebook group or something just to get people interested and talking about it first.

Oh, did I ever tell you about the weather we had last week? The sun was shinning so intensely that I was half-expecting to see little green men from Mars coming down on Surrey Street. Ha! That's quite the vision, Linda! But speaking of weather, have you heard about the local charity fun run next month? Yes, did you know that they're using some of the proceeds to sponsor sign language classes at the community center? That's a great initiative. Really? That would be brilliant. You'll have to check it out, Mum. Oh, I've heard of that. Seems like a fantastic cause, just like the Sports Day happening at Emily's school. Ah, yes - Emily's Sports Day! That's going to be such an exciting day. She's been practicing the 100-meter dash non-stop. And I bet she's going to grab a medal or two. You know she's always been quite the competitive one. For sure! We should make it a family day out. We're planning to go support her as much as possible. I'll have to check my schedule. It's peak time at the store, so it might be a bit tricky. Oh, don't worry, the sports day is on a Saturday. We can shift our plans around. Can we also talk about your sign language classes, Linda? How are they going? They're going really well, thank you for asking. I'm loving every minute of it. It's so fascinating to learn about a completely new language and culture. That's great, Mum! Have you thought about what you might want to do with this new skill? You were always interested in helping out in various community initiatives. Well, I was thinking maybe we could use it to benefit the local community in Birmingham. There are several deaf or hard-of-hearing groups there that could benefit from some support. That's a wonderful idea. We could take classes so we can learn too, and then we could all work together to create an event or project. Or perhaps you could teach a class once a week or just volunteer. There's always a need for more people to learn sign language, especially in local communities. Exactly. And it would help raise awareness too. So many people are unaware that sign language is a fully-fledged language, like any other.

I've heard of Cambridge University Press, but I have never actually been to their printing house before. You must have a really interesting job being an assistant editor there. Oh, yeah, I love my work! It's so diverse and it's great to see all the books go from being manuscripts to final publications. I've got a similar story. As a publishing assistant, I get to see the publishing process from a different perspective, but I don't get to be as involved in the editorial side. But even so, it's really rewarding to know that our work contributes to knowledge and literature being shared with the world. Definitely! I had a lot of fun last week when we did our week of non-fiction books. There was this one book about the history of Britain in the 19th century that was just fascinating. What about you, Speaker_4? What kind of publishing you enjoy most? Well, my experience is a bit different. As a temporary publishing assistant, I've worked across different projects and it's been a great way to get experience in various areas. I love the diversity, but if I had to pick a favorite, it would be editing children's books. There's something special about working on content that will potentially influence a young mind. That's lovely! I studied linguistics and I'm actually involved in language research, so I'm always fascinated by how language is used in different contexts, including children's literature. In fact, I've been looking at phonological development in children in Britain, particularly in the South East area where we’re from, and it’s really interesting to see how language can vary even within relatively small regions. That's so cool! I've always found regional differences in vocabulary and pronunciation really interesting, especially when I was in university. Did you come across anything surprising in your research? Oh, absolutely! For example, in areas like Kent and Essex, you'll find unique vowel shifts and certain words used that aren't common in other parts of the country. While I was studying, we even had a project where we went out to conduct phonetic fieldwork, recording native speakers in different age groups. It was incredible to see how pronunciation can vary across just a few miles, let alone throughout the entire country. That sounds like an intense but fascinating project!

Yo, mate, soo what did you find out about the visa application? I'm getting a bit worried we might not be able to get everything sorted out in time. Oh yeah, I've been looking into it and it isn't as bad as I thought. You just need to get your application in at least 4 weeks prior to the trip and then make sure you've got the right kind of passport photo and some decent fundraising evidence to show you can afford it all. Right, fund-raising. That's always the tricky part, innit? Think people would actually donate if we tell 'em we're going to Mongolia for a charity rally? Idk, mate. I reckon if you're in your early 20s, going to Mongolia for charity is quite a radical idea. You'd be surprised, though—people do support bold adventures, and especially charities. Maybe so, but we'll need some good looking photos and a strong pitch. Absolutely, good photos are key. We'll need passport photos. Someone should probably go to their next council meeting or something, see if they have a booth for this. Right, or we could even just get them printed from somewhere like Boots or The Body Shop, while we're out. They've got the right size photos at all the photo booths now, right? Yeah, or we can print them ourselves at home if we've got the right A4 paper. Speaking of which, we should really start placing ads on Gumtree for more donations and to find potential supporters, don't you think? That’s a great idea, but I'm not sure where to start with advertising the event. We might need some help finding the right kind of words to use, you know? Right. Saying we're just "going to Mongolia" won't lure anyone. We should mention what it's for and how it's for charity. Maybe couple it with a quick brief about the charity and why it's important. Makes sense. Any other ideas on getting more donations? Like, do you think it would be weird to ask local businesses for sponsorship? Not necessarily. If you can show them how it'll boost their local image, publicizing their name with our charity cause, they might bite. We should definitely include that in the ad. And maybe we can even post about it on social media?

Oh, did I ever tell you about last night? I ended up in the hospital because of my arm. No! What happened? Did you slip and fall or something? Just kidding. I kind of hurt it playing basketball with the guys from the uni sports team. I went to the hospital, they said it's fine, just a sprain. I was quite proud of myself for falling in front of everyone. Right, let me guess, you're blaming it on those new 'gym rat' friends of yours? Well, blame it on who you want, I just wanted to try something new. Everyone says we're in uni to have fun, right? Hence your stellar gymnastics skills you were showcasing the other day? Well, it was just an ill-advised grab for the ball. Guess it wasn't the best idea, but hey, I'm okay now. Okay, okay. So, how was the rest of the night? Did any fun happen despite that? Yeah! We had a bit of a hangover, but we packed up and went to get some grub at the uni's café. It was nice, you know? A bit chaotic but, you know, uni life isn't dull, right? It’s all part of it. I'm just trying to plan a nice quiet Friday night myself because I'm feeling pretty tired from midterms. You're not on your own there. Late nights can really take a toll. Did you sleep okay last night after that rave you were at? If by okay, you mean woke up before dawn with my phone buzzing non-stop and then couldn't get back to sleep because my mind was racing about my exams. Don't worry, you're not alone. Our generation loves to multi-task and overcommit, but it's alright to say no to things sometimes. 100% with you there. I could use a relaxing night myself. Maybe we could just chill in the kitchen and recover together? Since when did you become the wellness guru of our flat? Since late night company and conversation seem to be the only cure for the emotional rollercoaster we call university life. Alright, alright. Cooking together, that sounds like a good plan. What if we make something simple? Like pasta, or are there any new recipes you've come across? I did see this amazing one for vegetable fried rice, it seems simple but it was actually quite good.

Oh, did I ever tell you about the grousing Grace did today? She's quite the comedian. She was carrying on about how she's never talked so little in her whole life! Made everyone laugh. Ha! She just can't help herself, can she? I heard questions were flying left and right today! Yes, they were! "What did you mean by socialism?" "Explain artificial fractals!" All very advanced for GCSE! That sounds fun! Do you think she really understood all of that, though? Well, she's sharp as a tack but I think she was just pulling our legs. She's just trying to sound even smarter. Ah, that sounds like her! What about little Jack? How did he do? Oh, Jack did alright. He's looking for a challenging course next year, thinking maybe a STEM pathway? Really? That's ambitious. Is he good with that stuff? Yeah, he's quite the whiz kid. One moment he's building a robot and the next he's diving into the mysteries of quarks! The boy has a true curiosity. I remember when I used to think the same way. Maybe I should have stuck with it... Don't say that! You're doing great in your studies as it is! You should be really proud. I guess so. And what about you? How was your day leading the exam? Well, it's the usual checks, balances, making sure all the marking is fair and on the mark. People often forget how much the integrity of these exams relies on people like me. But it was just the usual. Do you ever wish you did something different? Sometimes, but teaching's in my blood. I loved it, but marking exams gives me a different kind of satisfaction. I guess you do it every year – do you find some students stand out? Oh, always. There's always one or two who are just exceptionally gifted or who persevere against all odds. It's wonderful to see. Yeah... I had one of those in my class this year. She was always so eager. I hope she does well. Likewise. And don’t forget, you still have a part to play in that. Your mentorship counts a great deal. I suppose. We had that earthquake drill today, you know? Remember? How could I forget? You looked so serious, pretending to drop to the floor.

Look Dad, we nearly forgot the water bottles. I was about to panic when I remembered I had this one in the bottom of my backpack. Ah, brilliant, because we're driving for ages isn't it? Through hundreds of miles and all those little towns? Yeah. I hope there isn't too much traffic. And do we have a plan for lunch? Think about something not too hot to eat in the car, right? Right you are. We can stop at some services. There'll be food there. Might just grab something to eat and carry on. Do we have pens? I need to do a bit of writing for my geography project. Pens? Of course, kiddo. You're always sketching or writing something. Let me check. Ah! Got it! Oh, I found the pen. And I think I have a few pens here too. Only if they don't run out, or better yet, if they don't explode everywhere like that time in Geography class. Alright, alright. Exploding pens. I remember that. By the way, have we planned where to stop for coffee? There's one just before reaching Cornwall called Holland and Barrett. You know, the one with the decent coffee and lovely views. Holland and Barrett? For coffee? Oh, I didn't know that. Yep, they’ve got a really good espresso machine. That’s a good idea. But not too much, or I might end up having another bout of IBS like I did on our last trip. Ah, sorry about that, didn’t mean to bring it up. We can just order something light and see how it goes. It's fine, Dad. Just something to keep in mind. But it's interesting how food has such a big impact, huh? It sure does. Food and travelling – two of life’s pleasures that can collide in less-than-pleasurable ways sometimes. Yeah. Speaking of which, we've been planning this move for ages, haven’t we? Been thinking about what to buy, how to arrange the house, and all that. Mhm. It's a big change, but we'll get through it. We’ll make our new home a home. And maybe we’ll have a least a bit more space, like that manor house you’ve always wanted to visit in Cornwall. Oh, that's right! Those big old places with history and everything...

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to transcribe that really boring talk from that conference last week? I swear it was thirty minutes of someone explaining the intricacies of bureaucracy in local councils. You do love questions like that, don't you? Ah, that sounds like the perfect pre-dinner conversation right there, isn't it? Yes, absolutely. It's comforting to be around people who understand such things. Well, at least you did your job. Transcription is not my line of work, but I can imagine it’s sometimes less exciting than one would hope. On the contrary, there are its own thrills in looking for the perfect word, the proper grammar, the tone of the speaker... Right? Absolutely! But that doesn’t mean it can’t be dull at times. Now, if I were the one who spoke at that conference, maybe I’d find it more interesting. Do you, really? What would you talk about? Well, I've always been interested in local history. I think I could give a good speech on the evolution of community engagement in our area. That’s a great theme, actually. Community engagement is a fantastic subject. How the dynamics between community and local government have changed over the years could be very insightful. Indeed. Especially given the national changes, blurred boundaries between local and national policies. Exactly! It could be really relevant today, especially with all the changes and challenges local communities are facing. Wouldn’t that be a good topic for our next dinner event? No? Actually, yes, it could be. And given the backgrounds we all have here... Speaker 1 has an eye for the local perspective, Speaker 4 could perhaps bring some insights from his community work, and you, Speaker 2, could put it into context with national trends, and I could maybe add some historical and educational angle. I love it. I've been involved in a few community projects that have often intersected with local government. There’s a lot of interesting stories to share. That would be fantastic. And if I guest lecture at a local community center or something, I could make it a bit more interactive, maybe share some of the history books I've come across in my transcribing work. That would be a great way to involve the community as well. I could see how this could tie in with some of our volunteer work at the school too, if we wanted to engage some of our students.

Alright sweethearts, what do you think? Should we start brainstorming some fun activities for Mother’s Day? Like going to forest school again! Yeah! Forest school was fun! We found a big beetle! Oh, that was indeed a fun day. I remember you two telling me all about the little creature's antennae. But what did your teacher say about why those antennae are important? They feel things! Like the wind and the grass. And sometimes other beetles. That's right, they help the beetle to explore its world. Hmm, maybe we should visit the forest school again if it's safe and possible. But for Mother’s Day, perhaps we can also plan something at home. Can we bake cookies? That sounds lovely! And while we bake, we can learn some fun new things. Did you two know that people often say 'break a leg' when they want to wish someone good luck? Why break a leg? That sounds like bad luck! Exactly! That doesn’t make much sense, does it? It's an idiom. In English, 'break a leg' means 'good luck'. We say it to people before a performance or an important event because, strange as it seems, it just became a tradition. Can we make lucky cookies then? We certainly can! And you can each draw a picture of what 'break a leg' means to you on the cookies. Can I draw a beetle for good luck? Perfect idea! And so can you, sweetheart. It'll be like we're telling each other to break a leg with beetle luck. Can we make the beetle cookies green? Absolutely. Beetle green cookies for good luck. How about we also use some red for the heart and some yellow for the sun for happiness and joy? Yeah! And maybe some spots like the beetle had! Great thinking! Let's make it a fun, interactive project for Mother’s Day. We'll write on the cookies with icing too, like 'Break a leg with beetle luck' and all our names beside each other. Can I draw my mom some flowers? And I'm sure your mom would love that. This will be such a special gift. I can mix the icing colors! You can definitely help with that. While we're working, would you two like to tell me some new idioms you've learned or heard? Sometimes they’re quite funny.

I was thinking of mom last night. It's hard to believe it's been two years since dad passed away and six months since she was diagnosed with cancer. Yes, it's been a tough time for all of us, hasn't it? I heard from Sheila that the treatment is going well so far, but I'd be lying if I said I wasn't worried. I know. It's never easy, and it seems like it keeps piling up even when you think it can't get any worse. This whole thing has really made me think about our own health a lot. I've started taking more care of my physical health and I've been seeing a therapist about some of my mental health struggles. You know, talking about it helps. That sounds like a great idea. I've been meaning to do the same. Sometimes I feel like I'm so caught up with being there for everyone else that I forget to take care of myself. Exactly! That's why I wanted to talk to you about it - you're one of the people I feel comfortable opening up to about this stuff. I'm always here to listen, and I'm glad you know that. It's hard for us women, isn't it? We often put our own health last because we're focusing on everyone else. Definitely. Like, my sister's children have been a huge help with mom, but sometimes it feels like I'm shouldering everything when it comes to family and all the worrying. I know what you mean. It's like it's always something new we're dealing with. The kids have been good, though. They're all doing their part and it's helped the family bond more. Speaking of which, did you hear that Tom is getting married soon? No, I didn't! That's fantastic news! When’s the big day? Noonie’s told me they're planning for next summer. Sounds like just around the corner, isn't it? It does. It'll be nice for everyone. Change of topic, though - did you hear from the doctor about mom's latest checkup? Yeah. She said things are stable for now. But she also stressed the importance of her mental well-being. She's stressed out a lot about the future and the treatment.

Yo, mate, did you manage to sort out your first year's timetable yet? I still can't quite wrap my head around all these modules and lectures. Oh, actually, I did yesterday. I had to fight off a few time clashes but it now looks pretty good, though a fair few of my questions are in the afternoon now. You? Yeah, similar. Mine starts at 10 AM but I’ve got a class at 4 PM as well. I'm trying to get used to it. Are you still considering taking a few extra languages? I’ve added Korean to my list. It was such an interesting module when our linguistics lecturer covered it. Ah, yes. I thought of that too. Our lecturer actually mentioned that the UK universities tend to be really good for linguistics, especially the South-East ones, due to the variety of dialects. That’s cool. I’ve heard that as well. But, do you know if the tuition fees are going to rise? And have you thought about applying for any scholarships or bursaries? Yeah, it's worrisome. We've discussed it on our student forum. There's a lot of pressure and uncertainty. I applied for a few bursaries and I'm waiting to hear. Fingers crossed. That’s wise, really important given the costs. It can be quite stressful, right? By the way, have you tried any specific language course or resources, like language exchange programs or apps? Yeah, I started using Duolingo a bit but it’s not always that practical when it comes to proper conversation and real-life uses. Totally, it’s good for basics but to get fluent you need practice with natives or in real situations. Exactly, which is why I was thinking of joining some of the language meetups on campus or seeking out exchange students for language exchange. That’s a great idea. Last year, there was a Korean meetup group on campus. You could try that. Yeah, I’ll definitely try that. Also, I’ve been reading up on Korean food. Did you know it’s quite vegan/vegetarian friendly? I might consider experimenting with Korean seitan recipes for dinner sometime. Oh, that’s interesting. I’d almost gone vegetarian at uni just for the variety of options. There’s actually a really good Korean restaurant near here that came highly recommended by a friend.

Oh, did I mention my first year's flatmate Grace brought this super cheap and decent flavoured vodka to last night's party? You mean that shaky bottle with the labels peeling off that now adorns our kitchen counter? Oh yes, the one that tastes suspiciously like cough syrup. I took a sip and felt like I was back in primary school, actually. Well, it was fun even if it wasn’t exactly premium, right? Definitely, and speaking of drinks, have you heard about the flavoured vodkas they have at Sugarhouse? They say the mango one is a must-try. Yeah, we should actually go sample them next week. That sounds like a plan! On that note, did anyone else catch that episode of The Big Fat Quiz? I was trying to explain the concept of the 'Chaos Walking trilogy' to Laura and Jack Whitehall got it so wrong. Oh, that was so cringe! I mean, it's not like he's read it or anything. It’s alright for him, he can always fall back on his English charm. Speaking of which, I saw Charlie Simpson on a quiz the other day. He was actually pretty good! I saw that too! I feel like we all should start doing more quizzes, maybe even try to get into University Challenge. That would be amazing! Have you taken part in the physics module assessments yet? Yeah, but it was tougher than I expected. Did anyone else notice the questions about the airport body scanners? I just had to try and recall all that physics again, blurred as it is after a certain flood year in Lancaster. Floods! How long has it been since we've all been together and not talked about the flooding? We should sit down and watch Cloud Atlas again sometime, though. I would love that! Have you guys heard of a new game called Heads Up? It's like Articulate but for phones. No! That sounds fun and chaotic. We have to try it this week during study break. We could also do Secret Santa soon. I was thinking about getting my Secret Santa a book, probably a thriller or something by Gillian Flynn. That's a great idea! You could even get a copy of City of Bones. I never read it because I was too busy with Twilight when it was first out, but I've heard it's good.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was doing my summer internship at the university? It was absolute chaos! I was working as a corpus administrator, and there was a mayor's visit. We had to prepare a corpus for his speech but just minutes before his visit, the system crashed! We had to recreate the whole thing from scratch! That sounds like a right mess! I've had my share of crises, as a consultant I'd say. Like the time we were rebuilding an old bridge and the structural engineers miscalculated. We had to redo some of the beams. Oh, I can imagine. Talk about a stressful week! But we managed it, even though I was fairly new to the job back then. Yeah, those are the days that test your problem-solving skills. It's amazing how quickly you can adapt when you have to, though. Absolutely. I learned a lot from that experience. Someone should make a motivational video out of it or something. Sure, I've had experiences like that too. Not to mention the initial days of my graduate studies. I had to learn everything so quickly. Speaking of which, I also really enjoyed the graduate program at university. It was tough, but it laid out a solid foundation for my current job. Though I feel, sometimes it's the silly things that we remember the most. Like what? Like the time our professor for a particular course had this... kind of a 'dad joke' kind of attitude. During exams if one of us failed significantly the first time, he'd say, "Well, that’s a fail, isn't it? The F for foundations. Grab another pint and try again." That's hilarious! I love that! Reminds me of the old lab days where our professor was known for his quirky sayings. He'd say things like "Well, if you can't handle atoms, how can you handle molecules?" when we struggled with lab results. It does lighten the mood, doesn't it? Even under pressure. Did you have any similar experiences? Actually, yes! I remember during my PhD. I was working on a project that had to do with temperature control in industrial environments. We were trying to get this new sensor to work but it just wasn't behaving. One of my peers, who was really struggling with the project, was sitting next to the fridge when suddenly the compressor kicked in, making a loud noise.

Bloody weather we're having, isn't it? Makes me feel like I've been dragged back to my youth. Remember when it used to rain this much back in Costessey? It does seem quite relentless doesn't it? I'm used to less rain and more sunshine in Norwich, but I suppose that's part of the charm of this part of the country! And it's not just the rain, it's how it seems to affect our bodies too. I've been finding it quite a struggle with my old bones. Oh, yes, I know what you mean. I've had to give up on the garden for now, it's just too much to handle with all this persistent rain. It's all about finding ways to cope with it, isn't it? How about those weather apps these days? So good for planning and knowing what to expect. Yes, but they're not always accurate, are they? I mean, I've seen forecasts completely change in a matter of hours. True. But technology's improved a lot, at least it gives us a heads up. And there's always the old-fashioned way of looking out the window , but I agree, apps can be hit or miss. Can't rely on technology for everything, especially when you're dealing with something as unpredictable as the British weather! Well, there's the old farmer's almanac or finding patterns in the stars for that, but I suppose we're all too far from the farm these days for that. The stars? I haven't noticed much pattern in them when it comes to the weather. But perhaps there's something to it, who knows? While you were dealing with the rain and farming, I was making sure kids were occupied and learning. And doing a fantastic job at that, by the looks of it. I mean, those children lucky enough to have you as their childminder are blessed. That's very kind of you to say. Though I do miss the chaos and energy they brought. Now, it's more about trying to keep these old bones from creaking. Well, for now, maybe there are other things to focus on that don't require as much physical strain. Like maybe some new gadgets? I've been looking at this new tablet that’s supposed to be good for reading and watching videos comfortably.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that awkward situation I had today? I was at work and one of my colleagues was discussing about our wedding plans, and he asked me if I had thought about children. It was so out of the blue. I just panicked and blurted out, "I don’t know, haven’t thought about it yet." Oh, right! Embarrassing. I had a similar situation too. I was at a sales meeting and one of the clients kept on asking me when I was getting married and stuff like that, and I responded clumsily. I have to say, it's just so invasive and I don’t know why people feel they have the right to ask. Exactly! It’s like everyone’s making life-changing decisions for us. And even if we’ve thought about it, it’s none of their business until we decide to share it. Yeah, but I get it. It’s because people are excited and interested. I mean, weddings and kids are exciting topics. Plus, it’s nice to be asked, right? At least they’re not being nosy in a malicious way. I know, I suppose. It’s good that they’re interested but sometimes it feels like the timing or place isn’t right. Absolutely. Honestly though, I started thinking about it after my sister got married and became a mom. She’s so happy, and it inspired me a bit. And with the pressure that comes from family and society... doesn’t help much Yeah, the pressure to have kids and all that can be intense. And let’s not forget about marriage – the expectations, festivities, and everything! Exactly. Speaking of festivities, did any of you hear about Sarah's next dinner party? She's planning a bonfire night party and I’m so excited. It’ll be our first time doing something like that without her husband though because he’s working abroad for a while. No, I hadn’t heard! That sounds amazing! Can we see if we can fit that into our plans? It’d be great to catch-up with everyone. I hope they serve those toffee apples. I was craving those during Halloween. Anyway, Sarah said something about a particular cake she wanted to try? Yeah, I remember Sarah mentioned a traditional British fruit cake she found a new recipe for. It sounded delicious.

Ah, lovely tea, thank you. You have outdone yourself again. Thanks, talked to my daughter the other day and she said they're all into some new video game called "Cyberquest". What's this all about then? It's questions all the time! Oh yeah, Cyberquest, "Pew, pew" they say . It’s quite popular among youngsters now. They can immerse themselves in these virtual worlds, get alongside with people from all corners of the globe. Technology's a mystery, isn't it? Used to be about the tractor at the farm, now it's about these virtual ones. Heh, yes. Used to read about virtual tractors when I was younger—if you even could call it that. It's a different world out there now. But sometimes I wonder... how does technology help the young when it comes to real life skills? You couldn't repair a video game, for example. Valid point. But technology can be a tool for learning, certainly. My grandkids use educational apps for maths and languages. It’s kind of neat, the way they pick it up. Still, I think the most substantial education is found in the real world, on a farm, fixing an actual tractor or working with animals – like equines. Oh, talk about horses! Reminds me of my youth. I used to help out at the stables in Costessey. There's nothing like the feel of a real horse under you. Horses! You should've seen the look on my grandkid's face the first time she rode one of those miniature ponies at the fair! Yeah, getting them out into the natural world, hands-on experience... that's something no app can replace. From fixing fences to mucking out stalls, it teaches responsibility and patience. Responsibility for sure. Our generation used to learn by doing, just like that. But I've seen kids these days, they're more comfortable with a controller than a bridle. That's almost too true. But you know, there's still plenty of horse riding clubs and things like that. Although, not all of them can afford it, is the problem. Things ain't cheap nowadays, are they? Money problems, speak of the devil. You know, we're all struggling to make ends meet. The cost of living, it's a challenge. My grandkids like these games because they're cheap entertainment. Maybe a welcome break from it all.

Ah, lovely to see you, Uncle Joe! How are you doing? I brought some Earl Grey, freshly made from my own garden. It's been a while since we last caught up. Ah, Alison! You're as lovely as ever and, as always, very considerate – thank you for the tea! I hope my garden's bounty didn't get too adventurous with that blend. No, no. It's fine! Quite nice, actually. I've been meaning to start my own little herb garden here but I've been a bit busy with lazy weekends – you know how it is with the retired life. I do know, even though I suppose I'm slightly busier in retirement than when I was working full-time. Teaching's a rewarding profession but requires a lot of time and preparation outside of class hours. Teaching! That's a challenging job, yet very fulfilling, I imagine. I've often thought about teaching Spanish – I picked it up a bit during my travels, but never had the chance to or took the time to really learn it properly. Spanish! That's a great choice! The different dialects across the Spanish-speaking world make it so fascinating. I love the way it's such a diverse language with influences from Latin and Arabic, to name a few. Indeed, very distinct – like the differences within the UK, perhaps? I noticed that, especially during your mother's recent travels in Wales. The way she'd come back with stories of the regional accents! Absolutely! Despite speaking the same language, English dialects in the UK are as diverse as the cultures in Spain. For example, my hometown of Hitchin in Hertfordshire has its unique accent compared to Birmingham here. An interesting thought, weren't we, Alison? The variety within our own little island is just as wide as another country's! It's one of the joys of language, really – it's a window into the culture and history of a place. It also makes teaching so interesting because it's a bit more than just grammar and vocabulary; it's about sharing cultures, and that's what I enjoy about my job so much. You're absolutely right. And I suppose it's good that you can share insights from almost all over Britain, having grown up there and having lived and taught in Birmingham now. I, on the other hand, had to travel a lot for my work.

Oh, did you both celebrate Valentine's Day this week? Yeah, I don't know, I think it's all just a marketing ploy. Totally. People get all caught up in the hype of flowers and chocolates, buying into the notion that if they don't spend a fortune, they're not "showing love" enough. But actually, I felt a bit bad for not doing anything. My boyfriend was away this weekend so it felt weird to celebrate it. That's a good point. It does creates extra pressure on relationships. I know! It made me wish I was just a student like you, free to do what I want without all that weighted expectation. I suppose. Though I still had my own share of issues, like choosing the right cinema and finding a good film for a date. What did you guys go see? Did you grab a bite at a fancy restaurant afterward? Actually, no, I'm not really that into fancy restaurants this time of year. We went to this cool little bistro that does great burgers. That sounds nice! Burgers can be so romantic if you make them right. Exactly. And it wasn't crowded or expensive. We just had a nice evening out without all the clichéd pressure, you know? Yeah, clichés can be off-putting. Although I do wish they didn't play "All You Need is Love" by the Beatles non-stop everywhere. Oh, have you noticed that? It's like, if you're not in love, the world will remind you about it every five minutes! True. Okay, enough about stress. What about you? What did you get up to last weekend aside from studying? Oh, nothing much. I went shopping for something to wear to our student ball. Student ball? No way, are you sure you're not feeling left out and decided to join in the festivities? Maybe a bit of that. Besides, it’ll be fun and it’s one less night spent stressing over exams. I can tell. Your accent changes when you talk about exams. Do you notice how certain situations bring out your London accent more? I suppose I do. You know how everyone has little quirks when they speak. I know exactly what you mean. I’ve always found it interesting how our accents reveal so much about our backgrounds. Right! I mean, from the way you say "film" instead of "movie" and your pronunciation, it's pretty clear you're from the Midlands at least.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen Grace's latest article for The Guardian? It's quite insightful on the intersection of racism and capitalism. Yes! I saw it. It was brilliant, as usual, but also kind of heartbreaking given how much of it is so close to home. I mean, have you seen the house prices in London these days? It's like the city is priced right out of reach for most people, especially young professionals like us. Absolutely. It's almost as if the housing market is designed to ensure only the wealthiest can afford to live here. And then there's the jobs market, despite our higher education, we're often competing with those from a bit lower socio-economic backgrounds who have less opportunity in the places of study or even the internships we need. Exactly! It's a catch-22, isn't it? Our education levels are higher, but the job market often seems geared towards people with connections or those already from higher socio-economic backgrounds. And those housing prices! So many people are forced to live with their families years after graduation just to make ends meet. And the funniest part is while the system seems designed to keep the divide intact, the politicians talk about "leveling up" or "opportunity for all." But it feels like empty words without real action backing them up. Honestly, as an architect, I've seen firsthand how in practice, gentrification projects often push out long-time residents, and all the while, we're "proposing diversity" but leading to community displacement. True, and the lack of affordable housing options only amplifies this issue. I've been covering some of these stories in my work, and it's surreal to see how systemic racism in property and finance just plays out. It's depressing to think about. But personally, as an architect, I've been trying to shift my focus towards more socially conscious projects. You know, working with local councils on designing community housing or public spaces that actually benefit the local population instead of just serving gentrification. That’s wonderful! How do you manage the pressures of working on such projects? It must be difficult given the current market trends. It is challenging, of course, but it’s the real job I want to do. There’s a little part of me that’s idealistic still, hoping we can make a difference.

Right, so I'm going to have to start thinking about going back to work soon. I still don't quite know what I'll do but it feels like it's been talked about for so long, and now it's actually happening. Aye, I remember you saying that a fair few times while I was still at uni. It seems like a big change though, and I suppose it won't be easy. It will, actually. I've been out of work for so long and it feels like I've got so much to catch up on, but at the same time, I really want to start getting back into a routine. It will be good for me, for [baby's name] as well. I think so too, but what about [baby's name]? Is she going to nursery soon? Yeah, she starts nursery next month. I'm a bit nervous, to be honest. I can imagine. Dropping her off for the first time must be quite a thought. It's like, she's still so little and now she'll be away from you for a few hours a day. Exactly! I keep picturing her crying when I leave, which I know she will, and I just can't decide if it's the right decision. It really is the right decision, though. She needs social interactions with her age group and you need to start getting back into your own life, you know? It'll be a bit of a shock for both of you at first, but it'll get better. That’s what everyone keeps telling me… but it's hard not to worry. I've been so used to spending every waking moment with her. I can totally understand that. But think about the independence you’ve given her so far! She’s growing up to be such a bright little girl and nursery is just another step for her. You're right, of course. She’s so smart and curious and changing all the time. Plus, you can spend all that time you’ll be at work thinking about all the new things she’s learning and just enjoying when you’re together. It might even make those moments feel more special. That's a good way to look at it. I hadn’t considered it like that. You also mentioned thinking about weening [baby's name] off.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my day? I had a surprise call from the police today. It was about a statement I gave last week about that little incident at the bookstore. You know, when that person was trying to leave without paying for their items? No, I didn't hear about that. But I knew you mentioned you had to make a statement. What happened with that? It seems that my store's new system has minimized the problem so much that they're looking into its roll-out in other shops in the city. It's a bit unexpected, but definitely a nice encouragement. That's amazing, congratulations! I knew you were doing a good job but to have the police consider it an example piece of work is something else. Indeed, that's quite a feather in your cap. Though now, how about this EE phone bill that showed up? I saw the circular when I came in. That's quite the shock to the system, hasn't it? Oh, yes. EE really let me down this time. For no reason, my phone bill just suddenly doubled and it's been a bit of a struggle changing the plan. It's been on my nerves all day. That’s frustrating. Have you managed to get it fixed yet? Phone-billed zero-obtained nothing yet. They said it's a technical glitch, and they're 'looking into it', which in reality just means 'let's delay any meaningful action as long as possible'. That's no fun. I've heard EE can be a handful. You might want to threaten to switch providers if they don't get it sorted. Sometimes that makes them move a bit faster.

Yo, mate, welcome back to Bedford! How was the move's been treating you so far? I hope everything's settling in alright. Thanks, mate. It's been all right. Just adjusting to the new place. It's nice to be back though and see the old sights again. Absolutely, Bedford’s changed quite a bit since I left, but it still has that homely feel to it. Have you watched any good TV shows of late? I've been obsessed with Peaky Blinders and it’s really immersing me into the whole era of the early 20th century. Yeah, actually. I’ve been watching Spartacus. I know it's a bit of a niche interest, but I love anything that’s got that epic Roman bit to it. Brilliant! Yeah, Spartacus - the making of the series and the actual history have always fascinated me. It's amazing how quickly the known world seemed to change back then. The paths of these historical figures were often cut so short, like the gladiators in the arena. Absolutely. I watch and think how many talented people died before they could even get to develop their full potential, you know? That’s so true. Musician-wise, did you ever listen to the '27 Club'? It’s this weird phenomena where a lot of notable musicians, like Jimi Hendrix and Jim Morrison, died at 27 for some reason. Yeah, I know about that. Almost seems like they burned out in their prime, really. Makes you think life is quite fragile, doesn’t it? Definitely makes you appreciate what you’ve got in the here and now. On a lighter note, have you tried this new café behind the town square? They’ve got the most amazing selection of teas. Never been there yet. But tea’s my favorite, so I'm definitely looking forward to checking it out whenever. It's really quirky, they have all these different blends you might never think of, and they'll even let you grind your own herbs in a little mortar and pestle to make your own unique cup. Plus, they've got these little snacks like artisanal crackers with chickpeas and so on. That sounds incredible! I love that kind of thing. Is it still good even if you're not much of a tea person? Oh yeah, the food’s good. I was telling you about my recent trip to China; they don’t use those fine-grained herbs and spices like we do here, but their use of chilies and whole spices is fascinating.

Yo, Lucy, did you finish reading that novel for English class? Yeah, I just finished it last night. I was thinking about it during my Art lesson today, the whole book had some really great imagery. I know what you mean! Our English teacher, Mrs. Jenkins, really encouraged us to pay attention to the imagery and symbolism. She's always going on about "show, don't tell," which I think is a right pain, but it does make me see things differently now. True!
