Well, the main character talks about feeling like she was stuck in a sort of weighted down life, and in French class, we were going over verbs that usually involve moving or changing. I made a connection with the idea of being trapped and finding a way out. That's actually quite observant, Lucy! And good for you for thinking like that. You will for sure score well in that essay. Hope so! Speaking of this, I'm a bit stressed about the upcoming test. It covers different parts of the English curriculum. You’re doing well though, I hope? Straining at the bit, to be honest, but we can't give up now. We’re nearly there. I know what you mean. I started re-reading the notes from all the lessons, but I need to keep everything fresh in my mind, and all the analysis and stuff. I know exactly how you feel. Going over it in the morning is the best thing. Memory works much better then. Except, unfortunately, I don't really have a morning routine right now. Same here, but I just tried to get a bit of practice every evening. We could maybe study together once or twice this week? That’d be perfect! I really need to get into a routine for studying. Definitely can do that. Plus, I need to finish revising for art and French too. Oh, speaking of which, did you see last week’s wind-band performance? No, I missed it sadly. I had a test the day before and I wasn’t well the next day. Yeah, I heard it was really good. Especially the new piece our teacher made us practice. You had a good part to play, didn’t you?

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to explain the difference between a Yorkshire and northern accent to my class? Well, let me tell you, it was quite the challenge. You two are from here, so you know better than anyone that sometimes people from the south get confused with our dialects. Yeah, I remember once, I had this friend from London who thought that everyone in the North spoke with a Geordie accent! Oh my, that's so true! I get it all the time when I speak to my distant relatives in London, they assume I sound like someone from Newcastle! It's just another case of people thinking the whole North is a bit of a monolith when really we've got so many regional variations. Like, the difference even between Newcastle and Hull is quite significant, even though they're both in Yorkshire! Really? What's the difference then? Well, it's all about the vowels and the way we say certain words. Like the word 'bath', in Hull we would say it more like 'barth', while people from Newcastle would say 'bath' in the more standard way. And of course, we also have 't' glottalization, where the 't' at the end of words or in the middle can be pronounced as a glottal stop - 'bu' instead of 'but'. It's pretty subtle but, you know, native speakers can always tell! Exactly! For instance, words like 'class' and 'path' would sound a bit different from Hull to Newcastle. It's all about the colloquialisms we use that make our accents unique. That's so cool! We never really paid attention to that detail before in school. I noticed that when I moved to Darlington, I had to adjust to quite a few local colloquialisms. Like instead of saying 'lift', you often hear people say 'pardon' around here! Indeed, that's a classic! And in Hull, we'd often say 'alright' instead of 'how are you'. So, speaking of local differences and education, have you kids noticed any changes in how we teach or learn over the years? Whether it's the way we teach or the subjects included? Yeah, definitely! More focus on technology now, especially coding and computer skills. We even have a whole new subject dedicated to that in school. And I can see that in your literature, even. My classes when I was a teacher were all based on books, now it seems like digital content is taking center stage.

I've decided I need to lose some weight. I've been hearing so much these days about obesity and how it's causing all sorts of health problems. Ah, you've really caught onto the health trends now, haven't you? I remember when being a bit thicker was kind of seen as healthy because it meant you weren't starving. But of course, times change. And the media doesn't help, does it? All these new diet fads and fitness videos keeps coming out. Makes it sound like it's so simple. Well, actually, it's more complex than that. It's not just about diet trends. There's a whole lot to do with lifestyle, genetics, and access to good nutrition and exercise facilities. It's not as simple as just picking up a new diet plan and hope for the best. That's true. I've been trying to incorporate more fruits and vegetables into my diet and doing some light jogging in the mornings. But it's hard. I'm a bit of a creature of habit, so it's hard for me to change my diet significantly. But I've noticed that when I do the odd bit of gardening, I genuinely feel more energised and lighter. Speaking of health, did you hear about the new studies on allergies? A friend of mine has a kid who's allergic to all sorts of things, really worrying for her. Yeah, I saw something about it. It seems like allergies are on the rise, and they reckon it's partly due to how we live now - all the cleanliness and excessive use of sanitizers might be causing our immune systems to act up unnecessarily. Exactly right. I've been reading about how our immune systems need some exposure to 'natural' germs to function properly. I always thought it was just my hay fever making me sniffle all the time. Maybe not. Funny how we just assume these things, isn't it? Did any of you hear about that new jigsaw puzzle the grandchildren bought for my daughter? It's one of those 5000 pieces and they say it's nearly impossible to finish. Oh, jigsaw puzzles are my wife's idea of therapy. We've got a whole bookshelf dedicated to them. I've never been much for puzzles myself. But I've seen the grandchildren get so engrossed in them.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you had a chance to learn how to use Moodle properly yet? Oh, the infamous Moodle. You know I've tried to navigate it, but I must admit it can be quite frustrating at times. I know exactly what you mean! I've been teaching a part-time course and it's been a real challenge to learn how to upload quizzes, assignments, and manage student participation. Right, it's like learning a new language, isn’t it? I've been trying to figure out how to embed videos and set up groups for discussion forums. Exactly. I had the same problem. But once you get the hang of it, it’s quite useful, isn’t it? It's useful, but the learning curve is steep. I found it really useful to watch some YouTube tutorials. There are some very helpful videos by the creator of Moodle himself or even other lecturers who have been using it for years. That's a good idea! I'll have to look into that. And then there's the good old trial and error method, which hasn’t failed me yet. Well, I guess it's always good to learn through practical experience. But isn't it bizarre how as academics, we often end up spending more time figuring out the technology than teaching the subject matter itself? But it's part and parcel of how we teach now. Just last week, I had to explain to one of my students who had issues accessing the course content. Seems their outdated browser was causing the problem. I had a similar issue with a student who couldn't seem to figure out how to attach files to their forum post. This generation takes digital tools for granted, doesn't it? I know what you mean. But in a way, it’s also a good opportunity to teach them some basic digital skills. That’s true! It's all part of preparing them for the real world. Yeah, plus it makes them appreciate the job we put into course design and administration. Absolutely. So, you figure out how to do those quizzes and assignments alright? Well, after much trial and error, I managed to set up some basic multiple-choice quizzes. But I still need to figure out the advanced features like adaptive testing or linking grades to the course gradebook.

Oh, did I sound like that much of a mess when I woke up early? Oh, you definitely did! Your tea-fueled ramblings were quite entertaining! Did the kids wake up too then? We need to keep them occupied until we head out to that play at the local theatre tonight, right? Yeah, they're downstairs, playing with those LEGO bricks. I managed to convince Sam to stop building for a bit so he could eat his breakfast. Well done! That's a good start. So you spoke with Emily last night about babysitting? Yes, she'll take care of them from 7 till we're back. I texted her to confirm in the morning, and she said yes - though we need to leave her some food for them and diapers just in case. Okay, great! Let me check on their room... And about next week, or whenever, we need to sort out who's picking up from school and who's doing dinner. I can do Tuesday and Thursday. How about you do Monday, Wednesday, and Friday? That works for me. Also, I need to finalize the leave request forms for the conference next month – I'm presenting. Ah, yes! Good luck with that. You've been preparing really well. Thanks. I know. It’s always a bit of a juggle but doesn’t feel that bad when it's for something I enjoy. Absolutely. Speaking of things you enjoy, did you check if the performance tonight is going to have any baby-friendly seats? Oh, I almost forgot! Yes, I did. We’re seated in the family section. It’s a small theatre, but they have monitors for audio if needed and there’s a baby room if they decide changing a diaper in the middle of a play might be necessary. I suppose that's standard for local performances these days. Either way, it looks like a fun show. I’ve read the playwright is quite influential. Right! And it’ll be good to be out of the house and almost back to normal after the trip. I know. I was reading about that jetlag. It seems the best way to deal with it is to regulate sleep and keep active. Hmm, I guess that makes sense. It’s not just that we’re tired from the travel – the time-zone change must be also messing with our internal clocks.

Ah, speaking of other countries, did you hear anything about your friend’s family in Kurdistan? I lent an ear to that article about the new oil pipeline being built. It sounds like it could significantly impact the economy there, right? Yeah, they’re all talking about it a lot – both the questions and the opportunities it’s bringing. The region could use the stability and the jobs. But, at the same time, they’re cautious about how this will pan out, as fractious past experiences with resources have often led to more troubles rather than solutions. True. That’s always the thing with oil in the Middle East, isn’t it? It’s a double-edged sword. You need it for development, but it attracts a lot of unwanted attention too. Absolutely. Everyone’s aware of the petroleum politics of the region. Some are optimistically hopeful, others are more cynical. It’s a complicated history you can’t quickly undo. That’s true. But, do you think that politically, the Kurds are better equipped this time around to navigate it all? It depends on who you talk to, really. Some feel that with oil income this time it could be an opportunity to stabilize and strengthen their political institutions. Others worry the expected political structures may not be able to handle the new pressure and benefits. That’s a fair point. It really depends on the governance at play. Here in the UK, for instance, while the media often focuses on the cynicism, I think we still tend to have a strong system of checks and balances for such things. I envy that sometimes. But you know, Kurds have been leading the fight against extremism in the region for a while now too. There’s a fair amount of experience with organized resistance and governance on the ground. That’s very true. Their fight against ISIS was pivotal, weren’t they? I always find it interesting how certain regions that face so much adversity can also develop unique strengths or resilience. Indeed. That and the knowledge that instability is a threat to everyone. You can’t help but admire that despite everything, Kurdistan's youth, for example – they’re often some of the most motivated people for change and self-improvement I’ve met, regardless of the local challenges. It must be incredible to see that kind of spirit in action, and even more so perhaps in circumstances where they almost didn’t have a choice in the matter.

I've decided I need to lose some weight. I've been hearing so much about this new workout routine that's doing the rounds. It's all talked about at work. What are you both doing to stay in shape? Just regular walks with the dogs, love. Nothing too elaborate. Although I do try and manage a bit of a workout whenever I can get into the swing of it. Oh, I couldn't agree more about needing to stay active. But even if it is as simple as a brisk walk in the park. It truly does make all the difference. Absolutely. I have to say though, I've just been feeling like I need to shake things up. Everyone at work seems to be joining this big group fitness class - Zumba or something, and they all say it's great fun. Zumba? Now, I know how much you love a dance, but I'm not sure if I can keep up with that. Don't worry, I won't force anyone to do it with me! But it sounds like it might be a great way to socialize and get exercise at the same time. I used to enjoy the Scottish Tablet we had after dinner. Do we still have some for later? It's nice to have something sweet after a good roast dinner. I actually got some from a fantastic little shop in town. It should still be in the cupboard. Why don't we grab a few pieces after you've finished chatting about your new fitness plans? Oh, that would be lovely! And let me ask you this, would you guys be up for joining me someday? Maybe on a weekend? If it means I get to try this Zumba without being embarrassed alone, I'd consider it. But honestly, I'm more for a quiet walk in the park on my own. No pressure, but I'm in for any of it. If it means spending more time together, I'm all for it. Though, if we do go for the sweet treat afterwards, let's make sure we have it with some tea. Perfect! I'll make sure I arrange something suitable, then. And remember, our tablets are from Scotland. You'll get all that extra strength and endurance from the Scottish air right in every bite. Scotland's already famous for its strong spirit, why not strong tablet as well?

Yo, mate, did you hear about that pasta bake last night's flatmate made? Yeah! It was bloody tasty! She said she got the recipe from her mum down in Surrey, right? Aye, yeah, that’s right! But speaking of tasty food, I just got back from the market and I saw some beautiful lamb chops. We could make a roast dinner if ye want? That’d be brilliant! But maybe we should figure out a bit better how to split the rent and bills. We’ve been kind of winging it, and I think it’s getting a bit messy. [laughs] Aye, you're dead right about that, just like the mess in our room. And can we finally sort out the weekly shop? We're always running out of stuff. Exactly! Maybe we could do a rota or something? Sounds good! While we're at it, let's discuss our university stuff. How's it all going for everyone? I'm still trying to get my head around this business studies unit. Oh, it's quite alright. Just plenty of essays to write and I’ve got a pretty big exam coming up next month. I hope I pass. [sighs] Do I even mention mine? [chuckles] Still looking for a job. It's like a job itself just trying to get one. There's always something new in Whitehaven, really. But you should definitely consider applying for that position at the bakery on the high street. I saw the ad the other day. True, I might give that a try. Just gotta make sure my CV is spot on, and maybe I should practice my interview skills a bit. [laughs] Oh, I can help you with that. I used to give mock interviews at Sixthform. Just couple of tips can make a big difference. While you're sorting out jobs, I’ve got family coming in next week from my Dad’s side. It's gonna be a hoot, they're always up for a laugh. That sounds fun, but I hope we can still have some peace and quiet here too. [chuckles] Again, unless they're baking. Then, they're more than welcome. We could set up a guest room. I’ll clear out that space in the loft if we don’t use it yet. You mean the room we all agreed to use as a study but that became the spare room for when we never used it because we all end up on laptops in the living room?

"Alright, today we're making simple scones. It's a good activity for young children, they get to measure and mix and of course, they can decorate their scones later. I thought it would tie into our lesson about baking measurements – do you have all the ingredients we need?" "Actually, Mum, I found out that we can find a very similar recipe for scones in that Tomodachi Life game on my console. Do you think we could maybe do some of those after baking? Even if there's no real baking in the game, it could be fun to try out the in-game recipe?" "Mum, can I help with measuring? I want to practice reading measurements, I didn’t do so well with that in school last week." "That's a great idea! Both of you can help with measuring. M, for the recipe, we need 250g of flour, 50g of sugar, 30g of butter, and 150ml of milk. We also need a pinch of salt, but the kids' measuring spoons are in the cupboard. And yes, Speak 2, we can do something fun with Tomodachi later for sure. Maybe a nice break from all this mixing and measuring." "Great! I'll get the flour for you." "Mum, I need the 250g, 50g is the sugar right? And the butter is 30g? Let me get those out." "Correct, M! That’s great reading! Now, for the next step, we need to mix the dry ingredients first. Can you both help me stir these together?" "Wait, changing the subject, but did you find that book we wanted at Morrisons? I think it was about the history of baking, something in the kids' section." "Ah, yes, I did find it. It has some sweet stories about how baking has developed over time and even includes some simple recipes. We could almost use this book as part of the lesson. We can put it next to Tomodachi if you like, maybe a little side activity for the kids." "And we can use those fun decorating tips from Tomodachi too! I really want to try making a face out of our scones." "That sounds awesome! Like, we could make animal faces or characters from the game." "Let's keep that as a fun part of the activity then. You both can come up with your designs after we've baked the scones, decorate them, and then present what you've made."

I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen Grace's latest Facebook update? It's about that new electric SUV she bought. Yeah, I saw it yesterday. I'm actually quite excited for her. I've been meaning to make the switch to an electric myself, but I'm waiting for my current lease to end and then I'll definitely consider it. Absolutely makes sense. The incentives and of course, the environmental benefits. But have you heard about that new one from Tesla? There's an even longer range and it's supposedly better in terms of handling and responsiveness. Yes! I saw a review for that earlier today. The design looks sleek and features are impressive. Exactly! So what about the performance? Was the reviewer impressed with that? Well, they said it's quite fast and agile. Plus, with the new batteries, its range on a single charge is much improved. That's amazing. I've always been a fan of Tesla but their prices... Yes, it's true. They do come with a hefty price tag. But if you consider all their software updates and the high resale value, it kind of evens out. True. I think the tech updates are a definite plus. It's like having a new car every year. Honestly though, I think it's time we start making a more significant move towards greener options. The planet is really suffering, and all of us need to do our part. Couldn't agree more. There was something else on my mind while we're on this. Did you hear about Facebook planning to rename the company? Something about expanding the brand? Oh yeah, I saw that on Twitter. I think it's Meta. Exactly! Meta. It's supposed to reflect their shift towards the metaverse concepts they're exploring. It’s quite ambitious, if you ask me. Building a whole new virtual world. Definitely ambitious, but also timely. I think we are at a point where we need to reconsider our relationship with social media and the internet as a whole. Absolutely. It's quite worrying sometimes the power these tech platforms have over our lives and freedom. Yeah. It's a bit concerning when you really think about it. I know. But at the same time, it's hard to imagine life without it now. How do we balance privacy and the benefits of these platforms?

Bro, did you see that??! We've hit jackpot today. Sales have been crazy, even for a Friday. Yeah, I noticed. I need to work out how to get all these into the till without messing up though! You've always been the expert with that tiny keypad isn't it? Haha, that's why I'm still struggling with why the report still comes out wrong! But seriously, even with keeps coming backwards, today was actually fun. We had this one customer who was just, like, really into our lazy tongs. Really into them? Yeah, like, was about to walk out of the store without them and then saw them - "Hold on, I need these", started acting like it's the most important thing they've ever known. That's quite the story. Anyway, shall we actually watch the film now? This kid's movie on is actually quite interesting - "Cloudy with a chance of meatballs"? I haven't seen it for ages, what's it about? Ah, it's quirky, you know, the whole 'food falling from the sky in a small town' concept. I used to think the core theme was just like, ‘dream big or something,’ but now I'm kinda pondering if there's a deeper message about, like, 'consequences of playing with nature' or something? Thoughts? True, I'd say there's definitely something there. Actually, that scene where Flint creates the food machine... I reckon it could symbolize how science should serve people, but if used wrong, just leads to... chaos. Yeah, and the mayor is this typical 'I just want to be popular' figure, really insincere, but he gets voted in because people are attracted to his superficial promises. You could say it's a bit of a comment on how politics works? Yep, that's a take I hadn't considered. It’s one of those films that are sorta sweet and fun for kids but have layers under the surface. Wonder what kids pick up on when they watch it. I mean, I remember my little bro got really upset when the machine went wrong and everyone hated Flint. But now, knowing more, I see it as more about learning from mistakes. Right, and his speech at the end? "Dad always said, 'It's okay to try and fail, but it's not okay to fail to try'. That’s pretty much a life lesson right there.

Ah, Phil, great to see you again! How was your day? I've been hearing so much about the Premier League lately. It's been alright, mate! Just the usual. Made some great journeys through the city today. Seen some interesting things though, the usual mix of drama and excitement in Liverpool questions. You'd expect nothing less. I've been teaching my students about the socialism in football and how it can actually influence politics, you know? Just had a lecture on how New Labour was so influenced by football culture in the UK, especially in its early days. Really? That's a fascinating angle. I always thought football was just about the match and the pint at pub afterwards. Oh, but there's much more to it. You see, Tony Blair actually used the "Cool Britannia" and "Third Way" concepts to kind of mirror the dynamics we see in football. You've got this balance between individual performance and teamwork, which in Blair's view, mirrored the society they were trying to build. That's really interesting, I never thought about it like that. Oh it's definitely there. When Blair wanted to balance between the different socio-economic groups, just like how a football team needs defenders, midfielders, forwards... they all have different roles but work together to win. It also aligns with the idea of individualism within a collective, which Blair advocated for in his politics. Makes sense, especially if you consider how different groups in society contribute to its functioning. But what about today? What are the current plans for Labour? I always hear stuff about reviving the party doesn't come across well. Oh, that's a fair point. The Labour Party has had its ups and downs since Blair’s era. But the current leadership under Keir Starmer is trying to revive it a bit, by focusing on the "socio-economic" team effort again. So, trying to bring back the New Labour ideas but with a modern twist? Exactly. It's about rebalancing the sense of team and individual contribution. But of course, there’s the challenge of moving people away from Corbyn's more radical approach. Starmer is trying to keep them together, but it's not easy. So, the battle for the Labour heart right now is about reconciling these two different styles? Essentially. And it's mirrored in football too, you know?

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was doing some BNC recordings in South London? It was fascinating! The varieties of accents and dialects there are so diverse, you'd be amazed. That sounds interesting! I've always been curious about how English varies across regions. You involved in researching for something specific, or just generally about linguistic diversity? I was actually working on a project looking into the use of different word endings in speech patterns. Like how some people say "gonna" instead of "going to". We got some really fascinating data, seeing how those localized patterns change even just within a few miles. It must be really cool to dive into those semantic nuances. It is! Also, we recorded some incredible samples from the London dialect which are almost like a language on their own sometimes. That's true! I've always been amazed by the English spoken in different parts of the UK. I barely understand some of the slang in Wales sometimes, let alone regional London dialects. For sure! We've got a ton of recordings from Swansea and Cardiff but London is a different beast. Yeah, I can't even imagine trying to learn that. Speaking of which, I saw you were on LinkedIn the other day. You must be very active? I'd say I try to be, especially for work. But honestly, sometimes it feels more like social media than a professional network. That's so true! Have you taken up any new social media platforms recently? I've been trying to navigate this new app called Beep. Haven't quite figured out what’s it's for yet, or how to use it for professional purposes. But it’s just me, I guess. I’m a bit old-fashioned in my networking style. I hear you. I’ve been meaning to join Beep but I’m not convinced it’s useful for my line of work. I think for us, LinkedIn for work and Instagram for relaxation usually works. Exactly! Though sometimes I see how people use it for work and it seems so... commercial and forced. Totally. There's also the issue of job postings being more like clickbait, you know? Totally. But thinking about this reminds me, have either of you ever thought about living abroad? Definitely thought about it lots of times! But practicality holds me back.

Yo, mate, did you finish reading that novel you've been banging on about? Yeah, I was just slumped on the sofa, talked about it for ages, unreal! Made me think about all the interns we've had. Still trying to get the system right though, huh? Exactly! We've had some talented ones, but it's about making sure they get enough support and feedback. I'm actually struggling right now, as I'm doing an internship myself at a publishing house. Right, get out of there, let me know if you need any advice! Will do. But seriously, I just had a bizarre encounter with one of the supervisors. What happened? You know how some people react to tattoos? Yeah, well, that's what happened. It's kind of a sensitive topic for him, I guess. It reminded me, though, we need to talk about our own plans. What are you guys up to for Christmas? Ah, right on time! I'm starving! For a moment there I thought it was just me who was hungry. Not to mention, the house renovation is kind of throwing everything off. We need to figure out what to do with the living area. Any thoughts? Well, I've been looking at some interior design ideas online. Maybe a nice mix of modern and classic? We could take inspiration from some of the recent trends in London design, really make it pop. I'm all for it. Food first, though. I saw some awesome doesn't-live-far-from-here London street food spots that I've been wanting to try. Except, we've been all busy and haven't had a chance. Food, then house together, and a few days off for Christmas. Sounds like a plan. If we're going to do that, we should plan it next week. Also, and this is important, let's make sure we'll have something that aligns with my dietary needs. I'm on this new plant-based diet and I don't want to end up at any of those old-school places we used to love, but can't go to anymore. Oh, don't worry, sis. I have a few great recommendations that are plant-based. And we can compromise on the house decor too. Maybe use some remodeled or second-hand pieces we can find around here? More eco-friendly and budget-friendly.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to explain the difference between 'lift' and 'elevator' to one of my students? They were so confused! Oh, yes, international language learners often do face questions like that. Absolutely, and sometimes it's about more than just vocabulary, it's about cultural nuances as well. But actually, that reminds me I bought a new recipe book and it uses so many words that are more common here in the U.K. than in other English-speaking countries. That's interesting! Are you planning to try out some new recipes? Yeah, actually. It just says 'flat white' as if everyone knows what that means. Then I have to explain that it's just a type of coffee and that coffee culture is quite different here. Oh, I know how it is. I've run into the same thing with American recipes - it's like they never use the same measurement units or ingredients! Exactly! For me, it's usually about explaining that we might use 'lorry' instead of 'truck' or 'chips' instead of 'fries' – it's these small things that can really trip a learner up. Absolutely. And do you find that it helps them to travel or live in Britain if they know these differences? Definitely. I've had students who went on exchange programs and they were much more comfortable once they understood all these little differences. Plus, they can't even order food without knowing what things are called. Oh, food and traveling, that brings me to, did you make plans to travel this year? More plans than actual trips, I’m afraid, but I am hoping to get to Spain. I've always wanted to see Barcelona and learn some Spanish too. That sounds great! Spanish is so useful and it's on my bucket list too. Yes, and I find it's also helping in my own cooking. I've started making tapas and it's fun. Though, I have to admit, I have a real weakness for English dishes like Sunday roasts and pies – comfort food. Those are classics. I do love a good pie or pasty when I'm feeling down. Totally. But thinking about recipes, I wonder what you've been up to food-wise? Any new recipes you’ve been experimenting with? I’ve been trying to be healthier recently so I’ve been making a lot of veggie dishes.

I've decided I need a teaching break. I have enough students today. Imagine lecturing to people who would rather be anywhere else but here. You're right. There's nothing like the blank stares or nodding heads without any interest. It's days like today that make me wonder if I'd be happier doing something else. But then I think about our students who really care and it makes it all worth it. That's true. It's always the ones who respond that make it all worthwhile. Speaking of, have you seen John and Sienna lately? Not recently, no. They've been pretty busy preparing for grad school. John is doing research and Sienna is planning her thesis. They're both so passionate about their work. I always hope they'll find success. Absolutely. They've worked so hard. What about Mark and Rachel? They've also been quite busy with their businesses. But I hope they're taking time to enjoy each other's company. I hope so too. They're such a busy couple with both of them working on their respective projects while raising kids. They make me tired just thinking about it, . Exactly. But I really admire their energy and dedication, especially to their kids. Indeed. They're both wonderful parents. I know. It’s always a highlight when I catch up with them and learn about the kids’ latest antics. Those are always the best stories. And let’s not forget about Emma and Dan. I’ve been seeing them a bit more, they always bring a smile. They do. It’s good to see them getting out of their usual routines. True. I think the four of us really need to plan another dinner soon. Definitely, that would be nice. On a completely unrelated note, have you noticed...blushes... No, what about them? They're just... I swear they're looking weirder by the week. Perhaps it’s the stress. I didn’t notice. Are they seriously that bad? Well, they’re...kind of odd. Weird, in a good way? No, maybe too long or something. They look fine to me. Oh, I just need to cut them, I think. You know what? There’s a salon near our place that I've been wanting to try. We could probably get a last-minute appointment. Oh, that would be great. A little pampering never hurts.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that film I saw last week? It's quite possibly the most absurd thing I've seen this year! Are you still into all the oddball films? Still into that? Oh yes! I just love the way they sometimes manage to make us question the status quo. It's like a breath of fresh air. Now, this film had a bizarre conspiracy theory at its core. Conspiracy theories? I always find those fascinating, even if they're not true. Like that one about the illuminati and celebrities. I used to be so into it. Though, let me tell you, even if there was something to it, it’s all probably just big business and showbiz making money on people's fear and curiosity. Absolutely. Still, it's fun to explore these ideas, right? But the film was so good at pulling off this “passing off” as legit. I mean, their research and whatnot was really convincing. Now that I'm a language teacher, I have to say I've come across all sorts of different media types in English classes. It’s interesting to see what the kids are interested in these days. Yeah, you can't underestimate the extent to which media shapes our discussions, especially among the youth. Like, my niece is obsessed with, you know, the silly dance challenges and all that... really bizarre stuff that never existed when we were that age. I know! I've had students who cite the most "Out There" sources as proof of some claims or theories, and you're left thinking if it’s educational or not. Definitely not a field day, I'm sure. No, but it does make for some interesting discussions. Speaking of changing times, any news on your graduate student life? Oh, I'm in the midst of collecting data and writing up my dissertation. It's on the impact of different dialects on language acquisition. It's been quite a challenge to set up the experiments, but it's good. That sounds like real meaty work. I can't imagine diving into corpus linguistics and all. How's it going? It's alright. I suppose it’s a bit of a cliché to say any PhD work is hard, but the um, the grunt work is really taking its toll. What can I say, a PhD is a beast of a task, I'm sure.

Dad, are you enjoying the scenery? We're already halfway to Cornwall! Yes, it's lovely, isn’t it? The fields of flowers and the birds flying over them. You’re right though, let's talk about the scenery. It's so different to what we have in London, isn't it? Definitely! I love how it changes so much from city to countryside. You get to see all the different types of fauna and flora along the way. It's like we're on our own little adventure! Absolutely. And the roads are so different too, like the colors of the road. Ah, what do you mean? Well, you see, the tarmac is so much more varied out here. We've had smooth and rough, black and yellow stripes, and then those bright blue marks that guide you in the night. Almost like the Yellow Brick Road in "The Wizard of Oz." You always make connections to books! That's so funny. I was just finishing the "Alice in Wonderland" book while on this trip. Lewis Carroll's descriptions of the English countryside are so vivid, yet here, it's like we're living it. Ah, nice to know you're enjoying classic literature as much as I do. Speaking of which, in Alice, the Queen of Hearts is from Wonderland, but in our world, if we were in "Wonderland," I don’t think we would need a car, it would probably be "Jamaica Inn!" Except, we're on our way to Cornwall, not Cornwall’s darker counterpart! More like "Jamaica Inn" than Wonderland, I think! But it's nice to think about alternatives. Speaking of darkness, have you noticed how wind turbines seem to pop up everywhere nowadays? You've a keen eye for that! It’s surprising how common they are. Makes you think about the old ways of generating power, like coal or even earlier, just using windmills. Exactly! Can you imagine having to send a message to someone far away without phones or the internet? Like those old Morse code telegraphs? Or the use of Braille for those who couldn't see, or even languages like Latin. Languages and communication methods have changed so much, haven't they? Yes, all these things seem so quaint now, but I suppose they were really important at some point. We rely so heavily on texts and internet now. Remember when we were younger, we used to send letters or use the old dial-up internet?

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time during my university days when I tried to cheat at a game and got caught out? You, cheat at a game? Never thought I'd hear that from the honest, hardworking girl from Sunderland. It's unlikely! It was just a harmless pub quiz, actually. We were playing Trivial Pursuit and I had a friend who was an absolute whizz at history. She was sitting across the room, and I was like, "Sally, you've got to help me here!" And what happened then? Well, we were in the middle of answering a geography question - "What's the longest distance swam without stopping in the English Channel?" - and I whispered the answer to her. But she decided to shout it out, thinking we were in a study group, not a competitive quiz! Oh, I can just imagine the looks on everyone's faces! Yeah, and worse, the quizmaster figured it out straight away. He's like, "Maria, did you get that from the 'interweb', or what?" Well, at least you weren't trying to cheat in your job, Maria. I'd have ripped you a new one for that! True that! Although I do wish they didn't increase the price of petrol so much. I was at the petrol station the other day and it's the highest I've seen it this year. I know what you mean. The cost of living really is shooting up. It’s strange because in my field, people are more likely to question the necessity of certain projects rather than just accept them automatically. Yes, that's right. Back in my day, it was very different. I grew up during and after World War Two. Petrol rationing was a thing of every day – you couldn’t just pick up a car like you can now. That’s so interesting, Grandad! I can't imagine having to ration petrol. It was a very different time. We made-do and mended, just like the Queen advised. You all take things like petrol and constant internet access for granted now. It's true. But at least our thinking about resources has shifted somewhat. I work with companies to help them implement sustainable practices – often, it’s not just about using less, but using differently. That’s great, though it can be tough when you’re a student like me, trying to save up for rent and all that.

Mum, I've been meaning to ask you - have you decided where you want to put the Victorian tea set from Granny's estate sale? It's been sitting in the box in the attic for years now. You were thinking of using it when we moved to the new house though, right? Oh, yes! I haven't forgotten about it. It's been something on my mind, but I've been so caught up with the wedding preparations of our cousin, Emily. Now that you mention it, I think we should set it aside a special spot in the new dining room alongside the fine china. We could use it for family gatherings and special occasions. What do you think? That sounds like a brilliant idea, Mum. And speaking of moving, how's the inventory list going? Did you get the kitchen appliances sorted out in the list? Well, the fridge, stove, and dishwasher are all planned out, but we still need to decide whether to go with the washer and dryer set we already have or get new ones. And remember that pair of good silverware from your late uncle's collection? We should definitely include those in the list. For sure! We should keep it on the list as well, it's still in good condition. Speaking of silverware, how are you handling all the packing? You seem so busy. If you want, I can come over and help you sort the library or anything else. I have some free days next week. That would be really helpful, dear. I could use some extra hands. The library in itself is a big task. And your help would be especially appreciated. We might have to prioritize some of the smaller items like the plates and cups for now. No problem at all, Mum. Just let me know when you're ready. And, if I may ask, have the marriage plans for Emily side of things gone smoothly? No last-minute dramas or jet lags to navigate? Surprisingly, yes! The wedding was lovely and everyone arrived before the ceremony without any issues. Although, Emily was a bit of a wreck a couple of days before from that lengthy flight from New York. Ah yes, that London-New York leg can certainly play tricks on you. I just got back from a week in Tokyo and I felt the effects for a few days too.

I've decided I need a new haircut. I'm so bored of my bob. Have you seen any cool hairstyle trends lately? Hmm, I've been following a few hair influencers on social media. There's a lot of experimenting with different textures and colors – like wavy hair with undercut and colorful streaks. But if you'd like something more traditional, a "shag haircut" has been making a comeback, right? Shag haircut? Oh, I've seen that. It could be a refreshing change. Though, I'm also really interested in seeing how long I can grow my hair out – always loved the look of long, luscious hair despite the trouble managing it. I wish I had that problem. Mine is thinning a bit now - oh well, the perks of being a researcher and staying up all night sometimes. Yeah, speaking of hair... how’s your research going? Completed any big milestones recently? It's been a bit slow, to be honest. I’m running into some issues with my supervisor about the direction of my thesis. We’re discussing some A-Level reforms that could have an impact on the policy area I'm focusing on, but he wants me to explore it from a different angle. It’s interesting, but it’s also really challenging. Ah, I know the academic life can be... A-Level reforms, huh? There’s been a lot in the news about that. Thought they were considering making the exams less stressful for students, but what’s the latest? Yeah, they're considering making it more project-based and the exams are supposed to be less content-driven. The idea is to reduce the burden of one-time exams and let the students showcase their skills through the year, rather than being judged on just one day. That sounds interesting. As someone who dealt with A-Levels, I can personally see the stress they put on students. But will it really change much if they're changing the format but not addressing the pressure to perform? Absolutely, that’s the challenge. I’ve read in some reports that while the format might change, if the structure of university admissions doesn’t change, the pressure remains. It’s like the students are preparing for the show, not the journey. True, and speaking of systems in need of reform... what about the NHS? Did you catch that recent BBC program about the crisis in the service?

Yo, lads and lasses. I'm pretty sure we've all hit some kind of wall with these GCSE and A-levels and university stuff. Right? Definitely, mate. You can't even get a decent voice in your head without it just pipping up, 'But what do you want to do with your life now?' Exactly, it’s a constant pressure. Whether it’s socialism, capitalism, or just actually dealing with the fact I can't afford the bus fare to uni. You know what's odd? Back when our parents were our age, it wasn’t this complicated. Like, most of them knew they'd be factory workers, lads. Yeah, but then again, I think there is this expectation among our age group that we need to be millionaires or something by the time we're 30. Exactly, and it's not just parents or society, it's sometimes our own peers too. Like, if you're not excelling in your dream career within a year of leaving uni, it's like you've failed. And it's not even just about jobs or financial success. It's this concept of 'personal growth' that everyone keeps throwing at us. I once tried that. I ended up in a Stampede-esque yoga session trying to 'find myself'. Ended up more confused than before. Honestly though, I think it’s good that we're all in this together, really. But does anyone else find the financial side of all this really stressful? Oh, absolutely. I'm basically living off pasta and beans and the loan that I might not pay back for years. Same here. I had to miss the trip to London for the weekend because I couldn't afford it. Plus, the fact that the local pubs charge a bomb now just adds to the stress. It's one thing to deal with the financial aspect but then there's also dealing with the stigma. You feel like you're somehow less if you’re not working 2 jobs on top of university. For sure, like we're supposed to be overworked and underpaid but still be zero-obligation millennials who want to save the world and eat avocado toast. Yeah, plus the whole 'mental health awareness' thing is great and all. But if you're actually struggling with anxiety or depression, good luck finding any real support or understanding.

I've been thinking a lot about friendships lately. I've realized that sometimes, you just outgrow people and you know they don't contribute much to your life anymore, but it's hard to just cut ties. That's so true. I've had friends who I used to see all the time, but over time, our lives and interests have just gone in different directions and it feels unnatural to keep forcing those connections. But still, it can be hard to end things, even if it's just a slow phase out. You start to feel like a bad person. Exactly! And what's weird is that sometimes these are people who were once very close. You share memories, laughter... but now, there’s just a sense of obligation to still be "friends". What's that phrase? An acquaintance you hope will never find you on social media, I suppose. Yeah, spot on. I've recently been dealing with it with this one old uni mate. We had a great time at uni, but now he's firmly in a different world than mine. Every time we see each other it's all about party stories and old times, and I just feel like I'm pretending to still be interested. It’s interesting, we sometimes think the right thing to do is to maintain these relationships even when they don’t feel authentic anymore, maybe for fear of being seen as unfriendly, or maybe because we feel a sense of loyalty or guilt about ending things. Definitely. And social media definitely doesn’t help. It keeps us in a loop of "oh, haven't seen you for ages, let’s catch up!" even if we both know neither of us actually wants or needs to. But the problem is, unlike romantic relationships, there’s no script for a "we've grown apart" conversation in platonic friendships. No, it seems so much more complicated. With romantic relationships, there's an end, but with friends… it's like a gradual disappearance that can feel awkward and guilt-ridden. Exactly. I've had friends who essentially just drifted away and I've had to deal with it, but I've never been the one to initiate a clean break. I just don't want to hurt anyone's feelings, and it feels easier to just let things fade naturally, even if it's over years and years.

So, aunty Lena, how was your week? Oh, it's been quiet as usual, love. Just doing a bit of drawing and reading, of course! I love that you've really found time for your art now, even after all these years. You always inspire me. You'd think I'd have gotten bored by now, but it keeps me young, and I'm grateful I have as much time to devote to it. And how about that exhibition coming up? You're still working on the pieces for it? Yes, absolutely! It's going to be quite an interesting one, dear. I've been drawing a lot of London scenes, looking to highlight the beauty of our city. That sounds fantastic. I've actually never seen your newer work. Do you have anything on your mind that's particularly progressed you as an artist? Well, as much as I love painting the London landscape, I've recently started incorporating some abstract elements in there. It's been a real challenge, but I find it really enhances the pieces. For me, as someone studying art history and criticism, I find it fascinating when artists mix different styles. It pushes the boundaries of traditional representation and interpretation, while still capturing the essence of the subject in a more modern way. Well, I'm glad you notice, then. It's been a bit of an experiment, but I believe it adds depth and emotion to the pieces. Absolutely, it does. I also couldn't help but notice that you're using a lot of bright colors. Is there a reason for that? Yes, I've always been drawn to brighter colors, but I think now, more than ever, I find the vibrancy important to the feelings I try to express. Perhaps because the world around us can be so grey sometimes. I totally get that. It's one of the reasons I loved your earlier works so much. The way you brought warmth and life into even the most mundane scenes. Ah, but I'm not just revisiting old techniques and styles just because. I'm trying to say something new. After all, isn't that what art is about? It absolutely is. And speaking of art, I swear those art history lectures you're attending must be fascinating. I'm always curious what you're learning. They are, actually. I just realized how much art can be influenced by the social and historical context of its time.

I've decided I need to eat before I head to the gym today. I feel like if I don't, I'll be out of energy halfway through. You're quite right about that. A quick snack can make all the difference, especially when you're not used to the physical activity. You've been staying pretty sedentary on this trip, haven't you? I'm afraid so. We've been doing a lot of driving and very little working out. But even so, it's been lovely, don't get me wrong. I just need to find that balance. Balance is key. I used to run into that in London too. Gym just wasn't fitting in with city life as much as I wanted it to. Yeah, London's always rushing somewhere. Even finding time to breathe is a luxury! True. But, you know, it's interesting how our perception of time changes when we're on a journey like this. One moment feels like an eternity, the next it's gone in a flash. Definitely. I find the sense of perspective coming from moving slowly through the countryside is quite liberating. Makes me realize how much time I waste on pointless stuff back home, really. It's like a different scale for measuring time. A journey like this, especially in a campervan, forces you to slow down. But you also feel like you're getting much less done, which is oddly refreshing at times! Well, I guess the lack of Wi-Fi helps too. There's a kind of mental detox, isn’t there? Definitely. Though the lack of gym opportunities hasn’t been just me, I've noticed fewer decent gyms in rural areas around Europe compared to cities. It’s a bit of a double-edged sword for us fitness fans. True, but changing the scenery and having more time on my hands might mean I do less gym, but maybe try more varied outdoor activities. I've been meaning to try hiking more. That sounds great! I mean, speaking of outdoor activities, have you ever tried a proper 5K run in the Polish countryside? Honestly, I've just been trying to keep up with the driving, really! But a hike or a good run in these beautiful landscapes would be amazing. I remember when I ran during my uni days in Cambridge. It was nothing like this, of course, but it was invigorating.

I've decided I need more hand-thrown mugs for our garden room. It's been ages since I've last made some myself. You love your pottery, Alison! I remember when you used to spend hours in the shed churning out mugs for the whole family. It's therapy! Plus, it means I can stop buying those commercial mugs that don't actually keep the drink warm. Oh, I always hated how keeps coming out cold. You know, when you're out in the garden, milk goes off pretty quickly if not kept chilled. Exactly, that's why I need more of your hand-thrown ones to line up around the garden table. How about the weather? It's summer, should be perfect for your little garden parties. It has been warm, but we did get a rainy spell last week. The garden needs a little TLC now. And last night we had a power cut. Almost an hour's wait for the electricity to return. For a moment there I thought it was the 80s again! I remember the power cuts back then. The candles and torches. Same. But this time we were lucky, nothing vital was on. Just a bit of inconvenience. I did see, however, a huge spider in the garden yesterday. Almost as big as my thumb! Spiders are quite normal around here, especially in the summer. Still, not my favorite part of gardening. Never measured spiders in thumb sizes, did you, mum? No, but I did measure the grass by hand back in my teaching days. Right, sure. Well, I was thinking of getting out the lawnmower soon if the weather holds up. Couldn't manage that now, but I'm sure your back would be grateful for some help. Maybe you can come over and sit this one out while I struggle? Always ready for that! Although, I did see your new garden bench. Looks very comfy. Yes, company and conversation seem more important now than playing gardener. Speaking of which, you've done well with the decorating. The room feels light and airy. Thanks! I've been meaning to paint it a while, and it really made a difference. And you've got all these lovely little touches, like the old gardening tools on the walls. Well, why not honour the past a bit? Thought it would give the space some character. Quite fitting for someone who's always been a bit of a do-it-yourself person when it comes to home improvements.

Mum, Dad, and Grandpa. I was thinking, since we've not had a proper family holiday in ages, what if we planned one for the holidays after our exams? Maybe somewhere coastal? Oh, that sounds lovely! Where were you thinking? Cornwall again? Or perhaps a bit further afield this time, why not? I've never been to Wales. They say it's beautiful. Yeah, or maybe something in Scotland? I've always wanted to see those lochs and castles. Well, Scotland's a bit far, isn't it? We'd have to consider travel times and costs. Right, but we could mix it up - maybe we could do a little road trip. Dad could drive and we could take turns reading maps, I'd do all the navigation! That might be a little risky, child! However, travel options are plenty. We could also look at the English coast, perhaps something like Eastbourne or Brighton. Oh, Eastbourne is lovely. And it's not as expensive as you might think. We could also stay at a nice B&B. That could be really fun. We can even take a train, right? It's like the perfect family adventure! Ah, but have we thought about what everyone's interests are, especially Grandpa? He isn't in the best of health for long trips, you know. That's thoughtful of you, dear. I don't mind a nice gentle holiday. But it's not just about the travel; I might want some music sessions or a local pub to enjoy some traditional folk concerts. Right. Eastbourne has plenty of festivities during the holiday seasons, so maybe that could be a good fit. If we're going to Eastbourne, perhaps we could plan to visit the Hastings Pier and then some beach days too! So, after watching that film, did you find anything else besides's Heath Ledger character that you'd want to talk about? Oh, definitely. I thought the whole unrealistic expectation of love and all that was quite odd. But also the way they portrayed the school, like portraying it as something very grand and kind of intimidating isn't really how I see my school. Like ours is a very friendly and small school, nothing like their fancy prep school right? Ah, absolutely. Our school is nothing like that! I mean, even our relationships among students aren’t nearly as dramatic. None of that “Puck” situation we had [laughs]. Hence, sometimes it's funny to see how they exaggerate everything. Exactly! But, do you think we could actually get tickets to the school play? Maybe even grab a few friends and make it a sort of film-inspired watch-along or something? That sounds like a brilliant idea! We should ask some friends if they’re interested. I’ve heard they’re doing some fun plays this term, but I’ve never checked what. If it’s anything like that film though, we’re in! [laughs] If it’s anything like that film, we’d need to take a few minutes to process it all afterwards. Seriously though, we should definitely check if there’s something worth going for. So, aside from all this, hows school been for you? Going alright? [sighs] It’s been okay, but I do have exams coming up and it's stressing me out. Seems like the teachers keep piling on more homework just when I feel like I’m keeping up. Same here. But we’ve had enough of stressing about school, haven’t we? What’s planned for the Easter break? I’m just nervous about what to pack because I want to make sure I look good if we go to some of the hotspots like Covent Garden and all that. Yeah, I’ve already made like 3 different outfits lists! But you’ve got to remember that London’s pretty chilly in spring, so don’t pack just shorts.

I've been meaning to ask you lot about this new thing called Facebook. I've heard it's where all the young folks are these days, sharing their pictures and chicken soup for the soul advice. Aye, yeah, it’s quite a phenomenon, isn’t it? I kind of got into it because my grandkids are always talking about it. It’s like a whole world that I’ve hardly touched. Oh, it's very popular for sure. But even I keeps coming across loads of odd stuff - most of which I ignore. Like, some people, they share every single thought they have about everything. Yeah, it’s a bit like the old village square but with everyone’s private lives exposed in the middle of it. But it can also be quite useful, connecting with old friends and family. And what's this thing about sharing chicken soup for the soul advice? I thought that was something you got from these American books. Oh, it’s still a thing. They say that sharing uplifting messages helps people on bad days. I've shared a few myself, mostly gardening tips or silly quips about life. Actually, I've found it quite useful for research and connecting with other people in the same field. It can be overwhelming though, especially when people keep sharing stuff like conspiracy theories or current affairs that end up making you feel worse. True, there’s definitely a downside to it all too. An overload of information and opinions. But it's like any other tool, you learn how to navigate it. I might just have to join this Facebook to see what all the fuss is about. Maybe I’ll post a few tales about my time growing up in Costessey. We’d love to see that, actually. Your stories are quite the thing. Speaker_3 and You know, back in my day, we didn’t need none of this social media to stay in touch. We’d just knock on each other’s doors, have a cuppa, and swap news. Still the best way, I think. No distractions. I still like that idea. Speaking of distractions, I saw something on TV the other day about OCD during the pandemic. Someone mentioned how for some people, it was like their symptoms were exacerbated with all the chaos and uncertainty. That makes sense, really. I remember times when life got too much and I’d get a bit... particular about things.

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about my stupid story from today? I lent a colleague my pen and she never gave it back to me. It’s just a pen, but it was my favourite. Oh, bless, another drama with your pen, Auntie Sarah! Like the time you "accidentally" spilled coffee all over your journal, right? Oh, that was even worse! I think it's a good omen. Like how lazy you’ve always been about keeping track of stuff, but I’ve been perfecting my organization skills. Yeah, well, let’s see how organized you are when you have a life-size, raging toddler running around. True! So, Sarah, you never got it back, did you? That’s just so like you. Nope! So, I'm forced to rummage through a dusty drawer for a new one. That's a good one! Speaking of lost things, how about we talk about good times instead? Like that holiday we had in Germany last year? Ah, the bratwurst, the beer, the language, all so good. Can you believe they never spoke English? I thought I was pretty good but... it was like trying to learn a new language in a real-life context. Well, Helen, you did pretty well! I mean, we were all stumped at times. Yeah, and weren’t we surprised by the dialect differences even within the same country? Absolutely. I remember we were in Munich and no one could understand my Cockney accent! It’s like when your granddad tried to speak French on that holiday before. I don’t know how we survived without laughter. Oh, Dad, if you're going to mock me Ah, come on, it was just a bit of fun! Did you know, though, that learning a bit of the local language can make a big difference in connections? I know. We met this lovely old lady in Cologne who spoke only her local dialect and a bit of English but any word we knew in German made her so delighted. It’s true. A bit of respect for the local culture can go a long way. Yes, and trying to learn a few words makes a big difference. I remember when we were going on that drive through Bavaria, we stumbled over what to call the trains but the conductor helped when he saw we were trying. And it wasn’t just the language; the food, the culture, the old history.

Yo, mate, been a while. How have you been since we last caught up? Yeah, it's been ages! I've been busy with work, the usual routine of kitchen life but I've managed to squeeze in some time for the things I love too. You know, I've been on the hunt for new culinary inspiration, maybe a new recipe book to challenge my skills. Cooking's always been your passion right? I never thought you’d pick up on it as a career though, I always remember how you were totally into drums when we were younger. Oh, that was a different life! I've always wanted to work behind the scenes in live entertainment, but kitchen life’s kind of consumed me. Though, there was this festival I worked at in Cornwall a few summers ago, that was a taste of it. We had a lot of bands playing, and it was pretty exhilarating. Really? That sounds great! It’s something I’m seriously considering as a career path after I graduate. Legit mate! Music industry’s full of opportunities. Did the internship open any doors or give you any new ideas for the future?

Alright, James, so first things first, have you got today's schedule squared away? Well, yeah, talked to Miss Brown this morning and we've got two more books to read for English and our project on the history of Durham due soon. Right, just so I can make sure I know where to pick you up this afternoon. Yeah, and I'm free actually, as soon as I pick up this coffee! Are you still on about coffee every time we meet? It's actually pretty fun. But I need some old pictures of Durham, might I have? Here, I've got some from a few years ago when we went to the castle. I'm sure they might help. These are great, Mum. I especially like the one of the town in the 1950s. Yeah, that's a good one. Shows how much it's changed while still keeping its essence, you know? Definitely. I've been thinking about maybe organizing a history session with the school, get all the kids interested. That's a great idea! You could even speak with Mr. Wilson about that. He's always keen on local history projects. Yeah, that could work. More people should know about our history! Absolutely. Speaking of which, have you checked out the town's new shopping list? It's full of great places to grab a bite after school now. Not checked it out yet, but might do so after this. You know, it's quite loud in here. Mind if I speak up a bit? Again, it's the 'mum volume', almost as if you're just being louder and louder! Well, sorry if I'm disturbing anyone. How can we discuss our plans if we can't hear each other? It's fine, Mum. No one's complained anyways. That's because they probably think it's just the usual mum and son chat. By the way, how's your friend, Luke, doing? Luke's fine, we've been planning a domino drive over the summer. A domino drive? That sounds fun! Do you mind if I join? Would love that! Really? Well, I'll think about it.

Yo, mate! It's been ages! How have you been? Hey! It's been ages too! I've been well, just been busy with work and all the usual stuff. How about you? Still enjoying life in England? Yeah, I am. I got myself a new flat in Sussex, just unpacking the last of the boxes. That sounds fab! Sussex is lovely. I'm glad you've moved somewhere nice. Thanks. It's been quite the move, changing jobs and all, but it's been worth it. What was your old job like? It's funny you mention it - I used to be a teacher, but then I decided to become an English Language instructor. It’s a good change, though I have to say the hours are better. Teaching can be quite a stressful job, you know? You bet it can. But I prefer it now, it feels more fulfilling. Although, I have to say, it's been a challenge adapting to what the students expect. They really seem to like learning about the common uses and changes in colloquialisms! Ah, I'm sure. Where did you train, while we're on the subject? I did my graduate degree in linguistics over in London. It was a bit of a hoot, had to get used to all the Cockney slang! I can imagine, mate! But you should've shown me the ropes! You know, I also plan to record some audio samples for a project, it's about regional accents and how they change over generations. That sounds super interesting! I might be able to help you. My side of the family has some strong West Midlands influences, so. That would be awesome! Could really use another voice or couple to get a broader sample. Sure, but what's the project actually for? It's for a research project I'm working on. We're looking at how some linguistic features - like certain sayings or pronunciations - just disappear when people move from one region to another. It’s all for a paper we're writing. That's intriguing and relevant right about now. I've noticed almost gone over to my grandmother in Bronsgrove and she still uses these complete old-timey phrases. Exactly! We've got all sorts of unique sayings in different parts of England. I've been trying to map these changes and why they happen. You know, we could even collaborate on a blog or something like that?

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to proofread the local paper for typos? I was literally slumped over my desk, exhausted, but I found a really funny one that read 'the rodeo will be held in the church parking lot' instead of 'rode'! That's hilarious, and such a good thing you caught that! Now, moving on to less laughable topics, how about you? How have things been coming along at work with the new support team? Oh, it's been a bit of a challenge. But we're getting there, slowly but surely. It's been a bit of a learning curve with online support, but we're adapting. Yeah, online support can be tricky. I've found that with my work, sometimes it's easier to talk to clients face to face, even virtually. Absolutely. But, you know, it's all about juggling. And it seems like we've all got more plates spinning than ever right now, or so it feels. I couldn't agree more. Speaking of busy lives, I was just thinking... you know, while the kids were at uni and my mum was still around, we didn't have much to worry about, health-wise. Now, though, it feels like everyone's got something going on. Health, yes. There's been a lot in the family, really. Your mum, your health issues, and I'm sure you're aware of some of the health concerns I've been dealing with myself. Oh, that reminds me... I was thinking about asking you, because you're someone I can trust to talk things through. You know about the cancer scare I went through last year? Yes, of course. I remember. That was such a shock to everyone, wasn't it? It was. And even though it was scary, and we did go through a tough time, I was so grateful that it was caught early. But after that experience, I've been thinking, when it comes down to it, how important health really is, not just physical but mental too. Absolutely. Over the past year, I've had to take care of my own health more carefully and deal with some pretty significant stress levels. Opening up with trusted friends and family like us can really help. I know. But I suppose what this whole ordeal made me realize was the importance of taking a step back, looking after ourselves, and not taking anything for granted.

Alright, boys, who was your favorite subject at school this term? I hope it was something more interesting than my old business studies class! Mine was definitely science. I really enjoyed our practical experiments. We even made this reaction happen with vinegar and baking soda. It was quite explosive! Ah, that sounds exciting! I loved our class on sustainable ecosystems, where we learnt about pollinator gardens. Our class set one up at school and planted lots of wildflowers. It was amazing to see all the bees and butterflies visiting it after a few weeks. I’m glad you enjoyed it. I struggled a bit with math this term, but I think the extra help sessions after school were helpful. What about sports? Anyone actively playing tennis or football? My team is going to the town cup finals at the weekend, so if you're free, you’re more than welcome to come. That would be great! I’ve been playing for the school team as well. I’m a bit nervous but excited. I’ve been practicing hard. That’s wonderful, I’m sure you’re doing well. Speaking of which, did either of you hear about the local tennis coaching classes starting up? Do think you’ll be interested? It’s a bit pricey, but very good quality. I think it sounds good. I’ve always wanted to improve my forehand. But is it too late for this year? Maybe not if you start soon. They usually open up spots as the term progresses. Plus, even if you can’t start sessions this term, it’s good to know for next year. Exactly, and it’s always beneficial to keep refining your skills. The coaches are highly recommended. Is this part of any bigger plan? Like if you’re looking at it as an opportunity to get a tennis scholarship or something? Good question. I think that depends on the commitment and if I can balance it well. But I have dreams of maybe getting an apprenticeship after school, perhaps in sports management or coaching. It seems like the UK has got some good programs. Apprenticeships are definitely a viable option worth exploring. There’s been a lot of support recently, especially in fields like sports and IT. And don’t dismiss those yet; they can lead to excellent careers. Hmm, I hadn’t thought of that. I’ve always thought about university straight after but any type of practical experience can’t be bad.

So, I hear you're planning on visiting Lancaster while you're there? I've never been but I've heard it's quite beautiful. It definitely is! I'm really excited. You know I've always been fascinated by the coastal towns around the UK, and this visit is a kind of weekend getaway for me. That sounds lovely! Speaking of the coast, have you heard about the recent cockle disaster near Morecambe Bay? I was quite shocked to hear about it. Oh yes! It is quite tragic. I guess it's a harsh reminder of just how dangerous some of those industries can be. It's a shame for the community, really. Definitely. I almost feel guilty considering just how much seafood I love, especially when I read about the lives lost from such a job. It's a bit of a wake-up call, isn't it? It makes me thankful for my office job, despite sometimes feeling it can be very routine. Absolutely. Offices can be stressful at times, but it's a far cry from the perils of jobs like that. Definitely. It's reminded me though to value what I have and perhaps to pursue some long-standing dreams. The coast is also great for 'fish and chips' so I'm hoping to make sure I get to try some, local, authentic ones. Oh, fish and chips, nice! I'd recommend avoiding the touristy places, if you can find a local eatery, really. But you should also consider the university, I'm sure they have some fantastic food places too. Good point, it's probably worth checking the university areas. As it happens, we might need to visit some universities, as part of my planning for my post-grad. Seems like the Morecambe Bay area has a few good language research programs. Speaking of research, how's your dissertation going? I’ve had my fair share of thesis writing, it can be quite a strain but rewarding when it's done. It’s going, slowly but surely. I've hit a bit of a roadblock lately. The literature review has been quite a headache, but I'm hoping to power through soon. It’s all about organizing ideas and structuring it properly. Again, it’s about those small milestones and managing your time well. Make sure to take breaks too. Stress can really hamper productivity.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new band that's been making waves these days? They're called The Archers. I've been listening to their stuff non-stop since I saw them live last Saturday down in Leeds. Ah, yeah! I heard about them, but I haven’t checked them out yet. What made you so into them? Honestly, the energy on stage is absolutely infectious. They’ve got this raw, gritty sound that feels really authentic. They’re from Sheffield, so it’s nice to see local talent getting a bit of spotlight. Yeah, that’s cool. Sheffield’s been putting out some great music lately, isn’t it? I’ve been listening to a lot of Arctic Monkeys recently and they’re proper inspiring. Have you heard any of their new stuff? Absolutely! I caught their new album release on Spotify and it’s brilliant. I loved going to the gig with you at the Leadmill for the Ronimo awards. Ah, that was a good night! I thought it was ace. Someone should make a roster of all the gigs we attend. It’d be a bloody good account of our weekend spent #rocking out. True that! The photographs from that night are still bringing a smile. Speaking of which, I saw there’s another event in the Sheffield arena coming up, aren’t there? Yeah, it’s probably the one with IDLES. They’re a new one for me, really, but they seem to be growing in popularity and all the buzz is that it’s going to be phenomenal. Okay, it’s a bit of the same arena, different event, but it seems IDLES are big on the Independent scene. I might give them a listen. Have you caught the Morecambe gig yet? I heard it was crowd of the year. No, haven’t yet. Just so busy with uni and all. But next time you’re in and around, let’s grab a ticket together for something. Definitely, I’m in. I was just on the phone with Sam last night and she said she’s trying to convince the group to go for it too so we might make a little gang for it. That would be brilliant! I’ll text her right now. How about we all meet up this weekend and finalize the plans? We could also catch up on what everyone’s been up to since we got back to uni.

Okay, so we all have one role and one action card each. Remember, don't panic, this is a collaborative game. Panic leads to more infections, you see.      Oh, because we haven’t seen that in the countless times we've played this. Seriously though, I've got the 'researcher', which always seems like a bit of a useless role for the first half of the game.      Not useless, dude. Your research can help identify the cure. Just try not to spread the infection to more cities while you’re looking for it, or we're all doomed.      Hence the importance of communication. It's not just about the cards, it's about working together as a team.      And good distribution of resources. Let's hope we can share the info effectively here. A bit like our charity work, really. Everyone working together to solve a common problem.      I assumed we’d be working together. After all, in a real pandemic, that’s what we’d need, right? Teamwork and coordination.      Exactly! Now, before we start, who's got the 'medical specialist'? Can we get that one to try and find the cure a bit quicker?      I don’t think anyone has that role. But it doesn't matter too much because we can always cooperate, right?      Cooperate? In commerce, sure. Here, it just looks like... ...like everyone's chasing their own goals.      It's designed that way to make the challenge interesting. Reality's more about strategy and luck.      I suppose. Our charity experience has taught us that sometimes we need to think several steps ahead, anticipate problems. Here, it's about anticipating where the disease might spread next.      That's almost like planning a new project in the classroom. We need to think ahead, work out who can travel where and when without causing outbreaks.      And all that while pretending to be a character that can cure diseases or fly a plane to any city. We're really pushing the boundaries of reality here.      Not if it helps us relax and bond, we're really having fun. Besides, a little imagination never hurt anyone.      Playing games like this can even help build teamwork skills. If we can coordinate here, maybe next time we can try something like Dungeons and Dragons?      Oh, you’re not talking about the tabletop game, I hope?      No, but that's been on my list to try.

So, children. We’ve got quite a few special days coming up and I thought we could start celebrating together – do you have any ideas? I want to have a big party like the one Daisy and I had last year? All her friends and us playing games and eating cake and cupcakes! Yeah! And can we watch some more CBeebies pantomimes? Maybe for your birthday, next week, we can plan something special.
