Right, so I'm considering moving out of London. The price's just getting ridiculous. Yeah, I hear you. I've been finding it pretty tough myself. Got some of the best-paying jobs in the city, but the cost of living, the stress, it’s kind of overwhelming. Exactly! I’ve moved back home to Hitchin, actually. It’s so much more relaxed and the cost of living is better, but the job market... I had to start teaching at schools. Which is fine, but not really what I wanted to do. That's a good point. I've been thinking of moving to the North. Maybe Manchester, or Liverpool. The tech industry is growing in Liverpool, right? Yeah, that’s true. And Northern places can be a lot more affordable. And the lifestyle, it’s definitely different from London. But there's also more cultural diversity, right? London’s creative and very international, which I miss when I’m up north. However, I couldn’t afford to stay. I think the cultural difference might be a big adjustment. We’re used to all the theatre, music, and art London offers. You’re right about that, but the 'diversity' of the North isn’t just cultural. I found people to be really nice, more friendly. It’s a different pace of life for sure. A slower pace of life, that's an interesting point. I've been trying really hard to keep up with my London friends, but it’s not the same from so far away. It's like a different world up there, isn't it? The North and South could be two different countries. But the food? Have you tried the food in the North? It’s just lovely, so different from anything we get here. Food is definitely better up there! And less expensive. True, but I’m actually changing the subject. Speaking of food, have we decided on anything for dinner tonight? I was thinking we could cook something new. I found an interesting recipe online. I’ve always wanted to try that Korean fried chicken recipe. That sounds good. Alright, Korean fried chicken it is. You two should consider looking for some good places to eat when you move. The food scene is growing in cities up North, especially Asian and other international food. You might be right. I often miss the variety of cuisine that's available in London but any recommendations?

Oh, did I ever tell you about my Dad's story when he took me to the market and bought me this plastic toy tractor when I was about 8? No, actually you've mention it occasionally. A bit of nostalgia, wasn’t it? Oh, and it was something durable, right? I mean, children can be quite rough with toys sometimes. Oh, indeed. It was very sturdy. And it even came with little plastic cows and a whole set of landscapes. You know, those miniature farms, barns… And what's more quintessentially British than miniature farmyard toys, I wonder. Well, when I think about it - oh yes! What's that phrase? "For little chaps and chapettes?" Ronseal equivalent for little ones, then. You know, I had something similar, though I’m a bit younger than you both? Maybe a few years younger. It was this plastic farmyard set from "Character World". My parents got it for me because they lived near a rather big farm in Peterborough. Seeing the real thing every day, but then having a model farm right in the house… Ah, that's nice. I'd love to visit a farm, especially one with an old barn. I've been meaning to plan a weekend trip to Norfolk or Lincolnshire and do some photography. I'd be right with you! Actually, that kind of aligns with what I've been planning. But the trip will have to wait until after this busy period at work. We’ve got some major auditing coming up so I need to prep. Of course, work first. That's always the priority. Though I hope we can make it happen in the summer. Definitely, let’s make it happen. And speaking of work, I have a bit of a struggle, though. As an accountant, I find sometimes the language we use in finance can be quite devoid of any personality, and it’s sometimes hard to connect with people in my region because of the dialect. Ah, I can understand that. Though sometimes our dialect gives us a unique connection, doesn't it? In HR, I’ve realized that often, it’s not just about using... universal language or um, “proper” English, but embracing our own dialects can make people warm up to you more. Absolutely, I've found that too. Especially when working internationally. So many times people prefer when you use local expressions or even your own dialect rather than trying to be "too" formal.

So, Mum, did you have any exciting experiences while you were away? I'm so jealous that you got to go on another trip! Absolutely, Dad! Can you tell us about it again? You've mentioned it a bit, but it sounds like the kind of holiday that's worth hearing about multiple times! Yeah, and I've got a few questions too. Did you walk a lot, or was there plenty of time to just relax? And what about food? Did you get to try anything particularly interesting or special during your trip? That's right. You'll tell us all about the long walks and the food. I heard about the walks earlier, but I’m keen to hear more details. Absolutely, please do share, husband. Unidentified: Thanks, everyone. So, I’d like to start with the walks. I managed to fit in some of the wonderful coastal walks you guys have always encouraged me to do. We’re looking at the paths around Whitby and Robin Hood's Bay. It was breathtaking! The scenery was just so different from what we have here in the village. That sounds lovely! For me, a good walk can make or break a holiday, you know? I’ve tried a few along the coast when we took our last holiday, but the pictures you sent looked incredible. Was there a particular route you enjoyed the most? Yeah, do tell. And did you get to try any local cuisine? I know you like trying new foods when traveling, especially if it’s seafood. Exactly! Tell us about the food. I know you’re going to reveal the absolute best places to eat. Yes, and maybe share the directions if possible. We might have to make a weekend trip out of it next time! She definitely was looking forward to trying a few treats, as always. One place I noticed in her emails was a little fish and chip shop couple of miles from Whitby. She raved about it in her letter, but I think you’ll want to hear from her about it. Wait, a fish and chip shop? I thought you’d be trying something more... exotic. But I suppose a good fish and chips always hits the spot. Exotic food is nice, but there's something timeless about the right fish and chips. However, this one must be special if you noticed it.

I've decided I need a new hobby. Been feeling a bit stuck in my job lately. Any suggestions? Maybe something engineering-related but not too deep into code? Oh, that's interesting. You know, one of my neighbors is into brewing his own beer. If you're interested in questions like chemistry and oxidation rates, you could consider that. But if you want something more hands-on, perhaps a DIY electronics kit? Speakers_1, actually, I've always been intrigued by CNC machines. Could be a fun project to keeps me engaged. I think it's a great idea. There's plenty of affordable starter kits out there. And with your engineering background, you'd pick it up in no time. Might just need to carve out dedicated time for it. I can recommend some resources if you like - I've got a friend who does this for fun and has some great tips. Speaking of which, I've seen some buzz about 3D printing too. What do you think about that? It's engineering meets art, right? You'd be surprised at what you can create. By the way, can anyone explain to me the mechanics involved in a pasta maker? I’ve tried a few times with friends, but it always comes out sticky or too dense. It’s all about the balance of the ingredients, the technique, and sometimes even the humidity in the kitchen. But for you, perhaps look into a device, like a good pasta extruder. It could be a really fun project to design or purchase one. I have a friend who’s working on his own design. Maybe we can get him in on a Zoom call sometime and learn the ins and outs. Then you can work on a weekend project to build one. Moving on to things that really matter : More food and drink-related conversations. Have you two tried that new Italian place Downtown? Just last week. The pasta was decent, but it's really just an overpriced carbonara. I stick with the local market for my pasta needs. I know what you mean. Quality in food for me has always been a must, but it's hard to find affordable, quality places around here for regular consumption. Agreed. But have you tried those new food delivery platforms? I've been using one for the past month and I swear the quality has taken a turn for the better.

I've used Google Maps so much since I've been here in Saudi. I swear, it's saved my life at least five times when I got lost. You're not alone, Sarah. I've used it too. But honestly, sometimes it leads me to some really weird places. Like the other day it took me to a part of the city I'd never heard of just because I typed “hospital” and it actually didn't know where I meant! Yeah, keeps changing its mind on the shortest route every time. You'll end up driving around in circles. I've had lazy colleagues who always rely on it for directions, refuse to use a map. Can't understand why they just don't like it. And sometimes it takes you to the wrong part of town! What's wrong with old fashioned maps? Nah, man, maps are okay but how often do you need to check? Google maps is pretty good. You just gotta trust it. Wait, but what if there's a better way? A more accurate Satnav? I've heard of some satnavs being more accurate in some areas. But in this part of Saudi, its pretty good. I guess it depends on where you are. Do you know anyone who's used a satnav other than Google? Like one of those in-built ones in cars? Yeah, some of the newer cars come with decent systems. But most people use it alongside Google just to double-check. I had a Garmin one in my old car. Was great. Extremely accurate, but it couldn’t keep up with the crowd of updates like Google. That's interesting. So which one do you think would be best then? You know, I’ve heard Waze is pretty popular too, especially for avoiding traffic. Waze, isn't that the one that uses crowdsourced information? Exactly. Its predictive capabilities can be helpful if you're in crowded cities. Clearly, there's no one-size-fits-all solution. It seems like a good mix of Google for updates and Waze for traffic could work. You could be on to something there, young lady. But remember, sometimes a bit of error is needed to find new spots. That’s true though, maybe too much accuracy can be a bad thing too. What about other topics? Like family and decorating? Or did you all want to keep on tech for now?

So, how about tonight? What have you two been up to since our last catch-up? Oh, just normal teacher things, of course. But I've been getting really into gardening lately. Which is quite ironic given how little time I get to actually garden outside of my small balcony. And here we are in one of the best gardens in the world, and you’re talking about your balcony. True! But as much as I love botany, I have to admit, it’s mostly about the relaxing atmosphere here. So, have you guys been taking care of yourselves? I mean, with all the weird lifestyle lately, it’s easy to neglect self-care, isn’t it? Honestly, I’ve been quite good about it lately. I’ve been following a pretty strict routine. Early morning runs, working from home most days... keeps me focused. But it’s funny how you notice the small things when you really pay attention to your life, right? For sure. I’ve been trying to focus on my diet and yoga the past few months. It’s funny how our lives kind of align on certain things despite our different jobs. But the past year has been quite the wake-up call in terms of health and what’s truly important. Speaking of which, have either of you tried any new wellness trends lately? I read about something called “forest bathing” in one of my teaching magazines. Well, we’re doing it right now – sort of. Although I suppose the Swedish people have been doing it for centuries just by being out in these beautiful gardens. True! The concept is all about the benefits of being immersed in nature. Some studies suggest it can reduce stress and even boost the immune system. That sounds like a pretty good excuse to spend more time outdoors, doesn’t it? Especially with us English folks thinking we can never get enough sunlight. Sure, but I suppose it’s not just about the cliché of “fresh air” or some spiritual mumbo-jumbo. There’s actually some solid science behind it. Like regulating your cortisol levels, improving your mood, that kind of thing. And it makes sense. I've been feeling the benefits myself. I’ve even started working from one of those outdoor coworking spaces in London. It’s made such a difference. That’s brilliant! And it’s a pity most of us can’t do that regularly, but what we’re doing right now is just as good, isn’t it?

I've been meaning to ask you, Dad. Do you ever wonder what the world sounds like to people who are not from the southeast of England? You know, all the different accents and various dialects we have here? Oh, yes, dear! I've always been very proud of the sound of our Kentish accent. I remember my childhood in London, we used to make a game out of trying to guess where people were from based on their accent. I'd say your accent still has a bit of that old Kentish keepsake to it, wouldn’t you say? Yes, and don't even get me started on the verbal tics and expressions used by people from Essex versus London. "Oi, what's the crack?" versus "All right, mate?" And then there’s the biggest challenge – understanding you, when you're into your Minecraft world with all the slang and creative names you come up with! Minecraft is a whole different tongue for sure! And ever heard any of the new voice recognition on phones struggle with different accents? It can be pretty comical. My phone often insists I’ve tried to order "bazooka" instead of "biscuits"! Indeed, technology has certainly got to catch up with the richness and variety of our speech patterns. And accents aside, speaking of speech patterns, I wonder if any of you remember visiting our old house in Gillingham in the summers as kids? The smell of fresh bread from the baker's and the distant sound of the Medway taken together, that was the sound of home. I do remember those summers! And the Sunday dinners at your Mum's...the arguments over football on TV or who could go the farthest without falling off their bike! Yeah, and the times we'd ride our bikes all the way to the next village just because it seemed like a big adventure! Speaking of large distances and adventures, I’ve been thinking about our next outing should we find some work. How about a long bike ride like the ones we used to take? Exploring the local scenic paths, maybe even all the way to the coast if we are feeling adventurous? Now, that’s a plan I can get behind! You know, those are among my fondest childhood memories. The freedom of the open road... Nothing like a ride outside to clear your head. Speaking of clearing heads, has anyone... ...noticed a bit of a... situation with me and John recently?

Alright, boys! As you can see, we've got baked Alaska for dessert tonight. Did you learn about this in culinary class? Yeah, miss! Made one in class once. It was really cool to see the meringue catch fire, but I kind of messed up the timing. Ours ended up more like a grilled Alaska. Ah, the perils of class experiments right? But that's part of the fun, isn't it? Learning from mistakes! Speaking of keepsakes, I still have my first ever baked Alaska from my training days. Remember when we used to make these for Halloween parties at our parents' place? Everyone would light the meringue together and then, as the kids dared, we'd sample from the defrosting center. Yes, those were some scary fun times! Let's leave that tradition alive tonight, shall we? We could even plan another party next year. Maybe with a baking theme - baking their own desserts or something. That sounds like a plan. I might actually learn how to do it right if we have enough practice with the rest of the class! Definitely. You know, learning how to make baked Alaska is not just about the food, it's about the techniques. Grating the cheese, for instance, might seem simple but you'd be surprised how much of a difference it can make in the final product. I'm not really sure. I always thought you just needed to grate it doesn't matter much. Not exactly, my dear. The kind of cheese you use, if it’s sharp or not, how finely or coarsely you grate it - all these little details can affect the flavor and texture. For example, if you were making a baked Alaska, you'd want to grate the cheese finely so it melts evenly and doesn't affect the texture too much. Can't believe I never thought of it. You learn more things when you cook with you than at school. Exactly! And speaking of learning, we should also talk about a bit more serious subject. Discrimination, and age of consent. How about we take a bit of time after dinner to discuss? I was reading about that topic in school. Good, it’s really important. But it's also important for us to talk openly about these topics. In the UK, the age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual activity, but discrimination is a far broader issue that affects many aspects of life, and everyone should become more aware of it.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my passport control story from New York? It sounds ridiculous now, but at the time it was quite embarrassing. No, actually you didn't. Was it the time they thought the picture was a definaling instance of questions? No, it was about a "security issue". Apparently, they couldn't verify my identity right at the start, and I had to fill out a very long form with details about my grandparents and even my birthplace address. Crazy stuff. Oh, that is indeed a classic! And today's day off here, staying in your lovely home, just like old times. How's everything been going with planning your flying lessons? Very well, thank you! Just got through the theory part. I’ve progressed to the simulator portion now. It requires more focus, but I’m enjoying it. What about you, have you been taking any big trips or doing anything exciting? Well, between marking papers and lectures, I haven't had much time. But last year I managed this fantastic trip to Japan, actually. We both met there. Oh, yes! Where did you go in Japan? Was it Tokyo or some of the countryside? It was a mix really, but mainly in the north. The soba noodles in Hokkaido were to die for, and Aomori was quite beautiful. But the highlight was visiting in Nagano, really. The food, the culture, the people... all so fantastic. I know what you mean! Japan is such a unique experience. I think it’s one of the reasons we became good friends, we both have that mutual interest in seeing different parts of the world. Indeed! It’s one of my favorite places. Do you think you’ll go back soon? Perhaps, but teaching is quite demanding, and traveling and planning everything can be tough when you're not retired yet. Speaking of which, my time here is valuable, but I'm enjoying a bit of rest. Well, I know a bit about that! How do you manage with such busy schedules? Ah, most days it feels like juggling. But I try to focus on one task at a time and use my postgraduate skills to manage time. I also love cooking when I can. It's a good relaxation for me. You do make excellent breakfasts. I like to think so. We should really share the recipe for that yorkshire pudding if you'd like?

I'm so late to this game, I've been stuck in traffic for nearly 20 minutes. I knew I should've taken the bus! You're late? You're the one who usually tells us that now, aren't you? And isn't that one of the most British phrases, "Sorry, I'm late, I got stuck in traffic." Yeah, but have you guys ever thought about the origins of that phrase? "Traffic" actually originates from the Middle French "trafiquer", meaning to trade. It started to be used to describe the congestion of people and cars sometime in the 18th century. It just shows how language is shaped by what we see around us, even in places as seemingly mundane as the streets we drive on. That's fascinating. I guess I never really thought about its origin. We just use the word so often, we take it for granted. And it's funny because it's so far removed from its origin, yet we still use it in the exact same context. We really don’t stick to the exact original meaning. True. And it's not just the words themselves, but the way they are used. For instance, the word "petard" - we use it in the phrase "to be hoist with one's own petard", but originally, it was a type of bomb used to blow up gates or walls in military engineering. I'm not sure if that’s "proper" conversation material for a Friday afternoon… No, it's perfect! It's like we're on one of those word origin podcasts. More like we're being hoisted by our own... fun banter. So next time you're late and stuck in traffic, thank the medieval French for the word. Alright, alright, let’s not dwell too much in the past. I just scored a decent word. "Serena" - 26 points! 26! That's impressive! What other words have you got planned? I’m trying to work with "Crook", but I need a certain letter. A good five-pointer could really help out. But that could also be a bit risky. Leaving too many useful letters on the board... True, always strategic thinking. Though, "Crook" rhymes with a lot - "brook", "joke", "shook"... Though, unless I can get a Q, U, or an X, it's going to be tricky. How about "qwerty?" We can use the I and E that are already on the board.

Ah, marvellous weekend we've had haven't we? The weather was just right. Felt like we were back in the 70s again. Indeed, it has been lovely. I've spent most of it in the garden. Nothing like fresh air to clear the mind, although I do have a bit of backache today. Speaking of the garden, have you noticed how the daisies have started to bloom early this year? Yes, they have. Seems like nature's got its own rhythm now. I've been meaning to get out and do some gardening but, you know, the body just doesn't want to cooperate anymore. I’m sure you're getting your share of rest just like me. You're right, but when you've spent your whole life making sure other people's days were properly started and ended, it's a bit difficult to fully retire. Still, it's been good having you here. You’ve kept me quite company. And you’ve done it for all these years. Childminding can't have been an easy or a lucrative job. No it wasn't, certainly not financially rewarding but it was very rewarding in other ways. Watching the children grow and seeing them learn new things every day. It made the long hours feel worthwhile. Absolutely. Though now, let's face it, we’re both at a stage where the jobs we had are simply not an option anymore. How are you finding it in retirement? It's quite a transition, I'm finding. Haven't gotten used to having all this time on my hands. I keep trying to find ways to occupy myself, but nothing seems as engaging as childminding was. I know just what you mean. Before I retired, I worked at the local market, mostly doing odd jobs, nothing too strenuous. I used to keep myself busy, but without that structure, it feels quite empty sometimes. I've noticed we both speak a lot about the past. It's good to sit back and reminisce but maybe it's time we make the most of these years too. True, we should, but it's hard to find something new to get into when we're not as spry as we used to be. That's almost too negative. There's plenty to do. We could start with things like local museum tours, or even volunteering.

Right, so I've been reading about this new app that's been making waves. It's like a personalized nutrition plan and fitness tracker all rolled into one. It's been talked about a lot in the local news. You two should check it out. That sounds interesting, especially after all the recent talk about healthy living and wellness. I've got a bit of a science background, so I'm curious about how they tailor the plans and if there's any evidence backing it up. Oh, I've got that. Apparently, it uses a whole bunch of data points from your daily routine, along with health metrics to create a custom plan. It also syncs with various fitness trackers. That does sound very involved, and it's nice to see health apps taking a more individualized approach. But do you think it's worth the subscription cost? Well, it's not cheap, but they offer various tiers. And from what I've read, a lot of users seem to find it effective for their specific goals, whether it's weight loss, gaining strength, or improving general health. I'll admit, it's impressive that it considers so many factors. One thing I'd love to know is how it handles different dietary needs or restrictions. For example, I know vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free diets are quite popular nowadays. Absolutely, flexibility with dietary needs is super important. And it must be very helpful if you're working to tackle specific health issues or simply trying to shift habits. Exactly, and I heard they have a decent community support function, too. So if you're working through a tough period or need motivation, there might be others facing similar challenges you can connect with. Very useful. And what kind of feedback do they get from users who have tried it for a while? The feedback seems mostly positive, although, as always, mixed. Some people find it too detailed and time-consuming initially. Others say it's quite game-changing once they get into the rhythm and it really helps them meet goals. It sure seems like a sophisticated tool. I might give it a trial run soon, especially since some of our habits could do with a bit of shaking up. I think that’s a great idea! And if anyone does give it a go, let's share our experiences.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new restaurant that just opened up on Grace Street? They’ve got an all-day breakfast menu that sounds superb. I've been craving some proper chicken and waffles. You into that? Aye, yeah, I saw a review on Instagram. That’ll be some kind of gingerbread waffle house, innit? Sounds sick. Exactly! I'm thinking of suggesting it to our group for lunch today. What say you? For sure, it could be a plan. You know our routine...picking up lunch and knocking off studies for a bit. Exactly, and I’ve been wanting to check out this new cinema near by, they have a new screening of 'No Time to Die' in 3D. It’s the last James Bond film, should be fun. Bond's cool, mate, but 3D? I've got my doubts. Will we need those cheesy glasses again? You're joking right? It's James Bond! Even with those glasses, I’m in. But jokes aside, it would be nice to do something different, see some new faces and all. I'm down for that. Makes a change from the usual games night. Speaking of which, how’s that new FIFA coming along? It’s alright, still getting used to the new features but I'm hooked. The graphics are brilliant, though. You started playing it yet? Nah, not yet, life is just too busy with all these seminars. I'm overloaded with Shakespeare analysis for my English lit course. But it's actually pretty interesting, how he ties into modern political themes and all that. Shakespeare and Politics eh? Sounds like a seminar topic straight out of More's "Utopia". I tried to get into a similar course, but it was way too advanced for me. Yes, it's quite confronting but it’s really opening my eyes to a whole new layer of texts. We could sit together for one of the sessions sometime, though. I’d be down for that. Funny enough, just the other day, my course mate mentioned he’s heading on a stag weekend to Budapest soon. Budapest, great city choice. Are you going? Not me, but I could swear off drinking for a month if someone included me! Haha. It's just too expensive for me right now, but funny thinking about it. Yeah, I know the feeling. I’ve been eyeing off some cheaper hols with mates anyways.

Oh, so many topics we've got to cover. I'm starving; these pastries look amazing here. Definitely! I've not been here before. Is it good? The cakes, especially the scones, are to die for. I see. I was thinking of getting a scone and a coffee. And the quiche... I had it once, truly delicious. Right, let me try... I need to lose some calories, but worth it. Oh, you're in London too often, just like me. You can't blame me. There's always something new to try, new places to see. So, how are you finding London? It's great, but exhausting. The job is good, but I spend a lot of time on trains and between meetings. And you, any news or changes on your side? Oh, just the usual. I've finally moved into a new apartment in Cambridge after finishing my degree. It's lovely, but the rent is beyond. I thought Cambridge was a bit cheaper, right? Well, relatively. It's worse in London. I’m managing, but it's tough as a project co-ordinator, really trying to keep everything together. That must be interesting and stressful. I get it, though - doesn’t sound much different from being in the marketing world myself. It’s different, but also similar. Late nights, tight deadlines, less sleep. The usual. The routine of a certain type of professional life. Exactly! So, are you seeing anyone or just focusing on work and travel? I was seeing someone after uni, but it didn’t work out. No real regrets, just moving on now. Ah, take your time. And your family, all well? Yeah, all good. Again, health issues are a bit of a theme... but we're managing. Sorry to hear that. I hope things get better for them. Thank you... Two scones, one quiche, and two... Two coffees, right? Yes, please. Can I also have a latte, please? So what are your plans for the future? Any big changes or moves ahead? I'm actually thinking of taking a break from the city life after this year. Really? Yeah, I've been thinking about a career break or maybe doing some volunteering abroad, seeing new things. That sounds amazing. I wish I could too. The nine-to-five sometimes feels suffocating after a while. Definitely. My marketing job is okay, but it's not my passion, you know?

I've decided I need more plants in my flat. I've been meaning to add more greenery around here for a while. I've been finding it soothing to care for them. Made me realize I need to expand my knowledge about plant care. That's great! Plants can really brighten up a place isn't it? I've got a few myself. Now, why don't I brew us some tea? Our very own homegrown tea from that keepsake cupboard? Oh, yes, please! That would be wonderful. So, any particular type of plant you're interested in? Yeah, I've been thinking about maybe getting an areca palm. They seem quite low maintenance and also purify the air, I've read. That's a good pick! They are quite hardy. And you can grow them indoors quite easily. But did you know that for them to do their best at purifying the air, they need a decent amount of light? Interesting, I didn't know that. I have good natural light most of the day in my flat but I guess it depends on where they are placed. Exactly! And also consider the humidity levels. They prefer high humidity so you might want to keep them in a less drafty corner or near other plants to create a microenvironment. Alright, I'll have to keep that in mind. I also saw a nice looking doesn't come from that, it's from another shop, but that reminds me... Have you read about that recent research on plant ownership and mental health? No, I haven't, tell me more about it. So, there was this study recently by a team at the University of Exeter. They found that people who spend time around plants and changing the natural environment in their homes felt a significant reduction in stress and anxiety. That's fascinating! Makes sense though. Nature has such a calming effect. Even my thesis so far suggests plants have positive effects on mental health too. Really? That's great! What's the focus of your thesis? It's about how socially and economically deprived communities can benefit from innovative green spaces and local gardening programs. The initial findings suggest it really can change attitudes and behaviors regarding health and wellbeing. That’s a really important topic. I know from this field, that's... Why don't we start a bit of a community project here in Cambridge maybe?

Ah, Phil, welcome back to the office! How was your weekend? I hope you managed to leave your marking books at home for a change. Ah well, you know how it is. It's always something. Still, it was lovely to have a bit of rest before the week starts. And did you catch the big match over the weekend? I was glued to my screen, watching those kids crack it for their teams. The little one already has a golden touch, judging by the nursery games video that's been going around. Yes, it's funny isn't it? I heard he's joining a local academy. Now that's pressure for someone so young. I can only imagine. Speaking of pressure, I saw that the new snooker rankings have just come out. Ronnie O'Sullivan is slipping down to the third, can you believe it? Honestly? I hadn’t had time to check. That does seem quite a fall really. But you never know, the old magic might come back. And with the World Championship just round the corner, anything can happen. True, and the prize money is always a huge motivation. Though, to be honest, all these players seem to be so young these days. Reminds me of when I started in the field. Exactly. The sport has certainly changed since we were young. Speaking of change, how's your gardening coming along? You told me you were taking it up as a hobby. Oh, it's been a struggle, but it's actually quite therapeutic. I've managed to finally get all my tomatoes to grow without them getting eaten by birds. Tomato trouble, eh? I hear you. I've had to deal with those darn squirrels eating all my tulips. Yes, wildlife can be a real nuisance. But it’s been worth it. I find it quite relaxing. Though, I do worry about the weather these days... It certainly is a bit unpredictable. Seems like we're always getting new extremes. Speaking of which, have you seen the new police recruitment numbers?

Oh for heaven’s sake, I just got back from another day of chaos at the office and now I have to deal with this... right now? We still don’t have a clear plan for Jess’s birthday party. It’s just keeps coming up and up, and I still can’t decide if it should be here, at a venue, or just a small family gathering. What are your thoughts, everyone? Alright, I'll start looking into that and some venues in Lichfield. Jess doesn’t need a huge bash, but... I do want it to be memorable, you know? Oh, I saw a really cute unicorn theme at that new party place downtown. Can we do that? It was really pretty on Instagram. As fun as that would be, I don’t know, isn’t that a bit too old for Jess now? Maybe for another year? True, maybe too old. And also, it's a little too commercial and expensive right now. How about we stick with games and a simpler theme for the party? We could set up a treasure hunt or something, that sounds more like what Jess would still enjoy. But not too many, we need to keep it manageable. I helped Jess with some homework recently and she was really into this new cartoon about animal explorers. Or different areas of the house for smaller groups? Ooh, and can we do it at my friend Emma’s place? They have a big backyard! I’m not sure if that’ll work, hun. Emma’s family might not want 20 kids running around their backyard.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we went to New York for your sister's wedding? It was absolute chaos! I don't know how we even managed to escape all the crowds. Aye, I remember! You were supposed to get the flowers and you ended up buying gingerbread instead because you thought it was a totally normal thing to do at a wedding! And didn't Dad get held up by the police for bringing a giant teddy bear into the church? I think it was supposed to be a 'groom's gift' to the bridesmaids, dear. I've heard the Brooklyn Museum is great, but I’ve never been. That sounds perfect. What about trying some new restaurants? I’ve heard about this place in Chinatown that makes the best noodles. Oh, I'd love that! Let's make some plans. We should probably start figuring out where we want to stay. Can we stay in that hotel with the huge view of the city? We'll see. Maybe the kids can try together to help research and find the best options. That sounds like a solid plan. Of course, this means we’d really need to start thinking about our budget and accommodation options. You mean we’re actually planning a proper holiday? Well, if I don't have to handle the florist again, I’m all for it. Oh, the florist incident will go down as a legendary family memory. Can we maybe go to a Broadway show? We could try for discounted matinee or off-peak performances. They usually have more availability. I like that plan. And maybe we can explore Central Park. Definitely. It’s peaceful and there’s so much to see. How about trying a picnic in the park this time? Yay, a picnic! Will we stay all day? If we don't get swept away in the fun, I'd say so. We can make a day of it.

Yo, mate, got a sec? I need some advice on this essay I'm doing. It's due next week and I'm still trying to figure out the main argument. Of course, what's been giving you trouble? Throw it at me. It's supposed to be about the questions of identity in Romantic poetry, specifically in Keats and Blake. I'm having trouble making his prose sound persuasive. That's actually quite a fractious subject. You're trying to tackle it for a literature course, right? Right, it's for my postgrad English lit class, and I want to impress. I've been struggling to structure the essay, sticking to the guidelines and all. Might just need to clarify your arguments first, mate. Tell me, in your opinion, what specific aspect of identity do you think these poets tackle most? Well, you see, I think they both contest traditional notions of identity as static and fixed, and explore it in a more fluid, evolving way. But how do I grab it in this essay without it sounding too vague or too dense? That's a good angle. We could develop it on that view. Perhaps start with a strong thesis that asserts this is the key contention. You could frame it like, while the mainstream idea of identity has long been seen as fixed and unchanging, Romantic poets like Keats and Blake illustrate a divergent perspective, one that sees identity as dynamic and influenced by the poet's subjective experiences. That's deep, but in simpler terms, really? Because I don't want the first paragraph to be too convoluted. Right, ease into it. Maybe something like, "While Victorian and preceding literary traditions presented identity as a fixed entity, the works of Romantic poets Keats and Blake suggest that identity is lived, felt, and subject to change. This essay argues that their poetry presents a form of identity that is evolving and personally derived, challenging traditional views." That's great! I can build from there. You sure about that thesis? It’s a good starting point? Yeah, for sure. Makes a clear claim about what the essay’s going to argue, which is super important. So then the structure would look like, the introduction with the thesis, then the body where I go through each poem and show how they illustrate the argument... right? Yeah. Each body paragraph could focus on specific lines, imagery, themes from a particular poem that demonstrate this fluid notion of identity.

Alright mates, so who first started talking about their dreams last time we all chatted? That sounds like a fun conversation starter, doesn’t it? I remember it was you, really. You were telling us about how you've always wanted to own a dog. Yeah! But then, you know how we get into these big conversations! It ended up turning into this big wishful thinking session about winning the lottery! True! I can imagine. Anyway, how would you like to continue discussing dreams this time around? Something new to share or maybe anything new about our dog dreams? You know what, let’s actually keep up with both. I think the dog dream has actually become a little more specific for me - I’ve been thinking of getting a golden retriever. They seem so lovable and active, perfect for our family dynamic. Ooh, I want to hear that! But what made you decide on a golden retriever? I’ve always loved dogs, but I've come across golden retrievers at parks or with friends. Their personalities seemed so great, friendly and loving. And seeing kids playing with them made me think - perfect fit for us! Well, if we had a golden retriever, imagine all the fun we could have, especially if we got one while we could still take it on all our adventures! True, but let’s not forget realistically - dreams and reality sometimes have a gap. I don’t understand... What do you mean? Well, I’ve always thought about a few things, and having a dog is one. But realistically, it's a big commitment - space, time, financials... Exactly, but changing the subject to something more fun - what if we did win the lottery? Oh, yes! I know! We could buy a big house and so much land for the dog! And we could even give some to charity or set up a little animal shelter! That sounds like a lot of fun and helpful! I would love to help with animals if we did win. That’s the spirit! Winning the lottery would certainly make a lot of these dreams seem more within reach... but let’s not forget this conversation started with dreams... True that. Speaking of which, I still have a few hopes I’d want to achieve regardless of the lottery. How about you, Tom? Any specific dreams or ambitions on your mind?

Yo, mate, did you hear about that A&E scandal from Sunderland? It was all over the news these past couple of days. Yeah, I talked to my cousin the other day. He said they're still investigating. It's all about lack of staff and poor maintenance, isn’t it? Exactly. It’s shocking really. I heard they even had to close the A&E at night a few times because they couldn’t handle the emergencies right. Absolutely outrageous. Where my cousin works, they keeps coming across similar issues with underfunding in public health. It really makes me sad – these are supposed to be the best places for emergencies, you know? Absolutely, it’s even happening down here as well. The whole system needs a good overhaul. And you know what’s even more frustrating? It's not just A&E either. My mum went to the dentist and it took her six months to get an appointment for a broken tooth! I’m not surprised. The NHS has been under a lot of pressure, especially recently. But that doesn’t excuse this sort of neglect. It’s not just neglect, it's a lack of resources too. I saw on the news how many staff they’re short of. It’s like they're trying to spin plates with half the coins gone. Absolutely – and while the media always focuses on individual A&E experiences, there’s a bigger systemic problem. It’s political, as well as resource based. I read an article saying that it’s not just NHS staff but also the community facing real challenges. But it seems like no one can agree on how to fix it. True. It’s hard when everyone has different agendas. On one hand, the government says they’re committed to a nationalized healthcare system. On the other, it seems like funding just isn’t matching up. It’s just so frustrating. We’re always hearing about cuts but never seeing the results of changing the system. It feels like there’s no end in sight. Well, that’s not entirely fair. There are people working on these issues every day, but it’s a truly complex problem. Maybe so, but that's not much consolation for the family who’ve had a night from hell because they couldn’t get the help they needed. No. I agree, it’s not a consolation.

Ah, George, did you hear about that business idea you were banging on about last time we met? How's it going? Oh, yes, Richard. Got some exciting developments to share. We’ve got a really good ally now on board and the prototype is coming along nicely. We’re on track for some kind of launch by the end of the year. That sounds brilliant, mate! Any chance of a return on your investment yet? Not quite yet, but it’s shaping up well. As you know, I’m putting a fair amount of my savings into it but I’m confident. It’s not just about the money for me, though; I’m seeing opportunities to really make a meaningful difference in people’s lives with this product. I totally understand that. You always have big ideas, George. What’s the product, if you don’t mind me asking? Sure, no problem. It’s a smart pollution sensor that helps households and small businesses monitor and reduce their carbon footprint. Right now, these people spend a lot of money on consultants and audits, but they often lack data or a clear plan. Our product simplifies that process. Interesting, sounds like it could be quite a game-changer. I can see why you’d want to invest in it. Good luck with it, by the way. Thanks, Richard. It’s good to talk through it with you – always a level head and helpful ideas. Speaking of ideas, have you had a chance to look at all the news about Brexit and the new policies they’re discussing? Just the headlines, unfortunately. It seems like it’s back to debating how we’re supposed to leave or remain or whatever. Honestly, I’m more focussed on things that directly impact my business side of things, but it’s all a bit concerning, isn’t it? Very concerning. Seems like they’ve been at this for years without any concrete resolution. I worry about the uncertainty it brings to businesses, especially for those dependent on European trade. Absolutely, though some of my suppliers are reassuring me they’ve got contingency plans in place and a bit of support from the government. But I guess it's always one step forward, two back with this mess. Either way, good on you for trying to stick to what you can control – in this case, developing your product and addressing those pollution and sustainability issues head-on.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that episode of Happy Valley today? The way that detective was so determined to catch the culprit was just riveting. You're quite the fangirl for that series, aren't you? I kind of lost interest after the first season. But I respect the dedication! Well, the story just keeps getting tighter and more gripping, right? And that fractious policewomen relationship? All very psychological. You mean like us, discussing everything under the sun, even if we've had our own differences? Exactly! Anyway, did you notice that the décor here is so nice? So much better than our local pub back in Edinburgh. It has a lot of character. I like the vintage feel they’ve kept. Yeah, it’s quite English, innit? Right down to the old oak beams and carpets. Almost makes you feel like you’re in a different time era. Aye, certainly different from the modern décor back home. I prefer the warmth and quirkiness of places like this. Speaking of warmth, I'm freezing to death in this place. Someone turn up the heating or lend me your overcoat? Considering the silly things you carry around, I think you need to invest in a more functional coat. We might have spoken about it before but you need one that keeps you warm and looks nice. There’s nothing silly about finding cute coats, dear. Plus, this one’s just right for falling temperatures. Oh, I get that. But come on, a fun warm coat is better for freezing cold evenings like this. You’re always so practical! But I think warmth and style can go together. You should see the cute ones on Zara next time you’re passing by. Either way, it looks like someone needs a new coat. Might be a good idea to get some recommendations from an administrator. Ha, administrator expertise in fashion. There's a revolution waiting to happen. Ah, now this is the kind of music to change your mind. I love it when they have live acts. Someone knew how to pick the tunes for the evening. True, the music's already setting a great atmosphere. Why don’t we get some food while they set up? Good idea. Shall we try the fish and chips? It's quintessentially British and fits perfectly with the theme of the pub. Mmm, that sounds lovely.

Aye, I'm absolutely enjoying my new Canon. Just got back from a weekend photography trip to the Highlands. Really? You haven't talked about that! What were you shooting? The snow? Aye, just the grassy, moorlands – acres of them. It was just so quiet, the snow made it feel even more remote. Ah, brilliant. I'm jealous, mate. I was thinking of doing a trip to Sutherland next week. Hopefully, the weather stays nice. Keep an eye on the forecast before you go, weather's been a bit unpredictable there lately. I will, thanks. You've been thinking of heading anywhere else soon? I did just buy a new backpacking trip to the islands. Planning to do it next spring. Hence the new camera gear. The islands? Which ones? Aye, the Hebrides, probably start with the Outer Islands. I've been reading up on it and the landscapes sound breathtaking. For sure! The Hebrides are stunning, especially if you're into coastal landscapes. Exactly, and I’ve also been wanting to try some seascape photography. Stunning at sunrise and sunset if the weather permits, of course. Absolutely – timing is everything in landscape photography, isn’t it? Aye, and the light really is key. I've been practicing shooting in different conditions – you learn a lot about how the conditions impact the shot. Well, you'll have to show me some of your shots then. I've also been experimenting with astrophotography lately. That sounds interesting! I’ve thought about doing that too, but the city light pollution makes it a bit tough here. Exactly, but if you can get out to somewhere dark enough, it's rewarding. I’ve been trying to plan a trip to the Cairngorms for a clear night. I’ve done that a few times before. If you're nearby when I’m over, I can join you. Might be a wee bit of help to have an extra pair of hands setting up and what not. That would be amazing, thanks! No worries, mate. Do you think the weather will still be good by then? I heard something about a low-pressure system coming through. Ah, I'll check that out. If it’s not too cloudy... We could even share the costs for some camping gear or something. That’s a good idea. I’ve got a decent tent and sleeping bag, can’t remember if I still have a portable stove though.

Right, so I was thinking we might need to reorganize our plans for the week. On Monday morning, I have that meeting at the community centre and I don't know if little Teddy's nursery is closed because of the snow. Oh no, now I remember! They did send out an email saying that if there was heavy snow they might close and they hadn't mentioned anything else. Let me check their website quickly. They haven't updated their website but that's because it's due to close at 3pm. You'll need to check back later, okay? True, thanks for that. Other than that, are we still on for Friday? Is your yoga class happening? Yeah, I read that in the email from last week. But let's maybe make an invitation to your mother for dinner while we're here? She's been asking about coming over more often. That's a great idea. How about after the yoga class? We could have her over for dinner. It'll also give us a chance to catch up and discuss or plan something for the baby's nursery before Christmas this year. Sounds perfect. And maybe we could have her help with the decorations. She always has great ideas. Exactly! She'd love that. Speaking of which, I saw there's this new documentary on TV tonight about local history. Would you like to watch it together? Sure, why not? There's not a lot in on any of the other channels that I'm interested in. It couldn't hurt, and we can always turn it off if it's boring. I know that one might not be your usual choice, but it's on all the time and I thought it looked quite interesting. Plus, it's good to try something new sometimes. True. Okay, that works for me then. What time does it start? It starts at 9 and goes until 10. We could have a quiet evening in then. Sounds perfect. I'll try and finish up some work I need to do for tomorrow before then and make some tea. I'll get started on making that dinner for your mother. You know how she adores your roast chicken. I know. She always says I should write a cookbook. She really liked your lasagna the other week too. You tell her that.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that one time I had to arrange for a conference for 500 people in under a week? It was chaos but it turned out really well in the end. Did the guests even get a fair warning? That sounds like some kind of logistical hell. That must've been quite a challenge. I'm glad you managed to pull it off. I had a similar situation at work. We're trying to implement a new production system and it's been a headache. Oh, that kind of stress is not foreign to me. But it's all worth it in the end, despite the stress. So what about the guests? Did they even get good food or decent accommodations? Yes, actually. We worked with an excellent catering service and a hotel that could handle such a large group. Plus, the conference was in York so it was good for everyone to experience the town. And you, speaking of experiences, how has the new production system been going this week? Not too bad. We're still ironing out some kinks but it's going. The team is learning quickly though. Learning from experience is key. It's like arranging a big event – once you've done it once, you become much more prepared for the next time. Yeah, experience is definitely key. I always feel like I learn something new every time I head a project. Speaking of projects, I'm wondering, have you two seen any of those new designs for next year's events? Seems like the trends are really leaning towards minimalism and sustainability, which I'm a fan of. Oh absolutely! The boss just rolled out new designs last week and honestly, they look great! We're changing the color scheme and décor to be more eco-friendly. Plus, we're using local suppliers where possible. Sounds like a good direction! How do you manage the sustainability side of things? Is it tough to find suppliers who can meet those standards? It can be a bit of a challenge sometimes. But there are platforms and networks designed specifically for events and events professionals to find sustainable suppliers. It's amazing how many there are. I wish it were as easy in my line of work. It’s not like workers can just decide to “go sustainable” overnight when you're dealing with hard, physical labor.

Ah, marvellous tea. I remember my first job's canteen had the best cuppa, just like what Jeannie here made. Oh, tea is a proper tradition, isn't it? I used to make a pot for the kiddies, now and then when they were at home. Speaking of traditions, do you all remember the history of our favourite beverage? It's quite fascinating actually, coming from China originally, and then... ... slowly brewing its way into our hearts and teacups, yes. I had to deal with a group of rowdy students who had a class on British history, including the tea trade. Must have been quite the challenge! And the railways, that's what really made it widespread, didn't it? My dad used to tell me stories of tea being as much a part of breakfast as eggs and bacon. Exactly! The Great Western Railway did a lot for it. And the English Tea Culture... what a cornerstone it's been. It's certainly provided a lot of comfort for many of us in the English-speaking world. Reminds me of when I used to have afternoon tea at my mum's; the clinking of the cups, the jam on the scones… Indeed, comfort food – and drink, of course. I remember visiting my grandparents in Norwich; the table would always be set with dainty cups and a selection of teas, and a slice of plum cake. I'd say doesn't come much more English than that! Perhaps we could revive those afternoon teas. It might cheer us up a bit, the way things are going. I’m game, as long as it’s a casual affair. Formality is a bit beyond me now, but a nice friendly meet-up sounds perfect. That’s what I’m talking about! We’ve got each other, and we’ve got tea. I’ll bring some of that lemon verbena I used to grow when I was childminding; it’s soothing, isn’t it? And maybe I’ll whip up some of those Dundee cakes. They could use a bit more texture in them, perhaps some fruit for interest? Oh, we don’t need fancy stuff! The simple things are always the best. Hear, hear! So, what about company? Someone to share a bit of gossip or hear about old times? Should we invite... I can’t think of anyone, if we’re keeping it low-key.

I've decided I need to take a break from cooking for tonight. Who'd like to order us takeaway tonight? It feels like it's been ages since we've had proper food from our favorite Indian place in Norwich. That sounds like a plan! Let’s do it. I haven’t had a good curry in weeks. As long as it's not too spicy, I'm happy. I won’t be able to handle it if it burns like last time we went to that new place in town. I love how we always have to check the heat levels with you, mate. It’s not my fault you’re among the chosen few who can actually handle a good heat. True that. Ordering now? Yes, go ahead. So, have any of you been following the recent protests in London? I heard it was quite a thing. Oh, absolutely. I see it all the time from my students. These protests seem to be happening more and more often. I had a student who came in late to the seminar this week because she was stuck in one of the marches. Well, it’s certainly a topic of interest. The whole issue about CO2 emissions and how we deal with it as a country is quite contentious really. But have any of you actually been to a protest? No, I haven’t, but I would say that it’s good that people are exercising that kind of freedom of expression and trying to bring attention to these issues. Yeah, that’s true. More people need to understand that climate change isn’t just a future problem; it’s a now problem. It’s quite heartening to see young people taking the lead and making their voices heard. As a lecturer, it’s interesting to see how our students aren’t just interested in activism but also in understanding the complexities of policy-making and climate science. Absolutely. Education, in its various forms, is key. It’s not just about understanding the science; it's also about understanding the political and economic considerations. True. There’s also the matter of job opportunities and how that can sometimes conflict with personal beliefs about the environment. That’s a very real dilemma. I’ve had to make similar choices when discussing career moves and job opportunities that involved working for companies that weren’t exactly eco-friendly...

Oh, did I ever tell you about my flatmate Grace? On the day before we went away, she was frantic about forgetting to book the tickets for her volunteer mission to Zambia! Made me laugh. Oh, Grace, bless her! She’s always so on the ball with her work, but sometimes her personal life is a bit chaotic. Yes! I guess she’s just got so much going on with her nursing work and stuff. So how was your holiday? It was amazing, I loved it. We had such lazy days – beach, sun, and just delicious food everywhere. The food – you've got to try their traditional dishes like the nshima and ifishika. Ah, yes, I've heard those are very filling. Hence your stellar tan and relaxed demeanor! Thanks, got me there. Anyway, we did some good work while we were there. We helped out at the local village school, teaching them some basic English. They were so cute and eager to learn. One moment they reminded me of when we were kids, trying to understand the English language. That sounds like such a fulfilling experience. I think it’s amazing what people can learn to do when they put their mind to it. Ah, totally. The kids were so patient with our terrible accents, it was lovely. Well, we British are known for our fantastic accents. Okay, okay. True that. Anyways, how has your new project at work been? I know you've been really busy. Seems like the company's expanding in some new areas? Oh it has! I'm co-ordinating a new project on sustainable supply chain practices. It's quite challenging but also really interesting. We’re trying to make sure we're sourcing materials more ethically and responsibly. That’s fantastic. Sustainability is something we can't ignore anymore. Exactly. And it’s also quite fun trying to find ways to measure and report on it accurately. Did you have any mishaps or ups and downs? Well, if you count the time I had to explain the difference between 'carbon footprint' and 'carbon offset' five times to one of the company executives... I suppose that’s a common problem across departments. Yup. But the hard part is really getting everyone on board, especially those who don’t see the immediate business sense of it. They’ll get there. What about you? How’s the hospital been?

I was thinking of calling Laura today. We have to check on her; it's been ages since we've spoken. Good idea. Are you still involved with the fundraising for her treatment or have they sorted the financial side now? A bit of both, I think. The charity event went well and they got a bit out of it, but there are still some out-of-pocket expenses. That's good to know. The fundraising was a brilliant idea, by the way. Thank you. It was such a lot of work, but it seemed worth it. She's been very brave. Absolutely, she is. How's she been coping with all of it? To be honest, it's been tough. She started chemotherapy last month and while the initial scan indicates it's working, she's going through a really tough time physically. Emotionally, too. But she's holding up surprisingly well. It's incredible, isn't it, how people can find strength even in the toughest circumstances? I remember this one time on our trip to Edinburgh, when we were walking up Arthur’s Seat, I thought I was going to die from exhaustion but the view was so worth it. It's like that with her, I suppose – the view may be worth it in the end. That's a good analogy. Though I hope, for her sake, the view can be enjoyed much more easily for her in the years to come. Of course. Anyway, speaking of toughs doesn’t come close to what she's going through. No, but you're right, it's just a reminder of the different scales. Shall we check in on her soon then? Maybe a casual call rather than a surprise visit? Different times for different people, after all. Definitely. I think it would be good to check in. You know how she appreciates knowing we're there. Right. I’ll set some reminders. Let's say we do it tomorrow morning just before lunch? Sounds good. I'll make sure she's free then. And while we're still on the subject of personal health and such, how's your back been? Last I heard, you were having those regular sessions with the physiotherapist. Oh, still a work in progress. I've made some progress but it’s a slow ride. But I suppose it’s a small price to pay compared to Laura’s situation.

Yo, mate, gotta say, I've been pretty frustrated with the management lately. They keep coming up with new policies and procedures that are less about keeping us safer and more about appearing comprehensive. Right! Exactly! I feel like every week there's a new report to fill out or questions to ask residents just so they can tick a box somewhere. "Like the other day, they said we have to make sure every door has its own report if we service it. What is it? Do we even get an extra pair of eyes with this job? Oh, totally. And you know what I can't stand? The moment someone complains about anything, we have to check in 15 times just to cover our backs. Cover our backs, but from what? It's like they think we're causing all these problems ourselves. Well, the other day, I went to help someone with a leaky faucet in the kitchen. Turns out, it was just because someone over tightened it. But we still had to fill out 10 pages or so on it. Now that was just a simple fix, but maybe they see us as overly complex problem-solvers or what. Exactly! Like we need to solve the world’s problems at 6am to please the authorities. And don't even get me started on the 'emergency response training'. Almost half the time it's in batches that clash with our actual shifts, or we’re asked to attend a training on something that’s already been covered a dozen times. Yep, and that reminds me of the 'behavioral management course' I had to take. I thought I knew the basics of being civil to the people I assist. But no, I had to learn the "proper" way to handle every potential problematic situation. Seems like they think we’ve all forgotten how to be human. That’s so true! And what's the deal with having to take on new responsibilities? Like, I'm not opposed to a bit more workload but some of these tasks are just not security or support related. It’s like they think we're superblokes. Right! Like the 'welcome orientation' for the new students. It was good the first few times, but almost every week now, just for the newbies. Clearly, they don't think we have any security stuff to deal with.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we bumped into Jennie and Sam in Barcelona? It was at a Christmas market, and neither of us even knew the other was there. You should've seen Jennie's face when she saw us. That's so funny! I've had similar experiences too. I went on a package tour to Budapest a few years back and ran into Rachel's aunt and uncle, right at the Parliament building. I couldn't believe it! You get a certain sense of comfort when you meet other English people abroad, don't you? Like there's this instant connection. Definitely. It's like you've known each other your whole life, even if you’ve only just met! Exactly. But it can also be a bit weird, hearing all the different accents and how we all seem to notice when another Brit walks in. It's a very British thing, isn't it? Absolutely. I remember on one of my few holidays, I was in Greece and heard a bunch of people talking in the accent that was so familiar...it turned out they were from roundabouts in Essex. The accent is like the international calling card. You don't even need to say a word; the accent does it all. It can lead to some amusing situations though. Like, have you ever been mistaken for a local in, say, Antwerp? I tried to explain to someone the correct way to get to the train station once, and they just kept answering in English anyway. Oh, yes! I've had that too. The only issue is sometimes they assume we're on the same page when we’re not. Communication barrier or no, it's usually harmless fun. I've had it worse though. In London, once, I got so lost trying to explain to a tourist from New York how to get to Harrow Road. I ended up changing the subject to puppies. Oh, you should have seen some of the looks in people’s faces when I tried to explain the difference between Herne Bay and Eastbourne shopping experiences on one of my trips abroad. Speaking of shopping, does anyone have any tips for Christmas shopping? Got almost two weeks off, just over the Christmas period, and I thought I'd complete some shopping if I can avoid the city. Well, I can tell you about the city traffic though.

Yo, Mum, did you hear about that equality vote last year? I was reading about it in history class today. Well, haven't talked about it much at home, but yeah, I remember it was all over the news. What did it mean? You know, like questions on same-sex marriage and gender identity stuff. It was kind of a big deal. Oh right, I think I heard of that. Now, with you being older and stuff, you probably understand it better than me. Can you explain it to me like a kid? Yeah, okay. So basically, there was a vote to see if Ireland would allow same-sex marriage. They decided 'yes' so now any two adults can get married, no matter their gender. Ah, that's brilliant! I remember, that was a couple of years ago when I was busy with so much, I didn’t really pay attention. But seriously, that's pretty good. You're right, it wasn't so long ago either. Yeah! Now that I'm learning this, it feels weird to see how some countries are still not accepting of this. You're right. Progress takes time, but it's happening. I'm glad to hear you're bringing it up at school. Ah, yeah. The whole thing about Ireland always seems interesting, especially since we learned about the Troubles and all... Alright, don't start on that stuff now. You can't learn everything in one day! But it is important to know about those things too. You're right. So, if I may change the topic, when will you start working again? I worry about things sometimes when you don't. Okay, okay, let's ease off on the worrying, kiddo. It’s just that being a full-time mom and taking care of our child hasn't left much energy for job hunting. We're making do. Don't worry, Mum. I'm sure things will turn around. I know it's tough. Thanks, kiddo. Your support means a lot to me. Anyway, about those kids you used to babysit, did you hear from any of them since you stopped? Not really. One of them, Emily, she sends me messages on Facebook sometimes thinking I'll still watch her during the summer. I wish I could, but I'm not sure that's... Do you think she remembers you, though? Oh, she might.

I've got an incredible story for you. Did you know my mate back in the old days, he did this mad thing. He once put his pet hamster in the microwave just to see what would happen. That's wild! I suppose he must have questions his sanity then! A hamster in the microwave? Seriously? I can hardly wrap my head around why anyone would do such a thing! Oh, I know it sounds nuts, right? But this was a time when microwaves were new to some, and people didn't quite understand them yet. Wait a minute. Is that a true story? You didn't actually know someone who did that? Ah, yes! Sure was! Lived down Costessey way, old Dave. Thought it would be a good prank or something. I hope the little creature survived! And what did it do in there? Well, I heard it ran around a bit, then slowed down, then... this is the best part... it started orbiting around the turntable. I mean, imagine it. A hamster orbiting in the microwave. That's a visual I never wanted! Well, at least the microwave cleaned up afterward, I'd assume. Oh, it did indeed. But really folks, that story is from the days when I was working on a lathe. You know, I've always been fascinated with things that spin. Lathe tools, you mean? You worked with those, didn’t you? Right. Worked in a factory for a bit, doing machinery. Learnt a lot about precision. Precision and hamsters in microwaves, huh? There must be a connection! You'd think so, wouldn't you? You know, for a retiree and a long-term unemployed person, you've certainly got some unique experiences. Well, when you don't have a 9-to-5, you've got plenty of time to think up the wildest things to do with your time. I did my fair share of experimenting. Speaking of thinking, did you guys see this new company that's making artisanal hams? I heard they're really good with curing... Oh, that sounds lovely! We could try some for tea one day. You know what I've always regretted is not learning how to make my own ham. There's something about preparing it, curing it yourself, that feels right at home for an Englishman. I've considered it, but it can be quite a process.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you ever heard of this thing called mirror-writing? You know, when you write normally but it can only be read correctly when you hold it up to a mirror? Oh yes, I have! Interestingly enough, questions have been asked about whether it could be a potential indicator of creativity and genius. But of course, most of us just write the way we were taught, right? Oh my, I remember when my granddaughter was little, she would try to write her name like that, thinking it was actually 'normal' writing. She was quite amused when she finally figured out what I meant by 'mirror-writing'. Yeah, we can't all be as creative or impaired as the likes of Leonardo da Vinci. Exactly! Now, on a more mundane note, have any of you noticed how the banks seem to have these ridiculous rules about deposits and withdrawals? It feels like they’re always finding new ways to charge you for the privilege of using your own money. Totally agree. It seems like they're running the show and we’re just along for the ride while they pocket everything. I've just written a detailed article about this for a forum I work with; it’s astonishing how much people are paying in extra fees without even realizing it. Speaking of things that are silly... I just heard that the new tax on plastic bags is meant to help, but all it really does is increase costs for the families who don’t have the socio-economic means to stock up in bulk. Makes the grocery shopping even more stressful. We should just bring our own bags from home. Seems like the simplest solution. Practical. I do that now whenever I can. However, what does baffle me is how people are still paying for paper statements and such in this digital age! It’s like they’re begging you to switch over – and then charge for the ‘online statement’. Exactly! And speaking of charges, what about the current real estate market? Ah yes, terrifying almost. Where I live, house prices are skyrocketing and it seems we’re heading into a bubble that could burst. It's discouraging for young families and first-time buyers thinking about settling down. That is disheartening. In my time, it wasn’t as crazily expensive when you were first starting out.

You know, I've read something about how this kind of gaming can be really good for problem-solving and creativity. But, why don't you two show me what you're up to? Maybe it'll inspire me to build a fantastic new world with you in Lego too? Oh, Mum, we're just at the end of a big battle! We just need to defeat the Lord of the Underworld to save Ninjago! Yeah! We've been playing this for hours and it's just so exciting! That sounds quite the adventure. But remember, it's good to spend some time with books too. They can take you on their own kind of adventures, don't they? For me, a really good book is like entering a whole new world! Nah, Mum. Books are too slow. They make me fall asleep. Yeah, and in Minecraft, you can build anything you want right there, like this temple we're making in our world... Alright, I get it. And that’s pretty cool! But why don’t we make a deal? How about after we finish this level, you both come and design a world in Lego? We could make it side by side, your Minecraft world translated into Lego. Really? We could? Yeah, that would be awesome! And maybe we can even write a story about it together? This world where we are heroes on a quest. Like a Ninjago story? Exactly! A Ninjago story with your own added ideas and adventures. Yay! That sounds like so much fun. We could start with this! There are so many pieces here that remind me of the landscapes in your Minecraft world. Look, I just defeated the Lord of the Underworld! Wow, that's... quite the victory! Now, shall we start planning our Lego world?  changes the channel on the screen to a Lego building demonstration video  Alright, let’s watch this for inspiration, then start planning! But remember, what we create, we get to tell the story ourselves! That would be so cool! Mum, look, isn’t this like a part of our temple? Absolutely! It does look similar. See, sometimes, inspiration for building something like that can come from real life or, in your case, from games like Minecraft. But Minecraft is a lot easier because you can just click to build and go places. True, but there can be something special about the manual act of building, piece by piece, and creating something from nothing.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time during our holiday? You know, when we were at the beach and you guys kept trying to build the sandcastle? Oh, mum. Still brings back memories! That was chaos! I just sat back and took notes on how not to construct a sandcastle. Now, you’re remembering! And how about that keepsake shell you still have at home? Do you still have it? Yes! I still treasure it. Remember when we all spent the day collecting seashells and you brought back this enormous one that just floated down to your feet? Definitely. That was lucky. It’s almost as if the sea wanted us to keep it. Well, the day was truly magical. What did you want to do today, mum? Any plans? Or is it just a relaxing day in Lichfield? Actually, I was thinking we could do a bit of a shopping trip this afternoon. There's a new boutique that just opened in the town center. I noticed they have this amazing tea set that would look lovely in the family room. That sounds lovely, can't wait to see. Ah, and maybe after we drop by Aunty Sarah, see how she's doing? She could use a bit of company. Oh, that's a thoughtful and kind idea! Sarah’s been on my mind since we last spoke. I’ll drive. If you two are okay with that, I can pick all of you up and bring you around. That’d be perfect. Thank you so much, darling. So, is the plan to head out after we finish this coffee then? Yep, should leave around 2. That gives us plenty of time to grab lunch after shopping. Definitely. What’s for lunch then? Haven’t decided yet. We could take turns choosing where to eat each time we go out like we used to do. I still remember the time you let me pick and we ended up with fish and chips at this quaint little place near the canal. I was livid! But you didn’t turn out too badly! You're right, it’s not every day you get a good fish and chips by a canal. I guess that’s the beauty of it. Each place has its own charm. So let's plan lunch for today, and then, maybe we can save the canal visit for another day.

Yo, lads, what've you got for lunch?? Me's had pasta from Sainsbury's, quite alright, but yours? Food sounds good. I had the chicken and garlic flatbread from Tesco, got quite a few leftovers so it was a good value, but a bit oily. Oh, isn't that one of my favourites?! I had the salad bar from Marks and Spencer, they’ve got a pretty good selection actually, quite healthy and I could pick what I liked. Yeah, keeps changing what I want, guess it's good. You game for a game of cards, then? Ace! I always try my best, but I never seem to do that great. What’s the game, though? Let’s try Uno. We can always switch if it’s not your thing. What’s new with you lot? Anything interesting at school? The school prefects are a right pain sometimes, acting all high and mighty. Yeah, last week we couldn’t even enter the common room for a bit after their meetings because they were 'having a serious discussion'. Seriously, this is a sixth-form common room! Oh, I’ve heard they pretty much just talk about who’s in the prefects' clique and what they’re doing this weekend. Never gets anything productive done, really. Have you seen the new season of 'Peaky Blinders'? Honestly, it’s been great so far. I’m a bit late starting it because I got busy with cricket, but the production and all is fantastic. I started it a few weeks back but haven't caught the last episode yet. There’s something about the atmosphere and the characters, Thomas Shelby’s all that and more. Right. Seems like the whole class went together to watch a few episodes, blurred the lines a bit between it being fun and homework. Speaking of homework, have you guys seen the long list of recommended reads for our English Lit course? Oh my God, yes. I thought I was gonna drown in that list. I’ve only read like three of them. Me too. I mean, 'To Kill a Mockingbird' and '1984' are great, but 'The History Boys'? That one almost lost me at the beginning. Wonder why they pick such heavy stuff for 17-year-olds.
