So, almost all of the options should be okay, just need to check the sauces and stuff. Chinese food tends to be a bit tricky with gluten since soy sauce is often used, but our usual place usually does gluten-free options if you ask.

Ah, I hear the NHS over in Finland is pretty first-class. I have some colleagues who’ve worked there and they say it’s all about community care and high-quality service. That’s certainly not always the case here, unfortunately. Yeah, it’s true the system’s very different there – more privatized yet still kind of universal. You hear a lot of praise for how they manage to deliver so much with a much lower cost. Exactly, and I think we can learn a lot from them. Part of the problem is money here, alongside a whole lot of other factors, I suppose. Even with the money, though, it feels like there’s still a lot of waste. I see it on the ward all the time, even with digital health systems that should streamline things. Sure, but even with that, the main issue is how stretched everything is. We're so short-staffed and it's affecting the quality of care. I once wrote a paper on this, actually, looking at how these problems are deep-rooted and not just about money. That sounds interesting. What was your main argument? It was about how the culture of the NHS, especially in terms of management and policy-making, doesn't always support the frontline workers. There’s so much emphasis on targets and compliance that it can sometimes overshadow patient care. And the bureaucracy can be quite overwhelming at times. That makes sense. A friend of mine, who’s a midwife, always says she spends more time doing paperwork than actually caring for the moms and babies. That's just not right. Exactly! I wish there could be more focus on what the service is actually supposed to deliver — quality patient outcomes, not just on filling out endless forms. Right. Seems like the administrators get more attention than the nurses and docs, who are the ones keeping the whole thing going. It's frustrating. But enough about work. How's life treating you otherwise? Kids all right? Yeah, they're great. The youngest is really into football, so we spend most weekends on match days. The second eldest is in his second year of university and he’s doing alright. The oldest is so busy with his band, always gigging around the city. That sounds great! I have two kids as well. The boy's gone through a phase of being into the classics – all the time asking me about Shakespeare, which is actually quite encouraging.

Ah, George, welcome back to the L8! How's life treating you these days? You've been quite busy, if I recall correctly. Ah lad, life's been livelier since I stopped workin' on the docks all those years ago! But I do miss the routine. Can't say I'm involved in much now though, except the odd bit of armchair politics! I can imagine! Speaking of which, did you hear about the recent allegations of police brutality in Merseyside? Pretty serious stuff, if true. Yeah, I heard a thing or two on the grapevine. These days, it's hard to separate fact from fiction in the news. Might just be the usual bit of city politics. Yeah, but it's important to address these things, isn't it? Especially when it affects our own community. Absolutely. But looking at it, it's not just our end. I heard the government's been talking about these new immigration laws. Some folks might not see it, but that could really affect what's goin' on in our area. We've always been a welcoming place, you know. True enough, George. Immigration has changed the face of Liverpool over the years, and for the better in many ways. It brought new vitality to the city, new blood, new ideas. Issues can arise, but they need to be dealt with fairly. You're right, but it seems the talk in Westminster is all about numbers and costs, not people and communities, if you take my meaning. That's a fair point. It's easy to forget about the human side when you're dealing with policy and figures. You've seen Liverpool change, though. I bet you have some interesting stories about that side of things. Oh, I certainly do! I remember when it was all fields around here, and suddenly we got all these new faces from around the world. Some of the young ones today don't even know the first time Liverpool was so mixed. True. Change can be slow to notice but it sure has happened here. Funny enough, just the other day, my university students were discussing how different accents and dialects are explored in British literature. It got them talking about identity and belonging and all that. Yeah, young folks today... they care about all that stuff more than we did when we were their age, eh?

Oh, did I just type that or say it? I'm getting so used to speaking to people around here that my Manchester accent's fading away. You wouldn't believe the number of times I've had to explain that 'gime' isn't the correct word for 'give me.' Oh don’t worry, I’m used to people talking about the regional variations in accent and dialect. As a language research co-ordinator, I have quite the ear for those kinds of things! That’s interesting, coming from someone who’s actually working in the field. I’ve always wondered about the nuances of different accents. It’s amazing how much your background and upbringing can shape the way you speak. Absolutely. I grew up in Pennsylvania, in the States, but now I'm working here in the UK, and I’ve started picking up some of these regional dialects, which is pretty cool. It’s fascinating how we all have our own distinct ways of speaking, even within the same country. Growing up in Leeds, for example, I always heard people calling oranges 'growns'. So I’m this odd mix of Yorkshire and American English, which can sometimes lead to amusing misunderstandings. I once worked on a project where they were studying how English as a Second Language learners struggled to pick up the difference between Received Pronunciation and accents from other parts of the UK. Like, 'bath' as in, you know, the place where you take a bath, can be so different from region to region. That’s exactly what I’m studying right now, actually. The effects of regional variation on ESL learning. There’s so much influence from the local dialect, but also on the other side, the effect ESL speakers have on the local dialects. More and more people are speaking a sort of, blurred, mixed variety of English. That is really interesting. As a corpus administrator, I deal with all sorts of language data, but I never really thought about it from an ESL perspective. Mostly we focus on collecting and cataloguing, but understanding how it gets used is crucial, right? Definitely. I’ve seen in my work that understanding regional dialects can really help in making ESL materials more accessible and relevant. However, it's also important to be aware of the variations within the standard varieties of English as well. Precisely. I work in publishing and we often get feedback from teachers about the language resources.

Ah, I hear you’re working on educating children in foreign languages now. How’s that going for you? Yeah, it’s been an interesting experience. It’s not just about teaching them grammar and vocabulary though, you have to handle behavior management and cultural sensitivity, too. Oh, absolutely! I've had some of that experience myself when teaching a module on cultural exchange at uni. You have to be very careful not to make assumptions, especially when discussing cultural norms or values. Right, right! For example, teaching kids about the different meanings of "no" in different cultures. In some, saying "no" directly can be considered very rude. Absolutely. And language in London, just the variety, it’s astonishing! So, how’s the planning for the new language learning platform coming along? It’s moving along. We’re trying to build a system that leverages the children's interests and incorporates more fun activities. It’s creative work, but also quite challenging. That’s a great approach. I’ve seen studies showing that engagement is key to language retention, especially at that age. So, are you using any specific methods or tools to keep them engaged? We are. We’re exploring gamification and using the internet to expose them to real-life language use. For instance, using popular TV shows to practice listening skills can be very effective. That makes sense, media exposure can really help with immersion. Speaking of which, have you seen the new TV series that’s really doing well? It’s fantastic for language learning and all. No, what’s that? It's a BBC series about different cultures across the UK. The way it explores local dialects, traditions, and all, it’s just brilliant for English language learners or anyone interested in cultural diversity. Oh, I must check that out. I haven’t heard of it. It's really well done. They have interactive elements too and it really promotes understanding and empathy towards different cultures. You’d like it. Definitely, I’ll try to catch an episode if I can. You should. Also, have you ever considered trying to incorporate regional dialects within the language teachings? That’s something I’ve been thinking about. It could be very beneficial for cultural immersion and authenticity. But I’m not sure how to best weave it into the program. A good starting point could be to use local children’s books or stories that incorporate different dialects.

Alright, Dad, Grace, today we're discussing how to sort out the garden and perhaps the house a bit. It's been a bit of a downer since Mum passed away, you know. Ah, yes, it’s changed things around a bit, hasn’t it? But I suppose that's life. What’s your thoughts, Grace? Erm, well, it’s just that the garden looks a bit... untidy, and it seems like it could do with some weeding, and perhaps a bit of renovation in the house as well. Like, the windows need cleaning, and maybe some new curtains. Well, we can sort the house out. As for the garden, I’ve always thought of it as a bit of a community project, you know? Get some family help. But speaking of which... how’s school, Grace? You’ve been studying hard, haven’t you? Well, yeah, it's been okay, but it's really hard with so much revision for my A-levels. I've been trying to stay on top of it but with everything else going on... Sticking at it, I see. That’s good, lad. It’s a lot to manage, school and everything else at home, but you’re doing well, I’m sure. You are, you know. Keep it up, and all this will help you in the long run. As for the garden, perhaps we can do it together. It’ll be good for everyone, kind of a family activity. Except, we’ll have to wait for when Dad’s feeling up to it, of course. Oh, I’m up for helping out with the garden. It’d be nice to get some fresh air. But first, let’s get something to eat. I was hoping for a spot of tea and a biscuit, if you don’t mind. That’s so typical of you, Nan! Tea is on the way. And Dad? You’re cleared for a bit of gardening, perhaps? Even if it’s just pruning some of the lower branches or something. A spot of gardening. That’s fine. Always enjoyed that. You know, while we’re at it, can we set up a small bench or something in the garden? Just something to sit on, enjoy tea or... or a book. Like, it could be our little reading nook from now on. That’s a good idea, Gracie! We could clear out that old oak tree over there and set up a nice little area.

Oh, did you take a look at those photos we took during our summer road trip? I was just going through them and thinking about how much fun we had. Yes! Those were some of the best days, weren't they? I miss that freedom of just putting some clothes in a bag and heading out on the road with no particular plan. Absolutely. And the unexpected surprises, like discovering those amazing roadside markets with local specialties. I even sent a few photos to my mum - she loved seeing us in all those different places. I did the same with my family. They were quite excited. It must have amazed them to see us among the UK expats, in the middle of China, discovering such unique spots. Definitely. It made me appreciate how much of the world there is left to see, despite having traveled quite a bit already. But, you know, it was also good to have people we knew in this new life. Our old friends from England - have you heard from any of them? Not really, actually. We've been a bit busy settling in here and getting to know people. But I did meet some great people while on those job lectures. You know the Johnson family, at the conference in Shanghai? They also moved here recently and invited us for dinner. Oh, yes! I love how we've become part of this little expat community here, really. It's wonderful to find people through our shared experience of living abroad. Exactly. But it's also nice to maintain contact with friends back home. Perhaps we could plan to make some regular video calls if it’s feasible during our schedules. An excellent idea! I just tried to call my friend Emily last week but we were on opposite sides of the world. It will be nice to have some regular check-ins. Emily changing the world byte by byte, I'm sure. She's always something. But seriously, she’s working on some fantastic projects. Have you seen the new virtual reality experiences they're developing? It's going to completely change education. I could have sworn you'd mentioned this before. Tell me more about it. They're creating immersive environments where students can explore and interact with historical sites or even complex scientific concepts in 3D. Emily was saying it could really help engage students with learning...

Oh, did I ever tell you about that night we had last week? We grabbed some food from that new Indian place near the campus after our exam, and then we just walked around town. You were right though, Jasmine, that food isn't the best now that the new owner took over. Oh, really? Yeah, I'd totally forgotten. But we've been so caught up with our papers and stuff, I'm just glad we managed to squeeze out a night. How about that exam? Pretty brutal, huh? Brutal, yes. I was stressing out so much beforehand. But passing that, I feel like I can finally breathe a sigh of relief. And just like you said, we were among the first to leave, even though we started talking about something irrelevant - oh, the memes that were going around that week. Oh yeah, that was hilarious. You were thinking about getting a pet, right? Ever thought about which breed? Yeah, between you and me, I’ve been wanting a dog. Probably a Jack Russell. They’re so energetic and fun, right? But I’ve also thought about different breeds. I even considered rescuing a dog too, I saw this adorable little terrier cross the other day. That’s really nice of you. I used to have a pet at home - a cat named Luna. She was really chilled and independent. Speaking of which, how’s your family in London? Family’s good, thanks for asking. Mum’s still working that job at the museum, and doesn’t come home till late. Dad’s always busy with his band, which is cool, but sometimes it feels like I never see him . And yeah, Luna, that’s a great name for a cat! It’s so apt! I miss having a pet sometimes. It’s funny, last time we were out, wasn’t it Julie and Tom you noticed were looking so great together? You mean they’re still going strong? Oh my god, I didn’t realize but I hadn’t seen Julie since before Christmas and she just looks amazing! And Tom too, I mean, he’s always been into fitness but last time we hung out, he cleared up about his gym routine and the changes in his diet. I swear, he’s taken it seriously, isn’t he? I mean, good for him but sometimes I feel silly for not trying to get into it too.

Ah, I hear you've seen Mary again at the last town's gathering. How'd that go? It was alright. She's still struggling, talked about her volunteer work but mostly talked about wishing she had more energy to visit her grandkids regularly. Yeah, I heard about that. I'd like to plan a visit to her soon, but I'm sure she'd feel bad about me taking a trip just to see her, right? Actually, she mentioned it. She hopes we could arrange it soon, especially since it's been ages since we've seen her. She's looking forward to a visit. Right, right. I was going through some old photo albums from my teaching years just the other day. You know, those kids... they grow up so fast. Makes me think about the grandkids even more. Definitely. I've also been trying to learn about this Fifa game they're all talking about. You know, trying to connect with the youngsters. [chuckles] It's not as hard as you think. I've been transcribing a lot recently. Now that I'm working more from home, I've had time to finally dive into it. [laughs] I can imagine 'diving into it' in your case, Karen. You're always so into the stories behind the transcripts. [grinning] Can't help it. Fascinating stuff, right, all those little details you find. True, it's quite the skill. Shows there's humanity in even the smallest of projects. Speaking of projects, it's a bit of the elephant in the room for us, but did we ever talk about that project proposal design for the town center? More like a donkey, a rather stubborn, blurred one at that. I've been delaying since retirement. [laughs] It's not just you, and it's not just retirement. We all changing gears. True, but I think we should discuss it soon, especially since some of us are in a new chapter of life and might just have something to offer. I agree. Can we maybe set a date? Maybe over dinner? Or even a quick lunch? I could bring the peas and chips. I love you for that, love. The peas and chips always remind me of our mum. [pauses] [nods in agreement] It'll be a nice way to reconnect. And maybe we can explore what each of us can bring to that proposal without the old obligations getting in the way.

I've decided I need a new laptop. The stupid thing just broke. I lent it to my sister and she managed to break it when she accidentally spilled her coffee all over it. Oh no, that’s just typical! Just like when I borrowed your old laptop and spilled some water on it. You gave me a hard time then, remember? I do indeed! I'm just glad it was just a coffee spill and not something else. But still, I need a new one and I’m not sure how much it will cost. In my day, we didn't have such gadgets. We were lucky if we had a Television. But then again, I spent most of my life not working so I didn't need one anyway. True, Uncle Jim. But times have changed. Speaking of which, I was thinking of going with a Lenovo because I heard they’re quite reliable. But my partner prefers Dell. We’re going to spend a lot of time arguing about it. Maybe look into reconditioned laptops. You can get good deals and it's also better for the environment. That’s a great idea! I hadn’t thought about that. I’ll definitely look at that option. By the way, did you guys hear about the bin strike? It’s causing quite a mess, especially in this area. Oh really? You working over there must be a nightmare during this time. True, but the council promised they're working on it. It's just a bit of a headache. Can't imagine standing for those strikes nowadays. We used to have strikes all the time. I used to go around Brighton to see if I could pick up any freebies from the bins if they were on strike! Uncle Jim, that was before they had all the health and safety rules, wasn’t it? Right. But, it was a different time. It does bring to mind, though, the types of water we drink. Did you know you can taste the difference between different kinds of water in the UK? Whether it’s from Devon or from London. Yeah, I've noticed that. Drinking water can change a lot from region to region. You could even get into a whole conversation about this when talking about different hobbies or interests. Like, I love DIY and I find I can pick up better when I listen to DIY podcasts, but I'll never forget when I tried to make my own dinner and ended up with a disaster!

Oh, I'm so glad we decided to have a cuppa here. It's been ages since I've had a proper English breakfast! Though, this coffee is not bad at all. You know I still miss some things from home, don't you? Like the right kind of beans, proper tea, and a proper pub! Absolutely, and decent football! I've been checking the FA Cup results as soon as I could, and it seems like it's been a bit of a keepsake cup this year, hasn't it? Oh, absolutely! Manchester United is going strong, despite their performance in the league. Though, football is not my main concern lately. Is something wrong? You haven't been well since... since moving here, have you? It's not just the language barrier, is it? It's the winter. And the people. And not having a regular job. Sometimes I feel like I've lost myself or something. A bit of a SAD spell, this time of year. Oh, silly. You’re doing well though, while I'm stuck here teaching kids to say "going to university" properly! Ah, teaching must be so rewarding though, right? How's your new student? I remember you were mentioning someone particularly challenging. Oh, she's actually quite endearing once you get to know her. And she’s working hard! But it's the exams that make things tricky - she’s worried about failing and the pressure is stressing her out. Sounds like a familiar predicament. The feeling of being responsible for someone's success or failure... It is a lot to take on. But it also means I have to prepare them better for confronting disappointments. She’s learning now, but I’m also teaching her that it's okay to fail sometimes. I used to work for a short while on a farm, when I first left university. There’s something grounding about working with the land... Oh, right. Did you enjoy it? Actually, yes! I enjoyed the physical work and freedom. But it wasn’t my calling. Though sometimes I wish I could have that connection with nature again. I’ve seen some great documentaries about urban farming lately - maybe there’s something like that you could get into here? Too much to think about right now, but it’s nice to consider, thanks for suggesting. You've given me something to think about.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that one time I had to arrange for a conference for 500 people in under a week? It was chaos but it turned out really well in the end. Did the guests even notice the chaos? As someone who does manual labor all day, I've had my fair share of chaos too, but of a very different kind. Oh, I'm sure they noticed, but they didn't care as long as the event keeps coming together. Speaking of putting something together in a hurry, did either of you try those new 'grab-and-go' meals they released at Tesco? I heard they are really good. Oh, those are actually quite convenient. But in all seriousness though, it’s the organizational aspect that’s challenging. And to be honest, it's partly why I enjoy it so much – its challenges and organizing a successful event is so rewarding. Hmm, that's interesting. When you're lifting heavy things all day, it's more about brute force than strategy, I suppose. For me, it's a mix. I have to organize people and resources, but if something goes wrong in production, most of the time it's still the manual labor that gets things back on track. Well, we can't all be event planners. Yeah, no, I'd rather not have to plan in advance much more than for the next day or so. That said, it's not bad to plan sometimes. I was thinking of planning a small trip for the next weekend. Maybe we could do it together? If you'd like, of course. Oh, that sounds fun! I'd love that. I just tried to relax over the weekend but I ended up organizing our niece's birthday party. Oh, really? I'm sure it was great! I actually missed the party because I was working on my own project. I'm building a new shed out of wood that I found for free. That’s impressive. I always take advantage of local thrift shops or yard sales if I need anything. They often have great stuff. That's very frugal of you. As for me, I swear I spend more time fixing things than organizing events! Well, at least our shed plans didn't turn into a crisis management exercise. That's because... because we don't invite 500 people to the build, I suppose.

Ah, I hear that you've also been involved with teaching English in China. What brought you to that? Yes, I've been teaching TEFL for a few years now. Mostly in larger cities, but I also spent time in the countryside and, believe it or not, even taught in Tibet once. It was quite an experience, really opened my eyes to how varied China is. Oh absolutely, I'm sure it did. I was just discussing with someone how Teaching English as a Foreign Language is increasingly popular even here in the UK due to the growing number of Chinese students coming over for study or business, and more companies wanting staff with Mandarin skills. Exactly, that's true. The trends are certainly shifting with China’s economic rise and more international interactions. And language learning can be quite a challenge, especially for Chinese learners. What were some of the most interesting cultural differences you found there? Well, one thing stands out - the concept of “face” in China is similar to “honor” in Spain. You have to be very careful with their dignity and never cause anyone to lose face in front of others. Sure, I've come across that as well. I find the diligence of Chinese students impressive too. And while on the subject, what about the landscape and wildlife in China - any memorable experiences? Well, the diversity is incredible. The pandas in Sichuan, for instance, are just remarkable creatures. A visit to the Chengdu Research Base is a must. And then there’s the rural areas - driving through those vast countryside, I was amazed by the amount and variety of wildlife. Bears, yes - doesn’t come close to the UK in terms of frequency, but still, quite thrilling! I would love to visit one day. And bears, really? That’s surprising. More common than panda bears I assume? Actually, yes, but they tend to stay away from populated areas. But personally, my highlight was seeing a boy catch and then let loose a pigeon in a park. It was such a heartwarming moment. That does sound lovely. Speaking of parks - Gordon Square here is lovely, and those lime trees. Beautiful, isn't it? Definitely. The way the sun filters through them is very soothing. It’s good to have such green spaces in the city. Indeed. We could all do with more green. I recently read about an interesting trend - using parks for birthday celebrations in China.

Yo, mate, did you manage to sort out the last bits of the plans for our trip to the Lake District? Yeah, I've been deep into it. Had the flight bookings finalised, and checked into some cozy little B&Bs up there, near the Lake Windermere – do you have a preferred kind of accommodation over there? Honestly, I've always been a fan of that quaint, rustic feel of a log cabin or a lodge. But honestly, as long as it's clean and relatively warm, I'm happy. Think about it, we'll have enough time to ourselves to enjoy those views. Right, I just need to finalise some of the picnic hike stuff. You keen to do the whole Kirkstone Pass thing? Everyone says it's one of the most stunning view points. I'd love to! What's the weather expected to be like up there, by the way? We don’t want rain on our parade... The forecast is good, but I've packed some waterproofs just in case. It's always best to be prepared, especially in the UK. Plus, we can always do indoor stuff if it’s a wash-out, like visiting the Beatrix Potter gallery. Aye, that's a great idea! I'd love that. Especially after we've done the hike, a bit of cultural stuff sounds perfect for relaxing. I've also managed to arrange for a little tea time at one of the local tearooms. They're famous for their scones. Smashing! That's why I love spending time with you - always know it'll be memorable and the plan-making effort always pays off. Thanks, love. I'm glad you're enjoying the planning too. It’s not just about the trip, just the fact we get to spend quality time together. Exactly. It’s been a bit hectic lately, what with my coursework and your consulting life. This trip feels like a much-needed hiatus. We could sit on the grass, do some reading, or even try our hand at some water sports if the weather permits. Perfect, take your book, I’ll bring the paddle board if the weather is fine! It’ll be funny watching you on the board. Ha! Yeah, well, at least the fall will be memorable. Do you need me to pick up anything for the trip before I head out? We're leaving early Saturday?

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about my week? Got a bit of a cold, and Jeez, was it dreadful! Are you okay now then? Colds can be so miserable. Yeah, I’m on the mend. But it’s so bad when you’re stuck indoors and can’t breathe properly. I spent most of the week sipping tea and watching Netflix, right? Teas and Netflix always provide comfort, even if it's just a temporary escape. Definitely, and speaking of comforts, anything new with you two in the romance department? Oh, bless you. I think the only romance right now is probably my relationship with my duvet. That’s understandable, given the circumstances, but seriously, anything going with anyone? Nope, not really. Been concentrating on work and recovering from the cold. You two? Been seeing someone a bit. It's new, so we’re just taking it steady, enjoying the small things at the moment. That’s lovely to hear, while I’ve been so busy at work in the production line at the factory, I haven’t had much time for anything. But that’s not to say you’re unlucky in love. It’ll come when the time is right. For sure. It’s all about timing and what you want, innit? I mean, doesn’t matter what others are doing. What about your health, though? As a labourer, you’re probably exposed to all sorts of things. More or less. But we get decent care, and I make sure to keep on top of hygiene whenever I can. Different job, but it pays enough. Speaking of jobs, I’ve been meaning to look into some courses on my time off. Anyone got any recommendations? For production controlling? Well, I know a few things about efficient working, but I’m not sure about courses specifically for that. Maybe look into a project management course? Or perhaps you could look at managing skills online. There’s plenty of free or low-cost courses out there. That’s a good idea. I’ll look into those. Maybe we could all get something new to do during our breaks. Free time is a luxury, huh? Definitely a luxury. But also, um, if anyone needs a hand with their event planning work, guest what? I’m always available! Maybe next event, how about a little help with logistics or something? Brilliant!

Oh, did I ever tell you about that awkward situation I had today at work? Not yet, but you're pulling a funny face. You look like you're about to spill the beans. What happened now? So there was this one new joiner who has been pretty out of place lately. Today, out of nowhere, he just decided to start explaining his theory on sustainable ecosystems to our fractious client. As if that’s what they needed right then and there? Exactly! The meeting was interrupted for a moment as everyone's faces just went into shock. It was really awkward. He doesn’t know when to keep his ideas in check, huh? Yeah, and I had to jump in and steer the conversation back on track. My heart rate was skyrocketing! Well, that's part of the job, isn’t it? I mean, in my line of work, I deal with all sorts of people and varying mental states. It's a whole different kind of awkward, but maybe it helps me deal with workplace situations. I'm sure. Where did you get that patience? You must have a special gene for dealing with the most challenging people and situations. Maybe. But seriously, it's all about understanding where people are coming from. I think that's why it's tough for me sometimes in personal relationships as well. What do you mean? Just the other day I was talking to a friend about breaking up with her boyfriend. She just couldn't understand why he didn't see things from her perspective or just listen without giving the ‘typical’ side of the story. I hear you. I used to go through that a lot when I was dating. It was like they were so fixed on their own narrative and it really infuriated me. Yeah, it’s like we are stuck in a one-way conversation. But sometimes I think it’s because they don’t know any other way. If they just took a step back, truly listened, maybe they’d see the other side of things. You know, in situations like that, sometimes even if you explain everything clearly, it just doesn’t register. Maybe it's just about being more patient and understanding. Exactly. And also being aware of how someone is feeling. We all get into our own bubble sometimes and forget that other people have their own experiences that drive their perspectives.

Alright, listen carefully everyone, we need to discuss the concept of good versus evil. In most of our stories, there's always a clear hero and villain, just like in the tales we've been reading tonight. Who can tell me what you think about the way the villains are depicted in the stories we discussed? I thought there were always good guys and bad guys, like in cartoons. Well, from what I remember reading, sometimes even the 'bad' guys aren’t purely evil. They just want something, and sometimes they do bad things to get it, but sometimes it’s because they’re hurt or scared. You’re so right, Speak 2. That’s a really good point. For instance, in this story about Robin Hood, he’s called a villain by some people because he steals from the rich. But if you look closer, the rich people he steals from don’t always treat others fairly. So, is Robin Hood truly evil or just fighting against an unjust system? So... maybe sometimes the line between good and bad isn’t really a line at all? That’s exactly right, Speak 3! It’s often shades of gray in reality, and stories reflect that too. Look at Cinderella, for example. The stepmother and stepsisters might seem one-dimensionally evil, but maybe they're just acting out of jealousy or insecurity? Perhaps if we understood their story, we’d see it differently? So, is that why in some of the stories, the villain turns out to be misunderstood or even changing for the better by the end? Exactly! Like in the legend of The Pied Piper of Hamelin, when the townsfolk refused to pay him for ridding the town of rats, he takes the children away. Now, that doesn’t sound very good. But maybe he’s trying to teach them a lesson about being fair and keeping promises. So, the 'bad guys' aren't always thinking they're bad? More often than not, no. They might believe what they’re doing is right or necessary for some reason. Remember also, in stories, it helps to make the villain seem like they have some real emotions or backstory so we can understand how they became the way they are. It's like if someone bullied you, maybe they're acting out of anger or pain too, right? They're not just 'evil', they might be hurting as well.

I've heard of strict directors, but coordinating film shoots for your school is no easy feat. How's the filming going for the kids? Oh, it’s been quite an adventure. We’ve got quite a few newbies amongst the team this year, so there's been a bit of chaos. But it’s starting to piece itself together now. I get to play a big part of it, right? Can I show them what I learned in drama class? Right you are, Ellie. I’ve seen your auditions, you’ll be great. I want to play a character like the cool guy, but what if I trip again? Ah, Anthony, don’t worry about that little mishap you had. It’s part of the fun of the project. You’re going to be an absolute star, just like how you were in the school play last year. But what if it's too cold at the night time filming this week? We have to shoot outside for some scenes. Don’t worry, the weather forecast says it should be warm enough. They’re even predicting a full moon to make it extra magical for those outdoor scenes. Ah, the full moon is a perfect touch for the finale, isn’t it? Hopefully, it will keep the kids really motivated to keep going even if they are tired. Mum, doesn’t the weather also affect whether you can see your shadow properly? Actually, that’s a good point, Ellie. Yes, it can make the shadows longer or shorter depending on how much sunlight there is, so we’ll have to keep that in mind for certain scenes. Oh, by the way, are you sure you’re insured for all these extra curricular activities? Yes, the school has all that sorted, along with some basic first aid. But Anthony here has been complaining a bit about his leg, from that soccer match last week. It's not just from soccer! It’s been aching for days and almost gone this morning, but now... Perhaps a bit of ice on it after each shoot. And maybe we should consider a bit of light stretching during break times. You know how I love my gym routines, maybe we can incorporate some that will help with recovery and any potential stress from filming. Like using the running machines at the gym? Though we mostly use them for cardio, the idea is similar.

Ah, George, it's good to see you! How's life treating you these days? You know, aside from the weather, that is. Always a pleasure, old friend. You know how it is. Life's been good. Still running the business, though it's a fair amount of stress, if I'm being honest. You? Stress and I have quite a relationship ourselves, especially with the elderly students I'm teaching. But I have to admit, I'm trying to keep up with the times, so to speak. I've been really interested in how the Green Party is shaping up this election cycle. Ah, yes, politics. Well, I've had my fair share of that too. I did try to convince some of my employees to vote Green, but... well, let's just say we have some mix of opinions around here. I can imagine. My students, they're more open-minded, but as for their parents, not so much. Exactly! But we're heading in the right direction, I'm sure. Definitely. For me, it's the youth that gives me hope. Now, how is your health? I heard you were having some issues recently? Yeah, well, it's the usual: the body creaks and groans a bit more every year. But I'm managing. Just had to keep myself fit and active, which isn't as easy as it sounds. Good on you! Fitness at our age is more important than ever. I've started walking a bit more and that’s been helping me a lot. But it's not just about the physical health, is it? How's the mental side? School can be draining if one’s not careful. Can't deny that. There are days when I feel like I'm trying to teach a whole new world every hour. But the students are what keep me going. It’s seeing that light of understanding in their eyes when you explain something complex. Right, sure. I find the same sense of satisfaction in my business. You know, when you see your efforts bearing fruit, it's rewarding. But it’s not all business, is it? How are your personal relationships coming along? Still keeping up with your niece or nephew? Oh, the family. They're all managing, growing up fast. It’s like... well, you know how it is. I was just thinking about my nephew.

I've decided I need more plants in my flat. I've been meaning to do this for ages. It's about time I stop living with just the little succulents my mum got me for my last birthday. Right? That's a great idea! Plants are such a breath of fresh air, literally! Yeah, absolutely. I'm thinking of getting some bigger ones, maybe some ferns or something. Do you recommend any kinds? Well, if you're looking for something easy to care for, a peace lily or a snake plant might be good. But if you want something more... exotic, then perhaps a fiddle leaf fig or a Monstera. They're quite trendy right now, but can be a bit finicky. Trendy? I suppose so! But I'd rather go for easy-to-care-for, to be honest. My last few attempts at taking care of houseplants haven't gone very well. So, you're not really that green-fingered, huh? Nope, definitely not. I'm more of a plant murderer. Alright, alright, we've all been there. What about fashion? What have you been into lately? I've been really into sustainable fashion. I've been trying to shop more second hand, support local designers, and generally, be a bit more mindful of what I buy. Well, that's the spirit! I've been looking at buying some of those reusable bags and tote bags for when I go shopping. More power to you! Have you checked out the Depop app? It’s a great platform for second-hand shopping. And there are so many small, sustainable designers on there. Oh, great tip! I’ll definitely check that out. I've been trying to do my part for the environment, especially after finishing that research paper for my PhD on sustainable practices in industry. That paper must've been such a challenge, covering everything from finance to waste management! It was. And terrifying almost as much as my supervisor's feedback. I can imagine. Research can be a real grind sometimes. How is your supervisor? Well, she's... involved. I suppose you could say. She's... quite the character. I remember when I was doing my master's, my supervisor was always so supportive, but she could also make things a bit too complex sometimes. Yeah, that's the kind of thing I'm talking about. Anyway, back to fashion.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you ever had your students surprise you with an unusual topic? I've had a few bizarre paper topics over the years but recently one of my students did a project on Killer Whales and their social behavior. It was fascinating, really! Oh, isn't that one of the most fascinating creatures out there? I mean, did you know that they're not actually whales, right? They're the largest members of the dolphin family and are incredibly intelligent. But even so, it must be a strange topic choice for an English literature class. Exactly! Even for a comparative literature module where we explore diverse texts, it's a very unusual choice. But I was so impressed by their analysis and research. It just goes to show, though, the power of inspiration even in the most unexpected places. Reminds me of when I was a kid, watching the TV show Blue Peter and getting so excited about their badges... Did you get any? I was never very good at achieving those challenges. For me, it was more about the dream than actually getting them. Though, I did once win a "Blue Peter badge" for making a model of the solar system. Quite proud of it in my childhood days! That's really nice. It's interesting how these kinds of childhood experiences shape our tastes and interests, isn't it? Speaking of shaping interests, have you ever considered incorporating more interdisciplinary approaches into your teaching? Mixing art and literature, for example. Absolutely! I was actually planning a module next semester that does just that. The theme will be about the representation of violence in Victorian art and literature, and how it’s perceived today in the media, such as TV and films. Oh, that sounds fascinating! The way violence is portrayed on our screens today is definitely a hot topic, especially following all those debates about its effects on children. Exactly! It'll be interesting to explore how things have changed and remained the same over time. I was also considering inviting a art historian to give a guest lecture. That's a great idea! And it might also be a useful discussion point for the students to look into the context of violence in entertainment. Did you know that some of the most violent shows on TV right now were inspired by Victorian literature?

Ah, lovely cup of tea, innit? I was just looking through some of these old photos. Reminds me of the days when our parents were both working so hard, you know? You two remember George's butcher shop? Oh, yes, I remember! He was always very proud of that place. And isn't it funny how times have changed? Like those abattoirs now, they're all so big and modern, not like the little ones our parents used to work in. And how about how they worked backwards and forwards, putting in those long hours? I always admired their industry, even if the smell of the abattoir did stick around for a while. Oh, you're right! My mum used to come home from her florist shop - oh, the dust and the smell of all those flowers. But she loved it, and so did I, being at the shop with her sometimes on the weekends. What about all these things they're doing with food now? Science and engineering, it seems like everything is so modern and automated. For sure! We're living in interesting times, certainly. My grandkids are always fascinated by anything STEM, science and maths and all that. I have to remind them that they owe a lot of that knowledge to the hard work of the past, like our parents' shops and the local industries they relied on. Like the old COH instructors at the school where your kids went, can’t recall the name of it now... It’s all part of the same narrative, isn’t it? The manufacturing and community spirit of it all. Speaking of old, do you remember those old cars we used to see on the roads when we were young? They were so simple. Nowadays, it's all about these new technologies and what-not. I do! I remember our first family car was this old Ford Anglia. It was so sturdy, but it had no air conditioning and we'd often melt on long trips. Like that trip to the coast when it broke down halfway! Our dad spent hours fixing it by the side of the road, but we made do with it. Those were simpler times, weren’t they? Simple, but hard. You could feel the pride and the work gone into those cars. Not like the throwaway culture we have now. Do you remember how George used to take us to see the new cars at trade shows?

Ah, James, I'm curious. I heard you've got experience working in recruitment before you started as an Associate Lecturer. How was that for you? Was it a big change for you moving from that kind of role into academia? It was quite a change, actually. I kind of stumbled into recruitment because I was looking for a way to utilize my communication skills and people skills, but I've always been passionate about education too. I loved the fast-paced environment and the sense of accomplishment when you matched someone with their dream job, but it got very repetitive and unsatisfying in the long run. I can imagine. So you must have found a very different kind of fulfillment here, then? I've been questioning the academic side of things lately, just trying to understand how to better evaluate the literacy skills of my students in a comprehensive way. It can be challenging making sure each of them has the same base level of understanding and ability to communicate effectively. Absolutely, that sounds challenging. In recruitment, it was quite straightforward - you either had the skills or you didn’t. But in academia, it's far more nuanced. I’ve found that a lot depends on how the course is structured and how it prepares students for their assessments and beyond. I completely agree. We have a curriculum that includes explicit literacy instruction, but it's in the more generic university-wide modules rather than individualized to the specific courses. It seems like sometimes students just don't realize how much work needs to be done on their own to be taken as seriously, especially if they plan on going into industry or further study. That's a common problem. I remember in my recruitment days, I’d have to work with candidates who didn’t realize that it wasn't just about the skills but also how to contextualize and apply them, especially in writing, which is so critical in academia. More and more in my field, I see students who are highly intelligent and motivated but struggle with academic writing. It's not necessarily because they can't do it but because they aren't taught or given enough practice in it from the start. Perhaps changing the way we evaluate these skills could help, but I'm not quite sure where to start. I think in recruitment, we focused on specific skills but it was all about adaptability and potential.

Oh, sorry I'm so late, I had to finish this assignment. I hope I didn't miss too much fun. You've missed nothing but introductions, honestly! We're still getting around the room, introducing ourselves, and sharing a little about who we are! That's totally fine, Sarah. We're all finishing up our studies and just hanging out. I'm actually looking for a study group for our marketing project next week. Oh, yeah, I could definitely use that, actually. I've been struggling a bit with the case studies. Do you think we could have our first meeting in your room then, just like the others? Yeah, that works for me. What's your name, by the way? I'm Sarah, from Bradford. Nice to meet you all, by the way. And you are? I'm Riya. Nice to meet you too, Sarah. We could meet there on Wednesday, see how it goes? Yeah, that sounds great. Wednesday it is then. Don't be late again, Sarah! I won't, I promise! Okay, so, really, everyone here is a student of sorts, and all from the North. I'm Jenny, from Bolton. I'm Riya, from... well, technically from England, but my parents are from India. I studied at the University of Manchester. Manchester! That's cool. I've always wanted to visit there. What's your family background like? Is it traditional Indian? Yeah, it's very traditional, actually. We keep up with a lot of cultural practices. Like, we celebrate all of the Indian festivals, even though we are here in England. That must be quite different mixing those two cultures, huh? It is. Sometimes it can be challenging to balance them, but most of the time it's wonderful. Yeah, I can imagine. We've got a similar situation with our family. We're from Yorkshire, but my parents' roots are in Ireland and Scotland. I like to say I'm a bit... a mix of all of them, I suppose. A cultural melting pot, right here! Speaking of culture, do you guys know much about Lancashire, where we're based now? I've always loved the dialect here, the way people say certain words. Oh, I love a good Yorkshire accent. It's so distinct! Oh, I've learned to appreciate it too, despite having a slight northern accent myself when I'm around my family.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that film I saw last week? It's quite possibly the most boring film I've ever seen! You're hooked on military films, aren’t you? Still into that? Yep! Can't help it! I guess it's something to do with the whole regiment and discipline side of it. It makes me feel a bit... right? Right? As in... right keeps coming right? Anyway, how was it? Oh, it was terrible. But I think that just proves my point about you needing to watch more of these. You might just like it. Well, when I need to watch something "regimented and disciplined", I’ll call you. Seriously though, it didn’t do very well in the film reviews, so I'm not surprised you haven’t heard of it. So, what makes it so bad? I’m all ears. The acting was poor, the plot was predictable and cliched, the CGI was beyond ridiculous. It felt like they wanted the money and didn’t want to put the effort in. Ah, the world of bad film production. I’m right there with you. It seems like quality in movies is getting really hit-or-miss these days. Exactly! I mean, doesn’t it feel like every month there’s another Netflix series that’s either really good or really terrible? There’s no in-between, sometimes. Seems that true for most things in life, doesn’t it? You want to keep up with it all because you feel left out, yet when you do, you realize you’d have been better off just living in ignorance! Definitely. I find my time might be better spent on magazines instead. At least there’s some art for the soul in there. Magazines, eh? Reminds me, have you checked out the new publication that's all about the military tech? It looks super interesting. No, tell me about it! They came out with a special edition focusing on AI and robotics in operations. Seems like they're really delving into all that stuff we discussed about AI and ethics last time. That’s right! That was a great conversation, if I do say so myself. I’d love to see their take on it, especially with their perspective from the military side. Yeah, and there’s also an interview with someone at the Ministry of Defence about what we might see in the next few years.

I've heard of this type of prejudice's rampant increase since Brexit; it's truly worrying. I've seen it even in our own social circles. Right! And it isn't just the now-prevalent, underlying assumption that everyone from London questions the status of being "truly" British or understands anything beyond, say, the Westminster bubble? I'm right there with you, guys. Just last week, a friend from London came to visit and someone keeps coming up to her saying how she "sounds funny" just because we have, you know, a certain accent in the north. It's disgusting. This "London-centric" mentality is as if the UK beyond the M25 doesn't exist or contribute to the culture we share. On that note, did either of you hear about this new documentary project Ronan, your cousin, is working on? It's about that exact topic—diversity in Britain and the overlooked regional contributions. No way? I haven't! Is he focusing only on regional accents or...? He specifically said it's looking at the 'diversity' of the entire UK, but with a regional lens. It's really ambitious, but I think it can make quite the impact. He's already filming in different cities, even Watford! I'd love to see it! Perhaps we could even pitch in somehow, get a shout-out from our own "provinces" I suppose. As long as it doesn't get lost in some London-centric narrative or just focuses on "regional characteristics" as side notes, I'd be all for it! Same. It would be interesting to see if it can educate people about the cultural richness outside of London and challenge some of these stereotypes. Definitely. We could perhaps even guest appear or do an interview, though that depends on the format. I'm sure we can talk to Ronan and see if it's possible, but truly, I'm just happy it's happening. It's so rare to see projects that focus on this perspective. Agreed. However, this leads me to wonder... Boys and dating. Did you both catch that BBC comedy special about dating in 2021? It highlighted something fascinating about the dating scene outside London. Sure did! I found it quite relatable. It made a good point that dating platforms don't necessarily cater to the nuances outside the capital, often giving regional options the short end of the stick.

Ah, so I heard mom was a bit startled by the utility bills when she first arrived. Well, she's talked about it a few times. Thinking about adjusting to the cost of living out here compared to London. She just can't get over how much more we pay for electricity and gas. It's understandable. Energy prices can be quite steep out here in the South East compared to the cities. I'm right there with her, always trying to reduce our bills as much as possible. Yeah. I joked about it being like a 'rental fee' for living in the countryside – with bonus tractor noises! You're too quick, ! But seriously, we can share some tips if mom wants. I've found that switching to a more efficient provider and being mindful of usage does make a difference. Ah, switching suppliers? That sounds like something you youngsters are good at. I remember when all we had to worry about was the gas meter. Oh, no kidding. Well, if anyone needs help or wants to look into it, I’d be happy to help. I’ve got some tips from my time at work. Although, let's also not forget the benefits side of things. ) If you’re eligible, that could help significantly, especially if your income is a bit in the red as it is. Exactly. We might have spoken about it already but there are quite a few schemes out there for older people, especially if you're on the lower end of the socio-economic scale. I don't really... . We've managed so far without government handouts. But maybe I should look into it. The bills are a worry. If you think it will help, by all means. It's always worth exploring what's available, but we should also make sure changing energy suppliers and using less are our first steps. Speaking of shopping, did you pick up any spices when you went to Brighton last weekend? I’ve been meaning to try some new seasoning for the chicken we baked last night. Oh! Yeah, I got this lovely garam masala. Got almost tempted by the new spices in the health food shop. Ooh, that sounds interesting. could you share the recipe? Sure thing. But I should also tell you, that store... I was surprised by the range of nuts and dried fruits they sold.

Yo, mate, did you seen any of that latest social media's online shenanigans? I mean, talk about drama! Oh, you're talking about that unreal video on YouTube right? Yeah, I saw it. I mean it just goes to show, even with all the new regulations, there's still a lot of bad content and trolls out there. As an administrator, I'm often on top of the big stuff, but sometimes it feels like a never-ending battle, eh? For sure keeps changing right? I mean, I've worked with some of the stuff we had to deal with on the day-to-day – it's like trying to keep the floodgates plugged at times. I hear you. But you know, as someone who just finished their postgrad in civil engineering, I'm making sure the infrastructure that supports this all stands up. It's a whole different kettle of fish, but at the end of the day, it's about how we use the systems we have. That's true. It's got to be tough sometimes though, I bet. I mean, especially with the politics that comes with it. Politics is a whole separate bubble. I mean, with the current climate and everything, sometimes I wonder if we'll ever actually get to the good stuff, like substantial infrastructure improvements, or if the debates are just going to be endless. Ah, the weather's no less predictable, is it? Look at this year's forecast – can we trust any of it? Haha, true. And with the "beast from the east"s and whatnots, you've no idea from one day to the next. Though, as a civil engineer, I've got to say, I do find it fascinating the way we adapt and build in anticipation of such changes. Adapting’s the key word, innit? If we can't adapt to the weather, we're in trouble! Indeed! Speaking of adapting, how's your cooking going? I was thinking of trying out a new recipe, something a bit healthier after all the lockdown comfort food. Ah, I'm always down for that! And I finally found a zero-waste recipe for some sweet potato falafel that was a game changer. Super easy, you know? Zero-waste recipes are the dream! I've been into that, too – especially after watching some of those environmental shows. It's amazing how much waste our daily routine can produce without us even realizing.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my day at work? We had the most hilarious situation. A patient was clearly under the weather, and his family just wouldn't STOP arguing about what to be served for lunch! That sounds quite the situation. I had one of those days where everything got totally disorganized at the office, but my colleague just spilled coffee all over our project proposal right before the meeting. And here I am, coming home to a quiet evening after a whole day of helping people with their daily tasks, but I had one patient who wouldn't stop talking about their dog, dear old Max, despite Max being in a far better condition than they were. I feel you! I had a session today with someone who kept on about their neighbours and their latest party, which made me think, do people really care that much? It's crazy how similar our days can be despite our different jobs. You know, between the elderly folks and the never-ending complaints at the care home, sometimes it feels like it's all quite universal. Absolutely! The day-to-day can be so funny. But don't even get me started on our new doctor who hasn’t the foggiest idea about the pharmacology chart or the patient file system! I can relate. I have one colleague who still can't figure out the new dosing charts, really frustrating. I had a similar problem with the system over at my care site. We're talking real basics that you'd assume would be easy for them to pick up. Absolutely. I just had to step in and fix that myself. It’s astonishing sometimes. But, I guess we all learn as we go along. Right? It's like we're all winging it in different ways. From technical issues to emotional overload, changing the world one patient or client at a time. True. I spent most of the day navigating the complex emotional needs of my patients today. Some days it feels like I'm more of a therapist than a care assistant! And I found myself mediating a family squabble more than giving them actual care this afternoon. Wonderfully depressing. Well, at least we're not alone in this. And sometimes our daily dramas can actually turn into great stories when we chat over a cup of coffee.
